## Ch. XL — The voyage home.

They cut the rope. Fa-hien took passage in a large merchantman with more than two hundred men aboard, towing a smaller vessel on a rope as a provision against damage to the large one. Three days out they met a great wind, the vessel sprang a leak, and the water came in. The merchants wanted to get into the small boat, *but the men on board it, fearing that too many would come, cut the connecting rope*.[^61]

**What a person is, at the moment the rope is cut, is a number that will not fit**. Fa-hien records it in one clause and does not comment. The merchants, greatly alarmed and feeling their risk of instant death, threw their bulky goods into the water, and he threw in his pitcher and washing-basin and some other articles.

What is worth having is what he did not throw. Fearing the merchants would cast overboard his books and images, he could only think with all his heart of Kwan-she-yin and commit his life to the church of the land of Han: *I have travelled far in search of our Law. Let me, by your dread and supernatural power, return from my wanderings, and reach my resting-place*.[^62] The prayer is addressed jointly to a bodhisattva and to the monks at home, and its content is the manuscripts.

How you know where you are, on that ocean, is by looking up. The great ocean spreads out, a boundless expanse; there is no knowing east or west, and only by observing the sun, moon and stars was it possible to go forward. If the weather were dark and rainy the ship went as she was carried by the wind, without any definite course. In the darkness of the night only the great waves were to be seen, breaking on one another and emitting a brightness like that of fire, with huge turtles and other monsters of the deep all about.[^63]

The sea was deep and bottomless and there was nowhere to drop anchor and stop. When the sky became clear they could tell east and west, and the ship again went forward in the right direction. *If she had come on any hidden rock, there would have been no way of escape*.

What makes things happen, on the second voyage, is a theory about Fa-hien. After a black wind and tempestuous rain the Brahmans deliberated together and said: *it is having this Sramana on board which has occasioned our misfortune and brought us this great and bitter suffering. Let us land the bhikshu and place him on some island-shore. We must not for the sake of one man allow ourselves to be exposed to such imminent peril*.[^64]

That is the same arithmetic Hwuy-king used on the mountain in chapter XIV — one man against the rest — turned around and pointed at him. How people should relate is settled by a patron who threatens them:

> If you land the bhikshu, you must at the same time land me; and if you do not, then you must kill me. If you land this Sramana, when I get to the land of Han, I will go to the king, and inform against you. The king also reveres and believes the Law of Buddha, and honours the bhikshus.[^64]

He does not argue that the storm has another cause. He tells them what will happen to them at the other end, and the merchants were perplexed and did not dare to land him. Protection here is jurisdictional: the reach of a Chinese king who honours monks extends onto a leaking ship in the South China Sea.

The shape of time on that passage is provisions divided by men. More than seventy days out from Java, with the provisions and water nearly exhausted, they used the salt water of the sea for cooking and carefully divided the fresh, each man getting two pints.[^65] Then the merchants took counsel: at the ordinary rate of sailing they ought to have reached Kwang-chow, and the time was passed by many days — must they not have held a wrong course? So they turned north-west looking for land, and after twelve days and nights reached the shore south of mount Lao.

How you know you are home is by the vegetables. They got good water and vegetables, and *seeing those well-known vegetables, the lei and kwoh, they knew indeed that it was the land of Han*.[^66] Not by a landmark, a coastline, or a star. He has crossed thirty countries and the thing that identifies his own is two plants he recognises.

What is real, in the last exchange of the journey, is a joke the text does not flag as one. Seeing no inhabitants and not knowing where they were, they sent a small boat into a creek and brought back two hunters, and called on Fa-hien to act as interpreter. He first spoke assuringly to them, and then slowly and distinctly asked: *who are you*? They replied: *we are disciples of Buddha*.[^67]

**The first men he meets on Chinese soil, after fifteen years, are hunters — and they answer a monk's question by naming themselves as his co-religionists**. He asks what country this is and they tell him: the border of the prefecture of Ch'ang-kwang, part of Ts'ing-chow under the ruling House of Tsin.

What is worth having, in the accounting he gives at the end, is a sum in years. Six years from Ch'ang-gan to Central India. Six more of stoppages there. Three on the return to Ts'ing-chow. The countries he passed through were a few under thirty.[^68] From the sandy desert westwards on to India, the beauty of the monkhood's demeanour and of the transforming influence of the Law was beyond the power of language to describe. *And reflecting how our masters had not heard any complete account of them, he therefore went on without regarding his own poor life*.

He then explains himself to the man who wrote it down:

> When I look back on what I have gone through, my heart is involuntarily moved, and the perspiration flows forth. That I encountered danger and trod the most perilous places, without thinking of or sparing myself, was because I had a definite aim, and thought of nothing but to do my best in my simplicity and straightforwardness. Thus it was that I exposed my life where death seemed inevitable, if I might accomplish but a ten-thousandth part of what I hoped.[^69]

*Read: lines 1750–1776.*

---

# Below the Line

*Everything above is sourced to the chapters named. Everything below is built rather than found, and is not measured by `assessgate.sh`*.

## Ch. XXXII — What Transfers `[SPECULATIVE]`

**A rule you write yourself into will be argued away by your own staff**. Asoka told the master of his hell to punish him as a sinner if he ever walked in, and when the moment came his lictors said *this is not a small matter, let your former agreement be altered*, and he followed them in. The Ceylonese king in chapter XXXVIII did the same job differently: instead of binding himself, he asked the monks to make a regulation excluding the king from the treasury, and attached a forty-year qualification for anyone else. *Applies when* you can foresee your own future temptation and there is a body outside your control that can hold the rule. *Fails* where the constraint lives only in your own word, because the people who serve you are paid to find you exceptions.
*Decision type:* power consolidation.

## Ch. XXXV — Roads Not Taken `[SPECULATIVE]`

**A live alternative, priced by the source**. The route into Dakshina existed and the terms were known: bring money and various articles, give them to the king, and he sends men to escort you, who pass you on at stages to others who show you the shortest ways.[^37] Fa-hien did not go, and he does not say why — only that he was unable to.

What that costs the book is measurable. Everything in chapter XXXV is hearsay, and he says so; and it is the only chapter where he reports something he cannot vouch for. Against that, the men on the wing were not going to be there when he arrived, and the villagers' answer to the pilgrims suggests the local account was already doing the thing accounts do at a distance from a famous building.

## Ch. XXXVI — Roads Not Taken `[SPECULATIVE]`

**A live alternative, taken by the last man with him**. Tao-ching stayed. His reasoning is on the page and it is not idleness: he had seen the rules kept properly and the dignified demeanour of the societies, remembered the mutilated state of the same rules at home, and vowed never again to be born in a frontier land.[^42]

The two men had identical evidence. One concluded that the good place is where you should be, and the other that the good place is where you fetch things from. **What settles it is not doctrine but what each of them thought the rules were for** — Tao-ching wanted to live under them and Fa-hien wanted them written down and delivered. Nothing in the source suggests either man tried to talk the other round.

## Ch. XXXVI — What Transfers `[SPECULATIVE]`

**When eighteen versions agree on the sense and differ on the procedure, take the fullest one and say why**. Fa-hien's account of the choice is four clauses long: they agree in general meaning, they differ as when one opens and another shuts, this one is the most complete, it has the fullest explanations. *Applies when* the variants are all in good faith and the differences are operational rather than doctrinal, so that completeness is a real criterion rather than a preference. *Fails* where the disagreement is about what the rule is for, in which case the fullest text is merely the most confident one.
*Decision type:* when to compromise a core value.

## Ch. XL — Counsel From Elsewhere `[SPECULATIVE]`

**A Stoic advisor on the leaking ship**. The dichotomy of control divides what is yours from what is not: your judgement and the quality of your action are yours, and your property, your body and your reputation are not. See [[ARCHIVES/concepts/history/stoic-dichotomy-of-control|The Stoic Dichotomy of Control]]. Fa-hien throws his pitcher and washing-basin into the sea without a word, which is the doctrine performed exactly. Then he prays, and what he prays about is the books.

The counsel would be that the manuscripts are in the same category as the basin. They are property, they are on a hull with a hole in it, and no amount of correct intention keeps them dry. What Fa-hien does instead is sort his possessions into two piles and treat one of them as not-his and the other as the thing he is for. **He is not failing the doctrine; he is refusing its scope**. A Stoic would say that fifteen years of work can be lost in an afternoon and the man is unharmed, and Fa-hien's whole life is the position that this is not true — that the mutilated rule-book at home is a real injury to real people, and the copy is the repair.

**And a Kautilyan advisor on the patron who saved him**. The *Arthashastra* reads protection as a function of whose reach extends to a place. See [[LAB/Worldview Reports/trautmann-arthashastra-worldview-archaeology|What a Mauryan Statecraft Manual Took For Granted]]. The patron does not defend Fa-hien's innocence of causing the storm, which would have been arguing on the Brahmans' ground and could not have been won. He extends a foreign king's jurisdiction onto the deck and offers his own body as the trigger for it. The threat is credible because everybody aboard is going to the same port.

Where the two advisors converge is on what actually kept the books dry, and it is not the prayer and not the rope. It is that one man on that ship had something to lose at the destination.

# What Runs Through All of It — A Record of Buddhistic Kingdoms

> **Closing pass across all forty chapter runs of Fa-hien, *A Record of Buddhistic Kingdoms*, in James Legge's translation.** Read from `RAW/books/A Record of Buddhist Kingdoms.md`, chapters I–XL. Written last, out of the finished runs.
>
> **Siblings:** [[LAB/Worldview Reports/faxian-worldview-archaeology-part-1|Part 1 — Chapters I–XIII]] · [[LAB/Worldview Reports/faxian-worldview-archaeology-part-2|Part 2 — Chapters XIV–XXVI]] · [[LAB/Worldview Reports/faxian-worldview-archaeology-part-3|Part 3 — Chapters XXVII–XL]]. No sibling thread map exists for this source yet.
>
> ⚠ **Supersedes** [[LAB/Worldview Reports/faxian-worldview-archaeology|the original whole-book report]], which merged the whole journey into one account.

*Source ingest: [[ARCHIVES/sources/faxian-record-of-buddhist-kingdoms|Fa-hien, A Record of Buddhistic Kingdoms]]*

---

## What Runs Through All of It

The whole book is one man checking whether a rule-book is intact, and it never once loses that thread. He set out because the Books of Discipline at home were mutilated and imperfect, and in chapter XXXVI, thirty-five chapters later, he finds a complete copy and takes three years to write it out. Everything between those two points is a survey of communities keeping the rules he came to verify. When he reaches the council of Vaisali in chapter XXV — seven hundred monks re-examining and collating the disciplinary books after a dispute over ten points — he is standing in front of an earlier version of his own errand.

**The single most repeated fact in the book is that the transmission held.** Kings from the Sandy Desert to Ceylon have been firm believers. The forms of ceremony and rules practised by the communities have been handed down from one generation to another without interruption. The places of the four great topes have been fixed and handed down without break. The laws regulating a monk's demeanour in sitting and rising are the ones practised by all the saints since Buddha was in the world. He says some version of that in five separate chapters, and it is what a man who came to check an inventory would say.

Strangers are provided for in advance, everywhere, by rule rather than by kindness. Khoten keeps rooms for monks from all quarters who have not arrived yet. Woo-chang supplies stranger bhikshus for three days and then tells them to find their own bed. Mathura's residents carry a newcomer's clothes and bowl, wash his feet, anoint him with oil, feed him outside the regular hours, and only then ask how many years he has been a monk, which is what decides where he sleeps. Even the ninety-six rival systems of chapter XX run free houses on the empty roads for travellers and monks alike, and the only difference Fa-hien records is the length of stay. **That infrastructure is why the journey is possible, and he almost never comments on it.**

Where the system breaks, it breaks on hospitality rather than on terrain. The party splits three times. At Woo-e, three men turn back because the local people neglected the duties of propriety and righteousness and treated them meanly. At the alms-bowl in Purushapura, three more go home and one dies. On the Little Snowy mountains a man freezes and orders the others to leave him. Nobody in this book is stopped by a mountain; they are stopped by cold, by illness, and by a town that would not feed them.

Objects decide who may have them, and kings accept the verdict. The Yueh-she king had won his war and could not move the alms-bowl with eight elephants, so he read the kneeling as a ruling on his own merit, was ashamed, and built a monastery instead. Asoka meant to demolish the Rama tope and a dragon opened its accounts and invited him to beat them, and he did his own valuation and went home. Buddha's pewter staff cannot be lifted by a hundred or a thousand men. **Three times a sufficient force stops on a non-military ground, and each time the man stopping is the strongest party present.**

Rules that bind a ruler come in two versions and only one of them holds. Asoka told the master of his hell to punish him as a sinner if he ever entered, and his own lictors talked him through the gate in two sentences. The Ceylonese king who caught himself coveting the treasury asked the monks to make it a regulation, with a forty-year qualification for anyone else, and it stayed. The difference is whether the constraint lives in your own word or in a body outside your control.

Two systems for making a grant outlast the man who made it, and both are metal. In Mathura the endowments — fields, houses, gardens, orchards, the resident populations and their cattle — are engraved on plates and handed from king to king, *without any daring to annul them*. In Ceylon, six chapters from the end, the king ploughs the boundary himself with a golden plough behind decorated oxen and then writes the grant on plates of metal, so that from generation to generation nobody may annul or alter it. **The same instrument at the two far ends of the journey, arrived at independently.**

A place becomes a place because somebody came back and identified it. Buddha tells his disciples that this is where he ransomed the dove; the people of the country become aware of the fact and rear a tope. He tells them this is where, in a former age, he laid down his bow and weapons; men subsequently get to know it and build. That is the mechanism behind most of the several hundred sites in this book, and the ground itself remembers nothing without the return visit.

The one thing that cannot be reproduced is a likeness. An artificer went up to the Tushita heaven three times to get Maitreya's height and complexion right, and came back with an eighty-cubit image everybody can see. Prasenajit had the first sandalwood image carved and Buddha told it to return to its seat and serve as a pattern to the four classes of disciples. But kings from every region sent skilful artists to copy the shadow at Nagara, and none of them could, and the shadow grows fainter the closer you walk. **The tradition can copy a body, a posture and a scale, and it cannot copy a shadow.**

## Which dimensions the book never reached

Fa-hien reports almost nothing about what makes things happen at the level of an explanation. The desert has demons and hot winds in the same clause. Dragons on the Onion range spit poisonous winds when provoked, and the local people call the range the Snow mountains, and both statements stand. A dragon at Sankasya holds the office of *danapati* and causes abundant harvests and rains in season. A robe brought out in a drought produces immediate rain. None of these is defended, connected, or ranked against the others. **He is a surveyor rather than a theologian, and the book has no theory of causes at all.**

Doctrine appears three times in forty chapters and it is the same doctrine each time. The bitterness and vanity of life as impermanent and uncertain, and the body as a bubble or foam on the water. That is the whole of what he reports anybody teaching. It reappears in the mouth of the bhikshu on the black rock before he cuts his throat, and again in the mind of the bhikshu in Asoka's hell, and once, at Jetavana, in Fa-hien's own account of his dead friends. He never explains it and never argues for it.

What a woman's life is like in these kingdoms is not in the range read (lines 228–1777). Nuns appear twice — Utpala, who is changed into a king so she can be first in the queue, and the bhikshunis who offer at Ananda's tope because he asked that women be allowed to leave their families. Ambapali gives a vihara and a garden. The woman on the wall at Vaisali feeds a thousand sons. That is four appearances in forty chapters, and none of them describes a life.

Nothing in any chapter reports what ordinary lay people believe, as distinct from what they do. He counts their monks, records their diet, notes that they use cowries and keep no butchers' shops, and reports that they build charity houses and set flower stalls outside a relic shrine at dawn. **Their observances are described in detail and their reasons never are.**

## Where two chapters pull against each other

Chapter XIII's uncopyable shadow and chapter VI's three trips to a heaven are the same problem answered opposite ways, and the book does not notice. In both, a king wants an accurate likeness of somebody not present, and both times the answer is to send a skilled craftsman to look. At Darada the method works after three attempts and produces an object that emits light on fast-days. At Nagara it fails for every artist every king sends. The difference is never named.

Chapter XVI's country with no magistrates and chapter XXVII's city built by spirits describe the same king from two angles. Asoka's Middle Kingdom has no household registration, no corporal punishment, a single tax on royal land, and people who go or stay as they please. Asoka's Patna has a palace no human hands could have built, an inscription recording that he gave away the world and bought it back three times, and a hell he commissioned with a specification. **Neither passage acknowledges the other, and both are Fa-hien reporting what he was told on the ground.**

Chapter XXX's suicide and chapter XXIII's demotion are the two places where a monk reasons his way past his own vows, and they land in opposite registers. The man on the black rock accepts the prohibition against killing himself and reclassifies the act as killing three poisons, and gets three ranks in one stroke. The devotee at Rama gives up the great prohibitions in order to be allowed to pull up grass, and founds a monastery whose head has been a novice ever since. Both men treat the rule as binding and find a legitimate way round it. Only one of them dies.

## What the by-chapter reading recovered

Reading forty chapters as forty worlds surfaces material a merged account discards because it happens once. The five hundred blind men whose staves grew into a grove. The rat carrying a lamp-wick that burned down a seven-storey vihara. The hundred topes that cannot be counted even by standing a man beside each one. Eight families with eight seals opening one door at dawn. A dragon carried down the seniority order in a copper vessel of cream, once a year. The fifteen-hundred-room monastery with a spring at the top feeding water past every door. The villagers who asked pilgrims why they were not flying. The fan of white silk in a stranger's hand that made a man cry in front of a jade Buddha. Two hunters on a Chinese beach answering a monk's first question with *we are disciples of Buddha*.

**And one sentence that only exists because the chapter was read on its own.** In chapter XXXIX an Indian preacher gives a complete future history of the world hung on the travels of an alms-bowl, and when Fa-hien asks to record it as doctrine the man says: *this is taken from no Sutra, it is only the utterance of my own mind.* A book about the integrity of a transmission ends four chapters later, and the sharpest thing in it is a man refusing to let his own sermon into the canon.

# What a Mauryan King Took For Granted — Prelude and Chapters 1–5

> **Prelude and chapters 1–5 of Nayanjot Lahiri, *Ashoka in Ancient India*** — the rocks at Erragudi and the problem of knowing anything, the prophecies invented for him afterwards, Pataliputra behind its wooden wall, Taxila's crooked lanes, the woman at Vidisha, and the march on Kalinga. Read from `RAW/books/Ashoka in Ancient India.md`. One full archaeology pass per chapter, sweeping all seven dimensions in every run.
>
> **Siblings:** [[LAB/Worldview Reports/lahiri-ashoka-worldview-archaeology-part-2|Part 2 — Chapters 6–9]] · [[LAB/Worldview Reports/lahiri-ashoka-worldview-archaeology-part-3|Part 3 — Chapters 10–12 and the Epilogue]] · [[LAB/Worldview Reports/lahiri-ashoka-worldview-archaeology-synthesis|What Runs Through All of It]]. Its sibling thread map is [[LAB/Threads/olivelle-ashoka-portrait-of-a-philosopher-king-threads|the Olivelle Ashoka thread map]].
>
> ⚠ **Supersedes the Lahiri half of** [[LAB/Worldview Reports/ashoka-worldview-archaeology|the original whole-book report]], which merged two books into one account and was built from the vault's Ashokan concept pages rather than from RAW. **The Olivelle half of that report stands** — *Ashoka: Portrait of a Philosopher King* has no RAW file in this vault, so the by-chapter rule cannot run on it. It is a re-ingest candidate.

*Source ingest: [[ARCHIVES/sources/lahiri-ashoka-in-ancient-india|Nayanjot Lahiri, Ashoka in Ancient India]]*

---

## Prelude — A waterfall of words on a low ridge

There is nothing to look at until you get close. A cluster of rocks sits on a low ridge near the village of Erragudi in Andhra. It rises perhaps thirty metres out of a patchwork of fields, with a bit of scrub on it.[^1] Then you walk up to the boulders and find more than a hundred lines of ancient Brahmi cascading down them. Large stretches are still perfectly sharp. Some has worn away, and modern visitors have scratched English and Telugu over parts of it. None of that takes anything off the impression of somebody talking to you out of 2200 years ago.

The reason that matters is that everybody before him is faceless. Kings came out of tradition around 600 BCE and ruled from the north-west frontier down to the Godavari. A great many of them wanted to be called chief king of all kings.[^2] Then most of those kingdoms got absorbed into one empire based in Magadha, and eleven or so kings ruled it before Ashoka arrived around 269/268 BCE. **What survives of every one of them is somebody else's version, written later**. The Puranas, some Buddhist and Jaina texts, and the classical authors — mostly literate men in Alexander's entourage, plus Megasthenes at Chandragupta's court.

So how you know anything at all about an ancient Indian king is by reading around him. Ashoka is the exception because his story is largely in his own words. Nehru said the edicts spoke to him of a man who, though an emperor, was greater than any king or emperor — and Nehru noticed the technical point too, that Ashoka was his own *sutradhar*, his own narrator.[^3]

Writing was not the normal way to say anything in the first millennium BCE, and the chapter is careful about what each civilization did instead. In Greece the rhetoric ran on logical argument, reasoned debate and persuasion, and it was direct and aimed at an audience in the room.[^4] In China speech was the medium for exchanging ideas, and effective speech was held to be a real instrument of government — but the man who found favour was not the one who spoke to make himself noticed by being different. In India debates were communal and group-oriented, and regulated along caste lines. Vedic priests and Buddhist monks alike went centuries without writing their texts down.

Against that, what he did was strange twice over. Other rulers inscribed things — the Achaemenid kings of Iran did — and their public inscriptions spend their space and their superlatives on how the enemy was killed and conquered.[^5] His do not. **And he did not put them where a king lives. He put them where the people lived and worshipped**, and sent his administration out with multiple copies so that the same words stood in Afghanistan and in Andhra, in Karnataka and in Kalinga.

What is worth having, from where he sat, was to be heard identically everywhere at once. The result is that his version of his own life is the one that was best known during his lifetime. No other ancient ruler's voice carried across a subcontinent while he was still alive to hear it come back.[^6]

Time here has a hole in the middle of it and the chapter says so plainly. There is no eyewitness. The stories of his birth and early years are in the *Ashokavadana*, a Sanskrit text of about the second century CE, and in the Sri Lankan Pali chronicles, the *Dipavamsa* of about the fourth century and the *Mahavamsa* of about the fifth.[^7] They shape what anybody thinks about his youth and they are centuries late. So a life of him written to modern biographical standards is not possible, and the book says as much rather than pretending otherwise.

**And the same hole sits under other famous ancient lives, which is the comparison that takes the sting out of it**. No account of Cleopatra's life was written in her own time. Her mother's name is not known. Her birth is unrecorded.[^8] Alexander's biographers work from narratives composed hundreds of years after his death, relying on earlier works none of which survive except in fragments.

How a king gets recovered, in the end, is by soldiers and clerks tripping over him. Military men, antiquarians and archaeologists came across writing in an unknown script on rocks and pillars all over India in the early nineteenth century.[^9] The lock opened in 1837 when James Prinsep, secretary of the Asiatic Society, worked out the key to the Mauryan Brahmi script. Prinsep unlocked Ashoka.

Not all the finders were European, and the chapter is deliberate about that. Bhagwanlal Indraji was finding Ashokan edicts in Maharashtra and Rajasthan at the same time as Cunningham's men were scouring the countryside. He is much less known because most of his early writing was in Gujarati.[^10] A gold prospector stumbled on the Maski inscription in Karnataka in 1915. The guru of a math at Gavimath reported another in 1931. One turned up at Ratanpurwa in Bihar in 2009. They are still arriving.

What later India wanted him for is the last thing the Prelude covers. Nationalist leaders looked for a political ancestor and found one, taking India's lineage of tolerance and non-violence back through the Buddha.[^11] Tagore wrote that countless great kingdoms had been razed to dust. The emergence of the power of benevolence in Ashoka, he wrote, had become a proud asset breathing strength into us. **A king is useful to a nation in the way that a king is not useful to a historian**, and the two demands pull in opposite directions on the same handful of rocks.

*Read: lines 242–415.*

---

## Ch. 1 — The prophecy that arrived four hundred years late

Nobody knows when he was born. Sometime around 304 BCE is certain. The day and month and year are not, because very few ancient writers cared about calendars the way we do, and his own scribes certainly did not.[^12] The way the date gets reached is by working backwards from his consecration. That date is fairly firm, because his regnal years can be matched against rulers elsewhere in Asia whose dates are known.

Then he did something with time that nobody in India had done before. He anchored every event of his reign to the year he was anointed, and **he is the earliest known Indian monarch to date events from his own consecration**.[^13] The Satavahanas in the west, the Palas in the east and the Cholas in the south all kept doing it for centuries afterwards.

What he would not say about himself is as marked as what he would. His epigraphs will tell you what was cooked in the royal kitchen and what he thinks of pointless social ceremonies, and they say nothing about his personal affairs.[^14] Part of that may be the events of his own early life. Part is that by the time he was writing he had developed a distaste for the ceremonies people hold at the birth of a son or the marriage of a child. And part is simply that no king before him had inscribed anything like this, so there was no template to follow.

Since he left no account, the gap filled up with prediction. **The strongest single thread in all the later stories is that his coming was foretold**, and the first foretelling happens in an earlier life.[^15] The Buddha, walking down the main street of Rajagriha with his begging bowl, sees two boys playing in the dirt, and one of them — Jaya, who will be Ashoka — puts a handful of dirt in the bowl.

The stories are careful about their furniture, which is what makes them convincing. Rajagriha really was the centre of Magadhan royal power in the Buddha's time, and it really had ceased to be by the third century BCE, when Pataliputra was the capital.[^16] The chronology inside the same text does not hold up — it says Ashoka lived about a hundred years after the Buddha's death while also saying eleven generations of kings separate them.

The prophecy repeats twice more with different prophets, and the second one arrives with the woman who becomes his mother. Her real name is lost — Subhadrangi in some places, Dharma or Durdhara in others.[^17] Fortune tellers told her Brahman father in Champa that she would marry a king and bear two jewel-like sons, one of whom would rule. So he took her to Pataliputra and offered her to Bindusara, who already had a substantial harem and an heir apparent called Susima.

Then the story turns on a razor. The concubines were afraid of her looks and kept her away from the emperor by teaching her to be a barber instead.[^18] She learned it so well that when she began to trim the king's beard and hair he relaxed under her hands, and she got what she had been kept from. When the boy came and she was asked what to call him, she said she had no sorrow — so he was *a-shoka*, without sorrow. Her second son was Vitashoka.

**His father disliked him, and the reason given is his skin**. It was rough and unpleasant to the touch, which is why the boy was at first unwilling to be examined by the Ajivika ascetic Pingalavatsajiva, whom Bindusara had asked to look over his sons and say who would rule best.[^19] His mother had known the answer for years and had kept it to herself, which is what a queen in a large polygamous household does when her son is not the eldest — every other wife has the same ambition, and Kekayi in the *Ramayana* is what happens when one of them acts on it.

The predictor's own sect is the most interesting choice in the chapter, and it is chosen for a reason you can check on stone. The Ajivikas are a vanished Indian religion — vanished because it has no modern adherents at all, unlike every other faith with ancient roots.[^20] Their founder Makkhali Goshala lived in the sixth century BCE, in the same wave of unorthodox teachers as Mahavira and the Buddha. His name was known in the royal circles of Magadha. The reason he turns up as Ashoka's augur is that Ashoka actually patronised the sect once he was king. The caves he gave them at Barabar near Gaya carry his donative inscriptions.

How you know the future, in this world, is by reading signs that were always there. The Rig Veda has the cries of certain birds foretelling events. The Atharva Veda has something falling from the mouth of a black bird.[^21] In the *Ramayana*, when Ravana is getting the better of Rama, the planets take the blame — Mercury standing over the Rohini *nakshatra*, which the moon favours, and so showing evil fortune. The *Mahabharata* reads the coming apocalypse off the sky, and a frightful comet standing over Pushya means terrible evil will visit both armies.

The people who read those signs were powerful and not much liked. Ascetics were forbidden to get their alms by foretelling the results of earthquakes, or of a throbbing eye or arm, or by astrology or palmistry.[^22] The censure did not reach the palace. The *Arthashastra* wants the king's chaplain to be a man of exalted family who has studied the Vedic texts thoroughly. He must **also** be trained in divine signs and omens, and capable of dealing with calamities by Atharvan remedies.

What all of it is actually for shows up when you line up who gets prophesied about. The Buddha's greatness was declared at his birth by the sage Asita. He took the child up, found the marks and signs his lore knew, and cried out that he had no peer.[^23] Harshavardhana, in the seventh century CE, gets a mother who while pregnant preferred to look at her reflection in a sword rather than in a jewelled mirror.

Neither Ashoka nor Harsha was the eldest son. **Neither had any claim under primogeniture, and both got a prophecy** — and the chapter names the function without dressing it up: the sacred is smuggled in as a prediction, and the prediction makes an otherwise dubious accession legitimate.[^24]

## Ch. 2 — A city inside a wooden wall

A Chinese pilgrim arrives 800 years late and writes down what the locals tell him. Xuanzang reached Pataliputra in the seventh century CE and recorded that Ashoka had moved the capital there from Rajagriha and built an outer rampart around the old city.[^25] That is wrong — the move had nothing to do with Ashoka, and Xuanzang may have confused Bindusara with Bimbisara, who had no connection to him at all. By the time he came, the old city was ruins and only the foundation walls were left.

What he was shown is a landscape that had been made into Ashoka's. There was the earth-prison, the hell the emperor was said to have built in his cruel years. Everyone who entered it was killed with no chance to defend themselves.[^26] There was a stone with the Buddha's two footprints on it, eighteen inches long and six broad, with circle-signs embossed on them and fish and flowers around all ten toes, which the king had enclosed. There was a pillar carrying an inscription saying Ashoka had thrice given Jambudvipa away as a religious offering and thrice bought it back with his jewels. **No Ashokan pillar we know carries anything of the kind**.

And the city itself had been prophesied, in a story that runs the same way as the ones about the king. The Buddha, on his last journey towards Kushinagara, looked back at Magadha, pressed his feet into the stone he stood on. Then he told Ananda that a hundred years hence there would be a King Asoka who would build his capital here.[^27] Earlier in his life he had seen thousands of magical creatures haunting Pataligrama, and read it as a sign that a fortress was going up. As far as Aryan people resort and as far as merchants travel, this will become the chief city.

The real place was made by a river and a war. It grew where people and goods crossed the Ganga, a little past the confluence with the Son, and the settlement ran in a line because the river did.[^28] The fortress went up because Magadha needed a base against the Vajjis, a republican confederacy on the far bank. Ajatashatru turned the village into the fortified city between 493 and 462 BCE.

Where a capital sits is a statement about what kind of power it is. Rajagriha was ringed by magnificent hills and had cyclopean walls run across them, and it was defended by its own landscape.[^29] Pataliputra is monotonously flat and swampy at the edges, fringed by marshes off the Punpun. **A state that had stopped hiding in hills and started reaching down a river moved out of the fortress and onto the water**.

What it looked like comes from a Greek who was actually there. Megasthenes went further into India than any foreigner before him, across Punjab and the Gangetic plains to the court of Sandrakottos. His *Indica* survives only in fragments quoted by later writers.[^30] He was prone to grandeur — he says the women of the Pandaian land bore children at six. He describes nomads with orifices instead of nostrils and legs contorted like snakes. On Pataliputra he is checkable, and he checks out.

The city ran about fourteen kilometres long and two and a half wide. It was a long narrow parallelogram girded by a wooden wall pierced with loopholes for arrows, with a ditch in front that took both the defence and the sewage.[^31] Archaeologists have found the wall. Uprights of strong timber turn up in excavations all over modern Patna — two parallel rows of posts about 4.5 metres high. They were paved with wooden sleepers and covered over with planks.

Wood sounds like the wrong material until you learn which wood. Sal is unusually hard and survives waterlogged ground, and Patna then had the same high subsoil water it has now.[^32] Ghosh's 1926–7 excavation at Bulandibagh had to bale deep ponds out before digging could start. And sal does not grow near the Ganga around Pataliputra — nobody knows which forests it came from, which means somebody hauled it a long way on purpose.

The posts kept surprising people who had no idea what they were. Villagers digging wells struck the great beams standing upright far below the surface, could not account for them, and usually abandoned the well.[^33]

**What a king is, inside that wall, is a man who cannot sleep in the same bed twice**. Megasthenes says he was not to sleep in the daytime and had to change his couch by night, because of the people plotting to kill him, and that his care was entrusted to women.[^34] The *Arthashastra* agrees: bow-bearing female guards when he rose, and female slaves of proved integrity working as bath-attendants, shampooers, bed-preparers, laundresses and garland-makers. At Bharhut, Ajatashatru rides his state elephant with a woman holding the parasol behind him and women driving the other elephants.

The living quarters in the manual read like a machine for not being murdered. A chamber in the centre built to treasury standards, or a maze-house with concealed passages in the walls, or an underground room whose opening is covered by a wooden image of a deity in a nearby sanctuary, with many subterranean passages, and above it a palace with a staircase hidden in a wall or an entrance through a hollow pillar, and a floor fixed to a mechanism so that it can sink.[^35]

Even the plants are vetted. Only certain shoots were admissible against poison and snakes. The animals allowed in were the ones that kill serpents — peacocks, ichneumons and spotted deer let loose in the grounds.[^36] The queens were frowned on as visitors to his quarters; he went to the apartments of the queen favoured that day, and only after she had been cleared of suspicion.

So the children may well have been barred from their father, and how they were educated is unclear. His days and nights were each divided into eight parts, with slots for income and expenditure, the affairs of citizens and country people, military plans and troop review, counsellors, secret agents, and being blessed by the chief cook and the astrologer.[^37] **No part of the day was set aside for his family**. The princesses were not thought worth educating at all, and no source says anything about Ashoka's sisters.

And the reason for all the locks is stated as a proverb about crabs. Princes are like crabs, creatures known to devour their begetters, and disciplined or undisciplined they were all held to be a danger to the king.[^38] The evidence was recent enough: Bimbisara of Magadha was murdered by his son Ajatashatru, and his contemporary Pasenadi of Kosala lost his insignia to his son Vidudabha.

The manual then turns round and coaches the prince on how to survive his father — disguise, refuge with a neighbouring prince, and parricide held back for the worst case.[^39] **What is odd, in a world where everybody expects to be stabbed by his own sons, is how tenaciously primogeniture held**. Kings guarded themselves to the hilt against their boys, and then handed the throne to the eldest one anyway.

## Ch. 3 — Crooked lanes on a plateau

A father sends his son to put down a rebellion and gives him an army with no weapons. The *Ashokavadana* says Taxila revolted, Bindusara sent Ashoka with a fourfold army of cavalry, elephants, chariots and infantry, and denied it arms.[^40] The servants pointed out the difficulty. Ashoka said that if his merit was such that he was to become king, let weapons appear — and the earth opened and deities brought them out.

Three readings sit on top of each other and the chapter keeps all three. It may mean a shortage of weapons rather than none, turning the success into one more miracle.[^41] It may mean Bindusara, who disliked this son, was sending him somewhere he might not come back from. Or it fits the later picture of Ashoka as an *ayashcakravartin*, an iron-wheeled monarch, who ruled India by the threat of the sword and not by its use.

**Whether he ever went is unknown, and the chapter says so rather than deciding**. He never mentions it, which proves nothing given how little he said about his youth.[^42] What is likely is that whoever wrote the legend knew Taxila carried his name — the greatest Buddhist monument there is the Dharmarajika stupa, and Dharmaraja means him.

What a journey is, at this distance, is two thousand kilometres of alluvium. The road existed and had a name — the Uttarapatha, the northern road, running from beyond Taxila across the Indus and Gangetic plains and past Pataliputra to the port of Tamralipti on the east coast.[^43] Traders, pedlars, caravan leaders, religious men and princes are the people you meet on it. Lapis lazuli from Afghanistan turns up at sites all along it, from Rairh in Rajasthan to Sravasti and Rajghat, along with tin and silver.

**Which is why Bindusara wanted Taxila quiet**. It was the premier city of the frontier, in a region so rich that Herodotus called the twentieth satrapy the wealthiest in the Persian empire.[^44] Its king had capitulated to Alexander, who sacrificed there, held a competition in athletics and horsemanship, and left a garrison behind when he marched east against Porus.

The book stops here to say what it thinks of the whole business, in one sentence it does not repeat. Conquest and empire-building have been called wonderful and great, and from a saner angle they are male megalomania of a revolting kind — and looked at through Ashoka's own lens of humanity and compassion and fellow feeling, these men of drive and ambition slaughtered thousands.[^45]

Now the city, which is where the chapter earns its keep. Taxila sat on the Bhir plateau, eighteen to twenty-one metres above the plains, about 1,097 metres north to south.[^46] The houses were flat-roofed and of varying heights, plastered with clay, and the clay gave the whole city one colour. The walls had changed from rough loose rubble to neat compact blocks of local hard limestone and the soft lime *kanjur* of the plains.

First Street is called that because it deserves the name — seven metres wide, more or less straight, and the city's main artery since the earliest settlement.[^47] Then you look at the rest of the plan and it is a mishmash of winding lanes at odd angles. Second Street starts straight and wanders. Lane 2 is blocked at its western end by a cross-wall. Anybody wanting to get from First Street to Second has to go round by Lane 1 or up to Third.

**And the strange part is the order it happened in**. The elegant street is the old one. All the crooked lanes were cut later, in the late fourth and early third centuries BCE, which is the wrong way round for a city that is supposed to be improving.[^48]

The explanation the chapter offers is about what people would not sell. The administration seems to have had to clear existing structures to lay the new roads. They ran into householders who would not give up their land and homes to make a street straight.[^49] So the planners agreed with Kautilya in theory and let the ground be settled by what was available. The lanes are haphazard and they are a citizen-friendly answer.

Then they fixed the consequences instead of the plan. Realising the corners were bad for the pack animals hauling goods, they put in wheel-guards — stone pillars set at the corners of houses, standing a little under a metre above ground with another half metre buried.[^50] Open squares were left at intervals. Big stone-rubble garbage bins stood in the squares; one on the east side of Square S is known by the bones and broken pottery dug out of it.

**There was no drainage system, and that is the difference between this city and the capital**. There are surface drains in Fourth Street and Lane 1 and nothing joining them to a main drain, so First Street worked as thoroughfare and wet-weather watercourse at once.[^51] Water off the higher lanes joined it, so a monsoon arrival meant parading troops up an inundation. Pataliputra had underground wooden drains. Harappa and Mohenjo-daro, two millennia earlier in the same north-west, had rather better.

What people worshipped is the clearest thing in the ruins. The city brimmed with deities and **the goddesses outnumbered the gods**.[^52] Miniature goddesses of clay outnumbered gods. The temple in the western part of the city has two courtyards, a pillared hall and some thirty rooms that were lived in, probably by the priests. There is also a room with a large square tank that was either an ablution tank or a fire pit — either of which belongs in a Hindu shrine and neither of which turns up in early Buddhist or Jaina places of worship.

The commonest object is a plaque you could buy across the lane. A turbaned male in a *dhoti* with necklace and earrings, holding the side of his shawl in his right hand. Beside him stands a female with ear pendants and a necklace and a long veil either side of her head, her left hand on her hip.[^53] The moulds were found in a shop opposite. Devotees bought them and offered them, most likely against a vow tied to recovering from illness or succeeding in business — the same trade that goes on outside Indian temples today.

**And that is the judgement the chapter reaches about what the emperor built later**. He put up a great stupa outside the city, on the rocky spurs east of the Bhir, and the worship there was a different thing from the rituals around the city's deities. Lahiri's own view, stated as her own, is that the goddesses of the Taxilans and the old rituals around them are likely to have carried more religious power and meaning for the citizens than the grand stupa built at their emperor's instance.[^54]

Who ran the place cannot be found. There are no names and no dates for anyone in public office, in inscriptions or in texts, and none of the buildings look administrative except by inference — Block A sits at a crossing and has a semi-octagonal frontage with a ring of rooms inside it, and that is the whole of the case for it.[^55] **Commerce is far more visible than government**. Seals of copper, glass, clay and stone turn up everywhere, and because they are not clustered anywhere there was probably no merchants' quarter. The same goes for the crafts: a crucible lined with burnt sandy clay, a precious-metal polisher, a chalcedony burnisher for gold and silver, scattered across the city rather than gathered into one street.

## Ch. 4 — A merchant's daughter at Vidisha

He is sent a thousand kilometres to govern a province and falls in love on the way. Bindusara made him viceroy of Avanti, headquartered at Ujjayini, and he seems to have spent about ten years there from around 282 BCE.[^56] The road there ran across the black soil of Malwa, rough and trampled by the feet of cattle.

**Where an empire sends its princes tells you what it is worried about**. Avanti had once been a kingdom with designs on Magadha — Pradyota attacked Rajagriha in Bimbisara's lifetime, and it was fear of him that made Ajatashatru strengthen the defences there.[^57] By Bindusara's time it was a province, and it was rich and connected enough to be worth a son.

The route had a name too. The Dakshinapatha, the southern route, carried the caravans up from the country south of the central highlands, and it was the road the physician Jivaka of Rajagriha took when Pradyota summoned him to Ujjayini to cure his jaundice.[^58] Along it the customs change: Avanti is described as a place where people attach great importance to bathing and where sheep-skins, goat-skins and deer-skins were used as coverlets.

How long it took is worked out from later caravans, and the arithmetic is the chapter's own. On the best Mughal road from Agra to Lahore, caravans averaged a little over thirty kilometres a day.[^59] On a harder traverse into Central India, thirty would be a steep target, so at twenty-five a day the journey runs to about forty days. Peter Mundy's caravan of 268 camels and 109 carts is what such a convoy actually looks like — he attached himself to a governor's escort to dodge local taxes, could not keep pace with it, and got caught at Khamva by a sandstorm and then heavy rain.

Then the country itself, which he would have found unlike anything at home. Jungle and cliffs full of rock shelters, long undulating plateau, riverine plains.[^60] The Rewa jungles in the nineteenth century were thick with sal, tendu, saj and khair, and full of tigers, leopards, bear, antelope and chinkara. **A boy raised on the near-monotonous alluvium of the Ganga would have been looking at another world**.

Devi is at Vidisha, and almost everything about her is missing. She was the daughter of a prominent city merchant and she was beautiful, and that is the whole of it.[^61] The pattern is the same one that produced his own mother: royal men notice common women when they are arrestingly beautiful, and nothing about their lives before that gets written down.

What the tradition wants from her is not the romance. The *Dipavamsa* is blunt — the daughter of a merchant, known by the name of Devi, having cohabited with him, gave birth to a most noble son.[^62] A later account adds that she bore Mahinda at Ujjayini and a daughter two years after. **It is the reproductive outcome that is the point of the story**, because Mahinda and Sanghamitra are the ones who carry Buddhism to Sri Lanka, which is where the texts telling this were written.

Whether he married her has been argued over for decades. Thapar holds she was not legally married to him, partly because no marriage is mentioned; the word initially translated as sexual relations outside marriage is supposed to mean co-residence.[^63] Lahiri's counter is a point about the man: a prince who broke primogeniture to take the throne is not obviously a man who would be stopped by a rule about whom he could marry.

Her religion is argued the same circumstantial way, and the argument is worth having in front of you. **Nowhere is Devi ever described as converting**. Ashoka converts. Her children take ordination. She simply appears as a Buddhist, leading her son Mahinda — a *thera* by then — up to the vihara at Vedisagiri.[^64] If she was a Buddhist later and nobody ever mentions her becoming one, she was probably a Buddhist when they met.

The places back it up. Vidisha is the pivot of the monuments at Sanchi, and Marshall's view was that the story of Sanchi was bound up from first to last with the fortunes of the city in whose shadow it grew and on whose wealth it depended.[^65] The largest stupa at Ujjayini, ten metres high and built of large Mauryan bricks, is locally called the Vaishya Tekri, the mound of the Vaishya caste, because Devi was a merchant's daughter and trade is a Vaishya occupation.

And then the ten years end in a killing. Bindusara fell critically ill at Pataliputra and Ashoka went home.[^66] The *Mahavamsa* is brief: he made himself master of the city, and after his father's death he caused his eldest brother to be slain and took the sovereignty. The *Dipavamsa* says a hundred brothers were killed, which is a stock figure meaning many rather than one, and it puts four years between the death and the consecration — long enough for the fighting to have been protracted.

The *Ashokavadana* tells it as a court intrigue and it turns on a joke. Susima, the heir apparent, slapped the prime minister's bald head in jest.[^67] The minister was not amused: today he slaps me with his hand, when he becomes king he will let fall his sword. So he pulled five hundred ministers away from Susima with the prediction that Ashoka would be a *chakravartin*.

Then Bindusara fell ill, recalled Susima to consecrate him, and ordered Ashoka out to Taxila in his place. The ministers said Ashoka was ill and urged the dying king to install him for the moment and swap him for Susima later, which made the king furious.[^68] Ashoka said that if the throne was rightfully his, let the gods crown him — and they did, and Bindusara vomited blood and died. **Susima came back to Pataliputra and fell into a ditch that had been filled with the live coals of acacia wood**.

## Ch. 5 — The victory written down as a disaster

A new king tests his ministers by asking them to chop down trees. The clique from his father's reign that had put him on the throne had started treating him with contempt, so he ordered them to cut down flowering and fruit trees and keep the thorny ones — and when they did the reverse, he cut off the heads of five hundred of them.[^69] The story is not free-standing invention. The *Arthashastra* prescribes exactly this kind of secret test, with agents suggesting to a minister that the king is impious and that they should set up another, and the minister who repulses the instigation being counted loyal.

The killings do not stop with the ministers. A stroll in a park east of Pataliputra in spring, a flowering Ashoka tree he greets as his namesake, a slight from the women of his harem, and mass slaughter follows.[^70] His prime minister, alarmed at how much of it the king was doing personally, got him to appoint a royal executioner so the killing could be delegated. The man found for it was a weaver boy from a Magadhan village called Girika, who already had the word "fierce" attached to his name, and who worked in a building beautiful on the outside and a very frightful place inside.

**The chapter names the literary machinery without pretending the machinery has no history behind it**. Sadistic cruelty is a trope in Buddhist hagiography, because a conversion story needs a brutish background to convert away from, and the *Ashokavadana* was going to show him as the ideal Buddhist ruler.[^71] What is nonetheless likely is that cruelty was close by in his early reign. He almost certainly got rid of an older half-brother and probably others who had backed the rightful heir, and the resistance was unlikely to have stopped at the palace.

The southern tradition writes the same years as a search rather than a slaughter. In the Sri Lankan telling he is a restlessly enquiring emperor looking for a spiritual preceptor, and the point of that telling is that he came to Buddhism by quest rather than by any natural leaning.[^72] The search ends on a Pataliputra road with a monk called Nigrodha out for alms — a handsome young man of tranquil appearance who walks the road like an elephant, fearless and endowed with the ornament of tranquility. It was the bearing and fearlessness, as much as the preaching, that made the king a lay disciple.

**And then Lahiri says both traditions are the wrong shape**. Her own view, stated flatly: his transformation had little to do with any search for a preceptor, and very little to do with spiritual matters at all.[^73] What changed him falls squarely inside material matters of state — and she says it with confidence because it is the emperor's own words on his own stone that say so.

What a king was for, in the manual he was raised on, is a list. Settle the countryside, by bringing in people from foreign lands or shifting the overflow of his own. Build irrigation. Put fortresses on the frontiers. Support the mines and factories, the ports and trade routes, because that is where the revenue is.[^74] Protect the subjects by wielding *danda*, the rod — for the Rod, used after full consideration, endows the subjects with spiritual good, material well-being and pleasures of the senses.

The last item on the list is the one that matters here. The king was to be a *vijigishu*, a would-be conqueror, with an ambition to own the whole world.[^75] The reasoning is not glory but arithmetic: **if you do not exercise power, somebody else exercises it over you**, so a king is only properly a king if he means to extend his sway over everything. He should follow the policy by which he can see that he will promote his own undertakings.

So the first act of his reign that he chose to record is a war. Kalinga, on the eastern seaboard, in what is now Orissa and part of Andhra, around 260 BCE.[^76] And the chapter widens out to say that this is what everybody was doing. Rome had just started the first of the three Punic wars in 264. Fifteen years after the Kalinga march, King Zheng came to power and by 221 had unified China. The Ptolemies had made Egypt the principal naval power of the eastern Mediterranean.

The expedition took a long time before it took a life. Ascertaining the enemy's strength, learning the terrain, working out the logistics, choosing the season — winter, in country that hot, which also suited the elephants.[^77] Pataliputra to Kalinga is some 900 kilometres, and at an army's average of about twenty a day it took five or six weeks just to arrive.

Then his own account of what he did there. **One hundred and fifty thousand deported, one hundred thousand slain, and many times as many who died**.[^78]

And the edict does not stop at the soldiers. It names the Brahmanas and Sramanas and other sects and householders living there, among whom obedience to those who receive high pay, obedience to mother and father, obedience to elders, proper courtesy to friends and acquaintances and companions and relatives, to slaves and servants, and firm devotion are practised — and says that to these happened injury or slaughter or deportation of their beloved ones.[^79] It goes on to the people who were not there: friends and relatives whose affection is undiminished, themselves well provided for, on whom the misfortune of others falls as an injury. It says this is shared by all men and is considered deplorable, and that even the hundredth or the thousandth part of what was done at Kalinga would now be very deplorable.

What makes it unlike anything else is not the sentiment. It is that this is the only surviving contemporary narrative of the catastrophe, from an age when such narratives almost never survive — the works of the men who marched with Alexander are gone.[^80]

**A king in that century, on that day, was supposed to swagger**. Kharavela of Kalinga had his own accomplishments cut in verse. Later rulers listed every territory they had valorously gained, from Sindhu-Sauvira to Saurashtra and Aparanta.[^81] The one and only account Ashoka left of a successful war turns state propaganda upside down. The triumph is recorded as a disaster, and he had it carved on stone, where it could not be taken back.

*Read: lines 1019–1139.*

# Below the Line

*Everything from here down is speculative by design. Above the line, every claim carries a footnote and a line range. Below it, the writing is allowed to weigh alternatives, run counterfactuals and hand the decision to advisors from other traditions — because that is the job of these sections*.

## Ch. 3 — Roads Not Taken `[SPECULATIVE]`

**A live alternative, visible in the ground**. Taxila's planners had a straight main street two hundred years old and a manual telling them how a city ought to be laid out, and they cut crooked lanes anyway. The alternative was open and somebody chose against it: clear the houses, condemn the land, run the grid. What stopped them was householders who would not sell, and the chapter reads the result as a citizen-friendly compromise.

**A constructed alternative**. Suppose they had forced it through. The gain is drainage — a grid can be given a main drain and a fall, and First Street stops being a river every monsoon. The loss is that a frontier city already rebellious enough to need a prince sent to it acquires a fresh grievance about property, in the decade before it rebels again and Susima has to be sent. The forecast is that the streets get straighter and the city gets angrier, and given how much of the empire's lapis and tin and silver came down that road, the trade was worth more than the drains.

## Ch. 4 — Counsel From Elsewhere `[SPECULATIVE]`

Take Bindusara's decision to post a disliked son two thousand kilometres away to a turbulent frontier, and then a thousand kilometres away to a rich province, for ten years.

**An advisor working from [[ARCHIVES/concepts/behavioral-mechanics/shih-and-strategic-depth|shih]]** — advantage accumulated in position before it is ever used — would say the father built his rival's power for him and called it exile. Ten years running Avanti is ten years of revenue, ten years of an administrative following, and a marriage into the merchant class of a trading city. The heir apparent stayed at court, where his experience of governing was watching it.

**An advisor working from [[ARCHIVES/concepts/behavioral-mechanics/indirect-agency-deniable-power|deniable power]]** would look at who actually decided the succession and find that it was not either prince. It was a minister with a slapped head, moving five hundred colleagues with a prophecy. The son at the frontier was reachable by that faction and useful to it precisely because he owed them; the son at court was the one who had humiliated them.

The two converge on the same reading from unrelated doctrine: **removing a man from the capital removed him from the one danger that killed his rivals, and left him everything he needed to come back with**. Neither advisor treats the posting as a punishment, which is how the chapter's sources present it.

## Ch. 5 — Roads Not Taken `[SPECULATIVE]`

**A live alternative, and it is the whole convention of the age**. Every ruler in that century recorded a victory as a victory. Kharavela did. The later Indian kings listing Sindhu-Sauvira and Saurashtra and Aparanta did. The Achaemenid inscriptions spend their superlatives on foes killed and conquered. Ashoka had a hundred thousand dead and a conquered seaboard, and the ordinary course was open, cheap and expected.

**A constructed alternative**. Suppose the Kalinga edict had been written the normal way — the territories gained, the enemy broken, the emperor magnified. He keeps the province, which he keeps anyway. He loses the thing that makes him legible 2,200 years later, because a boast is exactly the kind of document that does not survive when its dynasty falls. The forecast, and it is a forecast: the Mauryas end in the same century either way, and without the confession Ashoka becomes the eleventh faceless name in a Puranic list — recoverable by archaeologists as a ruler, not as a person. **The book's own opening problem is that every king before him is faceless. This is the decision that got him out of that category, and it is not clear he could have known that**.

## Ch. 5 — What Transfers `[SPECULATIVE]`

**Decision type: publishing against your own interest, permanently**.

The mechanism is the medium, not the mood. Plenty of rulers have felt remorse. What is unusual here is the combination of admitting the cost of a victory, doing it in the first person, doing it in the places where the governed actually lived rather than at court, and doing it in a form nobody can quietly withdraw. Stone in a village is not retractable. Multiple copies across a subcontinent are not retractable either.

**Scope conditions**. This works where the admission is made from unquestioned strength, and where the audience cannot use it to remove you — he confessed after winning, holding the province, with no rival left alive. It fails where the confession is made from weakness, because then it is not a moral position but an invitation, and it fails where the medium is retractable, because a statement that can be walked back gets read as positioning rather than as commitment. The cost is the point: **an admission is only load-carrying when undoing it is impossible**.

**Modern equivalent:** a signed public post-mortem naming your own failure, versus an internal one. Same content, different instrument, and only one of them changes what anybody expects of you afterwards.

---

## Evidence

Read from `RAW/books/Ashoka in Ancient India.md`, lines 242–1139: Prelude (242–415), ch. 1 (416–554), ch. 2 (555–718), ch. 3 (719–883), ch. 4 (884–1018), ch. 5 (1019–1139).

**Hagiography check, and this book runs it on itself**. Nearly everything about Ashoka's youth comes from the *Ashokavadana* and the Sri Lankan chronicles, written between four hundred and twelve hundred years after his death, by writers with a religion to advance. Lahiri says so at every turn rather than at the start only, and separates the parts that check out — Rajagriha and Pataliputra in the right order, the correct capital in the right century — from the parts that do not. Where she reaches her own view against the sources she marks it as hers: that the transformation was not spiritual, and that the Taxilans' goddesses probably meant more to them than their emperor's stupa.

**Where the source pushes hardest**. The book's admiration is open, and the sharpest line in these five chapters is the aside calling conquest and empire-building male megalomania of a revolting form. That is the author's position and it is reported here as hers.

**Bounded absence**. No claim is made about material outside lines 242–1139. The *Arthashastra* is used throughout as a contemporary manual and its own date and authorship are disputed, which the chapters state.

# What a Mauryan King Took For Granted — Chapters 6–9

> **Chapters 6–9 of Nayanjot Lahiri, *Ashoka in Ancient India*** — the first message sent out to the provinces, the bilingual rock at Kandahar, the long anthology of major edicts, and what each landscape did to the words put into it. Read from `RAW/books/Ashoka in Ancient India.md`. One full archaeology pass per chapter, sweeping all seven dimensions in every run.
