## Ch. 6 — The message read aloud to people required to listen

A little after 260 BCE a communiqué goes out to administrators from the Yamuna flood plain to the hills of Karnataka.[^1] It is short, and it is not about the war. He could not bring himself to mention Kalinga publicly yet. What he sent instead was the personal thing that came after it.

**How anybody heard it has to be guessed at, because nobody in India wrote it down**. There are no references and no reactions to Ashoka's edicts anywhere in the ancient Indian literature of the first millennium BCE.[^2] Not one. So the reconstruction has to come from the places themselves — where the words were cut, what people there were living on, and what a suddenly visible emperor could have meant to them.

The materials a king normally wrote on all rot. Palm leaf, birch bark, cotton cloth, probably wooden boards. Every one of them perishable, and no specimen has ever turned up.[^3] There is a single exception in the whole record. At Sringaverapura near the Ganga, charcoal of birch bark survived from the early first millennium BCE — **and it survived only because it had burnt**.

So the change after Kalinga was not what he said. It was what he said it on. He ordered his promulgations cut into stone in public places, and 2,200 years later several of them are much as they were made.[^4] Rajula Mandagiri in Andhra is on a flat horizontal rock. Maski and Nittur in Karnataka are on vertical faces. Sasaram sits on top of a hill in Bihar. Palkigundu crowns a high ridge you can only reach up a very steep climb.

Where a message goes depends on who it is for, and Mauryan practice already had a form for administrators. Two demi-official plaques of the period, from Mahasthangarh in Bangladesh and Sohgaura in Uttar Pradesh, carry instructions for distributing grain in drought and famine, addressed to the *mahamatras* who ran the towns.[^5] Ashoka's early edicts also address his administrators. **They were not only for them**, which is why the rocks chosen are in places people actually went.

The script was Brahmi and the language a mix of Prakrit dialects. Both were what the officials knew.[^6] Prakrit was not what anyone spoke in Karnataka or Andhra, where these inscriptions are thickest. So for the message to mean anything there, somebody had to translate it into the local language on the spot.

The second innovation is the one that is hard to see now. **Every copy went out in more or less identical form**. In a world with printing that sounds like nothing; in the third century BCE it meant a subject in Afghanistan and a subject in Andhra heard the same sentences in the same voice.[^7] What mattered to him was the sameness.

The people who actually made that happen are almost all invisible. One is not. Three texts in Karnataka are signed by the *lipikara*, the writer-clerk who prepared the exemplar, and his name was Capada.[^8] The three were cut within a few kilometres of each other and the hands are different, so more than one engraver worked on them. And Capada signed his own name in Kharoshthi rather than the Brahmi of the edict itself — a script used up around Gandhara, near the Afghan border, a very long way from Karnataka.

One more engraver shows himself through a quirk. The man who cut the Erragudi edict made part of it run boustrophedon — the lines turning right to left and then left to right, the way ancient Greek writing sometimes does.[^9]

Local officials also made additions, and one of them is why we know his name. He assumed his subjects would recognise him from his titles alone, and most edicts call him only Devanampiya, dear to the gods, or Devanampiya Piyadasi.[^10] At Maski in Karnataka and at Gujarra, the administrators putting up the message added the king's actual name to it.

**And after all the cutting, the delivery was oral**. A designated official read the inscription out, and the people who had gathered at the rock were required to listen.[^11] An inscribed message, disseminated by voice, in a culture where poets addressed audiences of listeners and that was how public speech worked.

Here is what the whole first edict actually says, in the Rupnath version. Two and a half years and somewhat more have passed since he is openly a Shakya. But he had not been very zealous. A year and somewhat more has passed since he visited the Sangha and has been very zealous.[^12]

> Those gods who during that time had been unmingled (with men) in Jambudvipa, have now been made (by me) mingled (with them). For this is the fruit of zeal. And this cannot be reached by (persons) of high rank (alone), (but) even a lowly (person) is able to attain even the great heaven if he is zealous.

Then the instructions. Have it engraved on rocks wherever the occasion presents itself, and on stone pillars where there are stone pillars. Dispatch an officer everywhere, as far as your district extends.[^13] And at the end, a line that tells you where he was standing: this proclamation was issued on tour, 256 nights having then been spent on tour.

What a king was supposed to say is the measure of how strange this is. Kingship was centuries old across his empire, and **a king did not confide the turning points of his life to his people**.[^14] He was warrior, protector and final arbitrator of disputes, and he was meant to look powerful rather than spiritual. This one dropped the grandiloquent titles and called himself beloved of the gods.

The graduated conversion has a Buddhist logic behind it that the chapter draws out. He says the initial adherence did not make him zealous, and that is what a lay convert normally gets — the powerful doctrine is not expounded straight away, on the assumption that a convert who arrives at conviction himself stays zealous longer.[^15] What made the difference, he says, was the Sangha, a year and a half in.

For the Sangha it was an enormous coup. The most powerful man in the region had gone over to a faith the state had largely treated as dissent against the Brahmanical order.[^16] The nearest western parallel is Constantine — and, as with Ashoka, roughly three hundred years after the religion began.

The claim about gods and men is the most Buddhist thing in the edict, and it is not explained. Gods and humans had been unmingled in Jambudvipa and are now mingled.[^17] John Strong reads it as a double utopia, gods and humans together on earth or later in heaven, carrying the resonance of what the Buddha is said to have created. **He does not gloss it, and he glosses so much else** — which suggests he expected the people who mattered to him to already know it.

The second minor edict does something different, and what it leaves out is the point. It lists obedience to parents, liberality, abstention from slaughter, and it invokes *porana pakiti*, ancient tradition, rather than claiming to start anything.[^18] Nothing in it is specifically Buddhist. Olivelle notices what is missing: there is silence on theft, murder, adultery and sexual offences, which were exactly what the law codes of the period cared about.

But that message did not travel alone everywhere. At Erragudi, Rajula-Mandagiri and Nittur it arrives sandwiched between stern imperial orders.[^19] The governor should pass orders in the words of the Beloved of the Gods. The *mahamatras* in the cities pass them to the *rajukkas* in the country, who order the people of the countryside.

**So one message becomes two messages depending on which rock you are standing in front of**. In the Chitradurga cluster, without the orders, it reads as loose moral advice rooted in tradition. At Erragudi, wrapped in commands, the same words can be heard as authoritarian — the emperor's private religion arriving in your sacred space as the law of the land.[^20]

And none of it was put up in the cities. Not one of these texts has been found at or near Pataliputra, Vidisha, Ujjayini or Taxila.[^21]

Maski is where you can see what that meant. In the third century BCE this was a sedentary farming settlement that kept cattle and goats.[^22] The houses are gone but the post holes remain, where wooden poles held up thatched roofs. Today it is potsherds scattered under fields of cotton and sunflower.

That is a village until you look at what passed through it. Beads of carnelian, garnet, terracotta and paste; lapis lazuli that probably came from Afghanistan; shell and coral that came up from the coast.[^23] A terracotta cylinder seal with a man driving an elephant. And gold under the ground — the Maski band of the Dharwar series, with old workings all around that show the deposits were being mined long before anybody wrote about them.

The people there had their own way of marking things, and it was not his. Nineteen types of graffiti mark turn up scratched or incised on the pottery — tridents, bows, careless crosses, V shapes, one like an arrowhead.[^24] Elsewhere in the south you can watch such marks give way to Brahmi over time, so some people at Maski may have seen Brahmi signs on goods coming up from further south.

The officials picked the biggest hill they could find and put the edict away from the settlement, under an overhanging ledge on the western side.[^25] Two reasons suggest themselves: the ledge would keep the weather off it, and the spot suited community ritual and local festivals. **Putting a royal message where people already gather for their own reasons is not idiosyncratic. It is the only thing that works**.

Then the chapter says what happened next, and it is the flattest sentence in the book. The Buddhist faith was not part of Maski's sacred landscape, and nothing in the king's message showed any awareness of what Maski already worshipped.[^26] No Buddhist stupa was ever built there, in his lifetime or afterwards. The people went on believing in the deities that had always protected them in life and death. **The emperor's strange message was read, heard, and ignored**.

Elsewhere the anxiety to be heard runs the other way. At Chitradurga the same message was cut in three places within a few kilometres — Brahmagiri, Siddapura and Jatinga-Rameshwara.[^27] It came from Suvarnagiri, the provincial capital, at the word of the *aryaputra*, a prince who may have been Ashoka's son, and of the *mahamatras* there, to the *mahamatras* of Isila, who must be wished good health.

At Brahmagiri, as at Maski, the rock sits at the edge of the settlement rather than in it — a place the people of Isila would pass, near a seasonal watercourse.[^28] Two millennia later that boulder was called *akshara gundu*, the letter rock, and washing it with water was held to give the water medicinal power. Siddapura's low hills were known as *Yenamana timmayyana gundlu*, the buffalo-herd Timmayya's rocks.

Jatinga-Rameshwara is the one that shows what they were prepared to do. The engravers did not use the base of the hill. **They carved it on the summit** — a climb made easy today by some seven hundred steps and steep and strenuous then.[^29] Nobody carries an important royal message up a hill nobody visits, so people were going up there for their own reasons. The hilltop is now tied to Jatayu, the bird that fell trying to rescue Sita, and there is a pond up there with human footprints in the rock around it, some of them called *Sita pada*.

What happened to that hill afterwards is the chapter's own irony and it does not press it. By the time the edict was found in the late nineteenth century, the rock was called *balegara-gundu*, the bangle-sellers' rock, and it had holes punched in it to hold the posts of a tent put up for the annual fair.[^30]

Panguraria in Central India is different again, because the audience was already converted. It is a forested tract of rock shelters, with paintings of animals and monkeys and hunters made many centuries before him, in the same line of shelters where his message is cut.[^31] Stupas of dressed stone are spread across the hillside. That pairing is everywhere in Central India — Talpura has the same, and at Sanchi a line of rock shelters with prehistoric painting runs along the old road to Vidisha.

Two things here happen nowhere else. He addresses the local governor directly, a *kumara* called Samva — royal family, but not a son.[^32] And he says where he is writing from: on his march to the Upunita-vihara in Manema-desha. **That is the only glimpse anybody gets of where the 256 nights were taking him**, and it was a Buddhist monastery.

*Read: lines 1140–1471.*

---

## Ch. 7 — Two foreign languages on a rock outside Kandahar

Around 259 BCE a message goes up outside the subcontinent altogether. It is at Kandahar, on an east-facing outcrop of the Kaitul massif, close to the road to Girishk and Herat that traders used constantly.[^33] Anybody passing would have noticed men preparing a trapezoidal panel on the rock.

The place had been somebody's province for centuries before it was his. The Achaemenids made central-south Afghanistan a province in the sixth century BCE and Kandahar their bastion, and from then on the administration ran in Aramaic thick with local Iranian terms.[^34] The province was called Arachosia and it was worth fighting over. Then Seleucus failed to hold it and made peace with Chandragupta — ceding Gandhara, Arachosia and Paropamisadae in exchange for 500 elephants and a female relative for a marriage alliance.

**So the edict is in Greek and Aramaic, and neither is an Indian language**. Everything else he sent out that year was Prakrit in Brahmi.[^35] Here he used what the local administration already worked in, which is the whole explanation — a pragmatic decision that took the trouble out of getting the thing understood.

There were Greek speakers there to read it. A Greek inscription found a few hundred yards from the bilingual rock, on a statue base, names a man who describes himself as the son of Aristonax.[^36] Aramaic had been the working script of officialdom across the Near East, from Assyria to north-west India and into Egypt and Asia Minor.

What he says to them is a different man talking. Ten years of reign completed, king Piodasses made known the doctrine of Piety to men — and from this moment he has made men more pious, and everything thrives throughout the whole world.[^37] The king abstains from killing living beings, and other men and the king's own huntsmen and fishermen have stopped hunting.

**There is no confession in it at all**. No metamorphosis, no personal experience, no reason given for the mission, no Buddhist convert, and none of the moral demands he made of administrators and subjects at home.[^38] It is a summary of spiritual success, delivered by a man who has already finished converting people.

The Greek is not the Greek of a stranded garrison. Paul Bernard says it does not read as a language languishing in exile and barbarised by misuse — no hybridisation, no dilution, alive to contemporary usage, at home with the vocabulary of philosophers and of politics.[^39] The translator found *eusebeia*, piety, for *dhamma*, and *diatribe*, a school of philosophy, for *pasamda*, a sect. Mortimer Wheeler concluded there was a full-blown Alexandria at old Kandahar — writers, philosophers, teachers, not a tired vestige of an army that passed through.

And then the words do not quite fit, which is what makes the rock interesting. *Eusebeia* means piety, and *dhamma* is not piety.[^40] It was the closest thing available in a language with no word for the idea.

The Aramaic below it is not a translation of the Greek either. Line by line the two do not correspond.[^41] In Greek the king makes known his doctrine of piety; in Aramaic he **promoted Truth**, *qshyt*. In Greek the king abstains from killing living beings; in Aramaic, for the feeding of our Lord the king, little is killed.

That second difference is the whole problem of governing at a distance, sitting on one rock in two scripts. **One version says the king has stopped. The other says the king's kitchen has cut back**.

Who decided that is the question the chapter puts and does not settle. Did an exemplar come from Pataliputra, or were the translators left largely free?[^42] What it does say is that a frontier is not a passive provider for a capital. It is where real people live, with their own languages and their own everyday spirituality, and their own resistance to whatever arrives from outside.

What people there actually ate is the last thing in the chapter, and it is put in on purpose. Afghan food is rich in carnivorous delights — mutton, the head and feet of sheep, chicken, skewered meat, hot mutton stock, dried meat.[^43] Hunting gazelle, markhor, ibex, quail, pigeon and partridge, and eating fish. The bones bear it out: domesticated sheep and goats and cattle in neolithic contexts, and at Mundigak 55 km north of Kandahar, ass and horse and dog alongside ibex, lynx and gazelle from the second millennium BCE.

**So the message is larger than anything the emperor intended, and the chapter means that as a limit rather than a compliment**. What a king said did not always define, or even much influence, the tenor of daily life. The populace will have found some of these exhortations most peculiar, and taken them with a large pinch of salt.[^44]

*Read: lines 1472–1599.*

---

## Ch. 8 — A hundred lines instead of twenty

The short messages were six to twenty-two lines. What comes next runs to more than a hundred, across several rock surfaces at a time.[^45] These are the major rock edicts, and they are a different instrument: longer, more elaborate, and mixing personal material with political practice at a length nobody had attempted.

They are at Erragudi in Andhra, Girnar in Gujarat, Shahbazgarhi and Mansehra in north-west Pakistan, Kandahar, Kalsi in Uttarakhand, and at Dhauli and Jaugada in Orissa.[^46] Some have not lasted. Sopara in Maharashtra has fragments of three. Sannathi in Karnataka has four.

The career he lays out in them has dates on it. Kalinga around 261/260 BCE, in his eighth year, and it is the only conquest mentioned anywhere in the whole corpus.[^47] Then the tenth year, a pilgrimage to Mahabodhi, and the start of what he calls the second part of his reign.

**And the touring changed name and purpose**. A *vihara yatra* was a royal pleasure tour, and hunting was what it was for.[^48] The *Mahabharata* has one, and the invitation reads: this also is an excellent season for thy son to go a-hunting. What he did instead were *dhamma yatras* — visiting Shramanas and Brahmanas and making gifts, visiting the aged and supporting them with gold, visiting the people of the country.

By 257/256 BCE the officials were carrying it too. The *rajukkas* and *pradeshikas* were ordered to add an inspection circuit every five years, on top of their ordinary duties, and preach.[^49] The content is four lines and every clause is a plain one:

> Meritorious is obedience to mother and father. Meritorious is liberality to friends, acquaintances and relatives and to Shramanas and Brahmanas. Meritorious is abstention from the slaughter of living beings. Meritorious is to spend little (and) to store little.

There is a deviation in that list worth having. *Shramanas* are ascetic renunciants, including but not limited to Buddhist monks.[^50] He names Brahmanas alongside them, every time, in a formula he keeps repeating.

In his twelfth year he announced that it had worked. For many hundreds of years slaughter of lives, cruelty to living creatures, and disrespect to relatives and to Shramanas and Brahmanas had increased.[^51] Now the reverse had increased, to a degree not achievable for many hundreds of years in the past. **Whether anybody believed him is the chapter's own question, and it answers it with a comparison**. Modern governments with far better communications and far more effective coercion have not managed simultaneous social transformation across the regions of India.

Then he tried to bolt it to the future. His sons, grandsons and great-grandsons will promote this practice of Dharma till the time of universal destruction.[^52] It became a standard formula in later inscriptions and he is the first to use it. To listeners in the third century BCE, familiar with sons who murdered fathers for thrones, it must have sounded like exactly what it was.

In the thirteenth year he built an institution for it. A new and very senior class of officials, the *dharma-mahamatras*, spread across his dominions.[^53] Their brief was to work out, among the adherents of Dharma, whether a person is only inclined towards Dharma, or is fully established in it, or is merely given to charity.

**And he made himself permanently interruptible**. Formerly there was no transaction of state business and no reporting at all hours. So he made an arrangement:[^54]

> The reporters should report to me the affairs of the people at any time and place, whether I am engaged in eating (or) am in the harem (or) in the bed-chamber (or) on a promenade (or) in a carriage (or) on the march.

The *Arthashastra* had wanted that too, and the difference is where it happens. The manual has the king always active, hearing urgent matters, never putting them off — and it designates places for public interaction, with audiences held in the assembly hall.[^55] The manual's other line runs even closer: in the happiness of the subjects lies the happiness of the king, and what is dear to himself is not beneficial to the king, but what is dear to the subjects is. The likeliest reading is not coincidence. A ruler in Pataliputra was very unlikely not to know that work at least by repute.

How the anthology got onto the rocks varies from place to place, and the variation is visible in the letter sizes. At Kalsi one part of a fine-grained rock was polished and the first nine edicts cut into it in very small letters, with the rest below in different lettering.[^56] Shahbazgarhi used more than one rock and Kharoshthi rather than Brahmi: the first eleven on the east face up a hill, the next on a separate boulder at the foot, and the last two on the west face. Mansehra copies that pattern.

Girnar is the exception and it looks like one. Thirty metres of a granite boulder carries all fourteen, in uniform writing, in neat columns, each edict divided from the next by straight lines with the compartments still clearly visible.[^57] **That is a single order carried out at once, by somebody who had the whole set in hand**.

At Erragudi he is called a king for the first time, added to the old title.[^58] And this king opens not with what he has built but with what he wants stopped:

> Here no living being should be slaughtered for sacrifice. And also no festive gathering should be held. For the Beloved of the Gods sees manifold evil in festive gatherings.

**That lands in a world where killing animals for the gods was how the gods were fed**. The megaliths of the Karnataka–Andhra belt put animal parts in with the human dead. In Hindu practice goats, oxen, rams and horses were common offerings, and the *Mahabharata* says animals killed in sacrifice with Vedic mantras went to heaven.[^59]

He knew it would sting, which is probably why the prohibition comes with his own kitchen attached. Many hundred thousands of living beings were formerly slaughtered every day in the king's kitchen for the sake of curry, and now, as this record is written, only three creatures are killed.[^60]

The rhetoric is built for the ear. Where war drums had sounded he was now sounding morality — *bherighoso aho dhammaghoso*, the drum of battle become the drum of dhamma.[^61] And "formerly, in the ages gone by" comes round and round through the edicts for effect.

The seventh edict wants all religious sects to live everywhere in his dominions. The twelfth goes much further, and it is not a request for people to leave each other alone:[^62]

> restraint in regard to speech, (which means) that there should be no extolment of one's own sect or disparagement of other sects on inappropriate occasions… Truly, if (a person) extols his own sect and disparages other sects with a view to glorifying his own sect owing merely to his attachment (to it, he) injures his own sect very severely by acting in that way.

**Praising your own religion loudly is described as damage to your own religion**. The tolerance being asked for is not cordial disregard. It is active concord, and he backs it with gifts and honours to men of all religious communities, ascetics and householders alike — given, he says, so that dhamma may grow among them.[^63]

The same anthology is far less patient about ceremonies. The ninth edict lists the rites he thinks superficial: the auspicious ceremony at an illness, at a wedding, at a birth.[^64] Which is a man telling people how to run the days of their own lives, and it sits a few boulders from the plea for tolerance.

The thirteenth is where he finally writes Kalinga down, and then does something else with it. He lists who has been conquered by dhamma instead — the Yavana king Antiyoka six hundred *yojanas* away, and beyond him Tulamaya, Antikeni, Maka and Alikasudara, and southwards the Cholas and Pandyas.[^65] Those were powerful independent rulers. **Announcing your sway over people you have not fought is still announcing your sway**, and some of them were states an expanding Mauryan empire had had designs on.

The limits get stated in the same edict, which is the honest part of it. The forest peoples are told plainly that pacification has not been ruled out.[^66] The *Arthashastra* is blunt about why: the Atavika, living in their own territory, are many and brave, fight openly, and seize and ruin. And the instruction to his successors is written for men he expects to disobey it — he asks that they not think of fresh conquests, and then, accepting that they will, asks that if they do conquer they take pleasure in patience and light punishment.

He even explains why some versions are long. Some topics have been repeated over and over again owing to their sweetness, so that people may act accordingly.[^67]

**And the last point of the chapter is about what he did not do**. Kings coined themselves — the Indo-Greek rulers put their names on coins in Greek and Prakrit. Others had themselves sculpted; the Kushanas were fond of it.[^68] There is no imperial portrait of Ashoka on a coin or in stone, and no courtly structure anybody can point to. The artefact that is indisputably his is the epigraph, and the empire has to be seen through those.

*Read: lines 1600–1833.*

## Ch. 9 — The same words, four different places

A British army antiquarian looks at Girnar before anybody can read it. James Tod called it the noblest monument of Saurashtra, speaking in an unknown tongue of other times — a huge hemispherical mass of dark granite protruding through the crust of mother earth like a wart, without fissure or inequality, which by the aid of the iron pen **had been converted into a book**.[^69]

He could not read a word of it and he had the shape of the thing exactly right. It is monument and inscription at once, an ancient rock made into a monument by the writing put on it.

The layout there had a practical consequence. All fourteen edicts on one compact face means an official on a platform could stand at eye level with them and read down to a crowd below.[^70] At Erragudi that is impossible — the edicts are spread across boulders at different heights, so nobody could have read the set aloud in one go.

What was around that rock is known only because somebody wrote it down 350 years later. Rudradaman's inscription records that the dam at Junagadh was built by Vaisya Pushyagupta, a provincial governor of Chandragupta, and that conduits were added to it by the Yavana king Tushaspha, who governed the province under Ashoka.[^71] **One of Ashoka's provincial governors shared his ethnicity with the Yavana rulers on the empire's north-western border**, and no Mauryan record says so.

The dam was found in the nineteenth century by a local official. Khan Bahadur Ardeseer Jamsedjee, Naib Diwan of the princely state, traced blocks of masonry running across the river from the north bank to the easternmost spur of the Uparkot rocks, with a breach thirty-six yards long.[^72] The lake behind it would have covered some 140 acres. In the Dharagir garden he found labourers digging out huge stone blocks forming a hollow pavement running north from the bank — the remains, most likely, of the conduits Rudradaman credits to Ashoka.

Why the water mattered is a matter of geology rather than piety. Wells in city areas have to go very deep, and the medieval *vavas* at Junagadh do — the Adi-Chadi Vava drops forty-one metres.[^73] **Wells that deep were not dug in Mauryan times**. Taxila is the parallel: the Bhir plateau stood too high to dig for water, so the city drank from a rivulet outside it. A dam and a lake are what a Mauryan administration could actually build.

And Girnar is missing something the poorer sites have. The whole set is there and the personal Buddhist declaration is not.[^74] The chapter's answer is that it did not need the rock space, because the landscape already said it. The Bhoria stupa stands on a knoll seven kilometres east of the city, a solid brick structure like the Mauryan stupas at Vaishali and Sarnath, and it gave up relic boxes of copper, silver and gold.

Large burnt brick keeps turning up around those hills — at Surajkund, in the Hasnapur dam area, at other spots in the forest.[^75] Put the sites on the topography and they begin to make sense as a circuit. **Girnar was a Buddhist landscape long before it was famous as a Jaina and Hindu one**, and the provincial capital would have been what supported the circuit.

Sannathi in Karnataka shows the reverse problem — a message whose place is lost. The edicts there are on a free-standing slab inscribed on both sides, and it was not found where it stood.[^76] It turned up serving as the pedestal of the idol of Kalikamba in the Chandralamba temple.

Two of the edicts on it had been known only from Dhauli and Jaugada in Orissa, which had made them look like something written specially for Kalinga.[^77] They were not. And the big habitational mound at Sannathi is named Ranamandala, which suggests a battlefield — on which somebody has built a case that the Mauryas conquered the region here. **Nothing in the emperor's own message anywhere refers to any such conquest**, which the chapter says is not enough evidence.

Orissa is where the editing is clearest, because the edicts there survive well. Three of the fourteen were left out at Dhauli and Jaugada: number 11, restating his idea of dhamma; number 12, the great statement on tolerance; and number 13, the account of the Kalinga conquest in full detail.[^78] Two new ones were put in instead.

The omission of the Kalinga edict in Kalinga is the one that explains itself. Only a few years had passed, and he was not going to rub salt into those wounds.[^79] At Dhauli they made a monument of it: a space specially cut for the edicts, and above them, on a terrace, an elephant hewn out of the solid rock.

The Separate Edicts speak to the officials at Tosali and Samapa by name, and they open with a sentence that is not about religion at all.[^80]

> All men are my children. As on behalf of (my own) children I desire that they may be provided by me with all welfare and happiness in this world and in the other world, even so is my desire for all men.

The officials are told to make people learn that the king is to them like a father. **And the chapter puts the obvious question: why here?** Nobody in Gujarat or the north-west was told this.[^81] The likeliest reason is that a newly conquered people were being handled roughly by Mauryan officials, and he knew it.

The borderers get the same treatment and a franker admission underneath it. It might occur to my unconquered borderers to ask what the king desires with reference to us.[^82] The answer: that they may not be afraid of me, but may have confidence in me; that they may obtain only happiness from me, not misery; that the king will forgive them what can be forgiven. **People who had just watched him go through Kalinga had every reason to think they were next**, and the edict is a man arguing against his own reputation.

Then the practical part, which is about judges. The passage is worth having whole, because it describes a specific failure rather than a virtue:[^83]

> It happens in the administration (of justice) that a single person suffers either imprisonment or harsh treatment. In this case (an order) cancelling the imprisonment is obtained by him accidentally, while (many) other people continue to suffer. In this case you must strive to deal (with all of them) impartially.

And then the list of what stops an official doing that: **envy, anger, cruelty, hurry, want of practice, laziness, and fatigue**. The root of all of it, he says, is the absence of anger and the avoidance of hurry. A man fatigued in the administration of justice will not rise, and one ought to move, to walk, and to advance.

The consequences are put in the only currency that reaches an official. Fail and there is neither attainment of heaven nor satisfaction of the king.[^84] Do it and they discharge the debt he owes — the debt to living beings he had claimed as his own in the Sixth Edict, now handed to the men who actually decide cases.

He also fixed the reading schedule and set a supervisor over it. The edict must be listened to on every day of the constellation Tishya, and by individuals on other occasions in between.[^85] Every five years a *mahamatra* of suitable character — neither harsh nor fierce, but of gentle actions — was to come and check whether the judicial officers had done what they were told. The same scrutiny was ordered at Ujjayini and at Takshashila.

**So the parts of the anthology that landed in the province he had wrecked are not about dhamma at all**. They are about running a court properly in a politically dangerous place.[^86] The message changes with the ground it is standing on, and the chapter's whole point is that the fixity of stone makes it look as though it never did.

*Read: lines 1834–2050.*

# Below the Line

*Everything from here down is speculative by design. Above the line, every claim carries a footnote and a line range. Below it, the writing is allowed to weigh alternatives, run counterfactuals and hand the decision to advisors from other traditions — because that is the job of these sections*.

## Ch. 6 — Roads Not Taken `[SPECULATIVE]`

**A live alternative, and the empire was already using it**. The Mahasthangarh and Sohgaura plaques show the working method for reaching officials: a portable inscribed plaque, addressed to *mahamatras*, carrying an instruction about grain in famine. That is administration, and it stays inside the administration. The whole existing machinery of palm leaf and birch bark was built for exactly that.

**A constructed alternative**. Suppose the post-Kalinga message had gone out that way — perishable, to officials, unpublished. He keeps the policy and loses the audience. The forecast is that dhamma becomes a directive rather than a confession, the *rajukkas* enforce it as they enforce everything else, and it dies with the dynasty because nothing carries it. What actually makes the difference is not the sentiment but the surface: **birch bark survived at exactly one site in India, and only because it burned**. He picked the medium that outlasts the state that issues it, and nobody had done that with a personal statement before.

## Ch. 7 — Counsel From Elsewhere `[SPECULATIVE]`

Take the Kandahar rock, where the Greek says the king abstains from killing and the Aramaic says that for the feeding of our Lord the king, little is killed.

**A Stoic advisor**, working from [[ARCHIVES/concepts/history/stoic-dichotomy-of-control|the dichotomy of control]], would find the emperor on the wrong side of his own line. What a man eats is inside his power. What a translator three thousand kilometres away writes on a rock is not. Issuing an absolute claim about your own conduct into a language you cannot read is handing the strongest thing you have — the truth of the statement — to a stranger.

**An advisor working from [[ARCHIVES/concepts/behavioral-mechanics/indirect-agency-deniable-power|deniable power]]** reads the same rock as competent rather than careless. Two texts, one stone, and the softer version sits in the language of the working administration. That is how an empire says an absolute thing in the capital's voice and a survivable thing in the province's. Whether he intended it or not, the effect is that nobody in Kandahar had to be caught out.

**They split, and the split is the useful part**. One says the discrepancy is the cost of governing what you cannot inspect. The other says it is the mechanism by which governing at that distance is possible at all. The book does not choose between them either, and says outright that it does not know whether an exemplar came from the king or the translators were left free.

## Ch. 8 — What Transfers `[SPECULATIVE]`

**Decision type: making a rule apply to yourself first, in public, before you impose it**.

The kitchen line is the mechanism. He bans killing animals for sacrifice — in a world where that is how gods get fed — and in the same edict publishes the count from his own kitchen: hundreds of thousands formerly, three now. The order and the placement are the whole technique. Not a rule with an exemption, and not a rule followed quietly by its author. A rule whose author's own compliance is inscribed on the same rock, in a number anybody can hold him to.

**Scope conditions**. It works where the author's compliance is checkable and costly, and where the rule touches something the audience will resent — the resentment is what the self-inclusion is spending itself against. It fails where compliance is cheap for the author and expensive for everyone else, because then publishing it reads as a taunt. And it fails where the number cannot be verified: three creatures a day in a palace kitchen a thousand kilometres away is not, in fact, checkable, which is why the technique is stronger as rhetoric than as evidence.

**Modern equivalent:** the executive who takes the pay cut first and says the figure, versus the one who announces the freeze. Same policy, and only one of them can be argued with on the numbers.

## Ch. 9 — Roads Not Taken `[SPECULATIVE]`

**A live alternative, and this one was actually taken**. At Dhauli and Jaugada three edicts were dropped and two written specially. The default — the thing done at Girnar, at Erragudi, at Kalsi — was to publish the anthology. In the province he had destroyed, somebody decided against publishing the account of destroying it.

**A constructed alternative**. Suppose the thirteenth edict had gone up at Dhauli with the rest. A hundred thousand dead, told to the survivors, on a rock beside the river, read aloud by an official on the day of Tishya. It is possible to argue that this would have been the more honest course and it is not obvious it would have been the better one: the Separate Edicts that went there instead are about judges who imprison people arbitrarily, which is the grievance the province actually had that year. The forecast is that publishing the confession there buys nothing a wounded population wants, and spends the credibility needed for the thing that might have helped. **Confession travels well to people who were not the victims**. The book has him omitting it precisely where it would have been heard by them, and that is a choice about audience rather than about conscience.

## Ch. 9 — What Transfers `[SPECULATIVE]`

**Decision type: writing one document to be read in many places you will never see**.

The pattern the chapter recovers is that fixity of medium creates an illusion of fixity of meaning. The same sentences cut on the same kind of rock in Karnataka, Gujarat, Afghanistan and Orissa were four different messages, because a message is finished by the place it lands in. At Maski it was parachuted into a landscape whose gods it did not mention, and it was ignored. At Panguraria the audience was a monastery that already agreed. At Kandahar it was translated into two languages that had no word for its central idea. In Kalinga the parts about dhamma were removed and replaced with instructions about judges.

**Scope conditions**. Local adaptation of this kind holds together only while the centre is willing to let the edges edit — and it collapses in the other direction too. Where the centre insists on literal uniformity, the message goes unread in places whose concerns it never touched; where the edges edit freely, the sender loses any idea of what was actually said in his name. The Mauryan settlement sat in the middle: identical core, local additions, local omissions, and a five-yearly inspection to check the officials rather than the text.

**Modern equivalent:** any policy issued centrally and executed in dozens of jurisdictions. The document is the same everywhere and the thing that happens is different everywhere, and the illusion that the document settles it is created by the document being the only artefact that survives.

## Evidence

Read from `RAW/books/Ashoka in Ancient India.md`, lines 1140–2050: ch. 6 (1140–1471), ch. 7 (1472–1599), ch. 8 (1600–1833), ch. 9 (1834–2050).

**How the argument is built, and where it is honest about being conjecture**. The core reconstruction — how the edicts were received — rests on the fact that no ancient Indian text of the first millennium BCE mentions them at all. The book says so at the start of ch. 6 and then reasons from the archaeology of each site instead. Where a reading is a guess, it is usually marked as one: the Maski ledge, the choice of the Jatinga-Rameshwara summit, and the reason the Separate Edicts went to Kalinga are all flagged in the source as hunches or possibilities.

**The strongest claims here and their basis**. The Junagadh dam is known only from an inscription of Rudradaman cut some 350 years later, and everything about Mauryan governance in Gujarat that follows from it inherits that distance. The Sannathi conquest theory rests on a mound's name, which the chapter rejects as insufficient.

**Where the book pushes back on its own subject**. The chapter on the minor edicts ends with a message read, heard and ignored, and the Afghanistan chapter ends with exhortations taken with a large pinch of salt. Both are the author's judgements and are reported here as hers.

**Bounded absence**. No claim is made about material outside lines 1140–2050.

# What a Mauryan King Took For Granted — Chapters 10–12 and the Epilogue

> **Chapters 10–12 and the Epilogue of Nayanjot Lahiri, *Ashoka in Ancient India*** — the caves and pillars he built, the animal edict of an old man, the queen and the half fruit at the end, and seventeen centuries of being remembered for the wrong things. Read from `RAW/books/Ashoka in Ancient India.md`. One full archaeology pass per chapter, sweeping all seven dimensions in every run.
>
> **Siblings:** [[LAB/Worldview Reports/lahiri-ashoka-worldview-archaeology-part-1|Part 1 — Prelude and Chapters 1–5]] · [[LAB/Worldview Reports/lahiri-ashoka-worldview-archaeology-part-2|Part 2 — Chapters 6–9]] · [[LAB/Worldview Reports/lahiri-ashoka-worldview-archaeology-synthesis|What Runs Through All of It]]. ## Ch. 10 — Caves cut for a religion that was not his

In 257/256 BCE he had caves dug for somebody else's ascetics. That is the same year he was issuing rescripts about proper courtesy to Shramanas and Brahmanas, and the caves are what those rescripts look like in granite.[^1] Barabar is the highest hill of a rocky ridge in Bihar, twenty-four kilometres north of Gaya, a day from Pataliputra, standing up out of flat cultivated plain.

There are four of them, and the names on them now are not the names he used. The Sudama cave was **Nigoha Kubha, the Banyan cave**, which is what his own short donative inscription there calls it.[^2] Two chambers, both polished to a lustre: a rectangular outer one with a vaulted roof, and an inner one, circular in plan with a hemispherical ceiling, imitating a thatched hut.

That imitation is the design idea. The caves have inclining walls and rounded roofs and they copy humble wooden and bamboo dwellings — **the sort of hut an ascetic would actually be comfortable in, reproduced in solid granite at enormous cost**.[^3] Karna Chaupar, cut seven years after the others and nineteen years after his coronation, was made as a shelter against rain.

You can still watch how they were made, because the finishing was not perfect everywhere. The tool marks in the Lomasha Rishi cave give the whole sequence.[^4] Chunks of rock came out first with heavy tools, working from bottom to top, the chisel edges between 0.7 and 1.3 centimetres. Then dressing with a lighter chisel into parallel straight grooves. Then pecking, to thin the ridges left by the chisel. Then grinding — the surface rubbed with coarse sand, water and a coarse-grained stone until every mark was gone.

The dimensions were not eyeballed either. They appear to be laid out on a grid using whole multiples of a unit of about 85.5 centimetres, so the interiors are sized to a measure rather than to the rock.[^5]

**Who got them is the point of the chapter**. The Sudama and Vishwa Jhopri caves went to the Ajivikas — the vanished sect, not his own.[^6] Karna Chaupar names no sect at all and could have gone to Ajivikas or to anybody. And the Lomasha Rishi has an architrave with elephants moving towards a stupa, which reads Buddhist.

So one hillside may be housing Buddhists, Ajivikas and unattached ascetics at the same time, at the same king's expense.[^7] That is what the twelfth edict's concord looks like when it stops being a sentence and becomes a building programme.

And here is a whole category of royal record that is simply missing. **Taxes, punishments and land grants were not, in his view, things to put on stone**.[^8] The subjects most emperors keep records about — which province is behind on its taxes, safety on the highways, complaints of harassment — are absent from his corpus entirely.

The building goes where the Buddha's life went. Mahabodhi first, in the tenth year, where the first temple is generally credited to him.[^9] Xuanzang, seven centuries later, says Ashoka walled the Bodhi tree round with stone nearly three metres high. A Burmese record of repairs from the eleventh century says King Dhamma Asoka built a temple on the spot where the Buddha took a meal.

Then the terai, in his twentieth year, on a circuit of three sites close together — Nigali Sagar, Gotihawa and Lumbini.[^10] At Nigali Sagar he had enlarged the stupa of Konakamana six years earlier, and he records that on the visit, along with his worship and the pillar he set up.

Lumbini had been sacred long before he arrived. Under the brick pavements are postholes marking out a sacred space going back to the sixth century BCE or earlier, with root features in the middle of it that the excavators read as a tree shrine.[^11] What he added was a pillar.

The pillars are the technical achievement of the reign and the numbers say why. Monolithic, freestanding, set on base-slabs below ground, admirably polished, tapered for elegance.[^12] They weigh from 8.6 tons at Lumbini to fifty-one tons at Vesali, with capitals of another two tons on top. The stone is Chunar sandstone from the Vindhya hills. **One kind of skill carves them, a second gets them from the quarry to the site, and a third stands them upright** — and the third is the one that is hard to imagine anybody doing.

What that does to a shrine is not neutral. The pillar he raised at Lumbini was monumental enough that it must more or less have eclipsed the original shrine it was honouring.[^13] Memorialisation and a display of political power in the same object, put down at the place where the Buddha was born.

And then somebody else did the same thing to him. In 1312 CE, sixteen hundred years later, a Naga king called Ripu Malla came to Lumbini and had *Om Mani Padme Hum* and his own name cut into Ashoka's pillar.[^14]

Gotihawa shows the other fate. Only a stump of the pillar there is above ground, and it used to be called **Phuteshwar Mahadeva** — worshipped, that is, as a broken Shivalinga.[^15] Its foundation slab carries a plain hill-and-crescent symbol of the kind considered typically Mauryan. The village underneath goes back to the ninth century BCE, and among what came out of it are fragments impressed with straw and reeds, accidentally baked when the huts caught fire.

Vaishali is where his programme is visible as an intervention into somebody else's monument. The stupa there began as mud in about the fifth century BCE — twenty-seven mud layers, each separated from the next by a thin layer of gravel, a little over three and a half metres high and about eight across.[^16] One of the oldest stupas in India, built after the Buddha's death with relics inside it.

Somebody cut into it in the first millennium BCE and took about three-quarters of the relics. What was left in the casket was ash mixed with earth, a punch-marked coin, two glass beads, a conch and a tiny piece of gold.[^17] **The breach is unmistakable and the motive is not** — it could be miscreants in unsettled times, or a rival sect desecrating it. What argues against both is that the casket was carefully put back inside.

Buddhist literature has him opening seven of the eight original relic stupas and redistributing what was in them. This is what that would look like in the ground.

His own capital, by contrast, has almost nothing. No inscribed pillar and no stupa ruin has turned up at Pataliputra.[^18] The one candidate is a pillared hall at Kumrahar in Patna — eighty monolithic pillar bases, fragments with Mauryan polish, a pillared porch reached by steps on wooden platforms. Some think that is where the Buddhist council under Moggaliputta Tissa met, and the chapter says there is no positive indication either way.

At Bairat he stops patronising and starts prescribing. The edict there, taken to Calcutta in the nineteenth century, has him call himself the **Magadha king** — and then give reading instructions to the clergy.[^19] He acknowledges that whatever the Buddha spoke was well spoken, and then names specific expositions he wants many groups of monks and nuns to listen to and reflect on repeatedly.

Sarnath is where that becomes law. The pillar there carries the quadruple lion capital that has been India's national symbol since Independence, and an edict about breaking up the Sangha:[^20]

> But indeed that monk or nun who shall break up the Samgha, should be caused to put on white robes and to reside in a non-residence.

**Putting a monk in white robes is unfrocking him, and the king is the one doing it**. Then comes the distribution, which is pure administration: one copy kept in your office, another deposited with the lay-worshippers, who come every fast-day to be inspired with confidence in it. Every Mahamatra is to attend that service too.[^21] And dispatch an officer with the letter of it as far as your district extends, and into all the territories around forts.

The same edict is at Kaushambi and at Sanchi.[^22] **A king with Buddhist inclinations has become a Buddhist head of government**, disciplining the clergy of a religion whose own texts give him no such authority — and the fact that copies went to every major monastic establishment means the Sangha was in real danger of splitting.

*Read: lines 2051–2296.*

---

## Ch. 11 — Bulls must not be castrated on Tishya

Thirty years into the reign, around 243 BCE, he goes back to speaking to everybody.[^23] Six edicts on pillars, mostly across north India: Lauriya-Araraj, Lauriya-Nandangarh and Rampurva in Bihar, one at Allahabad that probably came from Kaushambi, one near Meerut, one at Topra in Haryana.

The way they were cut says something about the man who ordered them. The fourteen rock edicts had gone out over about four years and been engraved in batches, in different letter sizes, as they arrived.[^24] **The six pillar edicts were not staggered at all**. They were engraved as a single prearranged bunch, from Haryana to Bihar, at around the same time. That is a set assembled by somebody looking back over what he has already done.

Once again he did not put them in the cities. Pataliputra, Hastinapur and Mathura were all bypassed.[^25] Two of the pillars are not even where he left them — Firuz Shah Tughlaq had the Meerut and Topra columns carried to Delhi in the fourteenth century and set up on the Ridge and at Firoz Shah Kotla.

Lauriya-Nandangarh is the only one of these columns still standing entire, and what is around it is not Buddhist. There are mounds, round at the base and conical on top, and they are burial mounds older than the faith.[^26] **The pillar went to a place where people already gathered for rituals and worship, which had nothing to do with him**. Traders and travellers passing would see it.

The routes are the other half of the explanation. N.G. Majumdar traced the pillars in that part of Bihar against the communication lines — one running from Lauriya towards the frontier at Bhikhna Thori, another along the Gandak to Triveni.[^27] The goods prove the routes: lapis lazuli beads from north Afghanistan turn up on one continuous axis from the Swat valley to Burdwan in Bengal, and sea shell from the east coast turns up all through the Gangetic plains.

What he says on them starts as a summary and then breaks into parts. Dhamma is **few sins, many virtuous deeds, compassion, liberality, truthfulness and purity**.[^28] Then the demonstration, in his own person:

> On bipeds and quadrupeds, on birds and aquatic animals various benefits have been conferred by me, (even) to the boon of life.

The third edict turns the list of failings on the ordinary person. Envy, anger, cruelty, hurry, want of practice, laziness and fatigue.[^29] **That is the same list he sent to the judges of Kalinga**, and here it is aimed at everyone, with the instruction to take responsibility for evil deeds as well as virtuous ones.

The fourth is a real change in how the empire is run, and it goes the opposite way from Kalinga. The *rajukkas*, the officials of the countryside, are given functional autonomy.[^30] The *mahamatras* who judged in the cities had been told to be more sensitive and even-handed and had been put under a five-yearly scrutiny. **The country officers get independence and the city officers get inspection**, and the chapter says plainly that the reason is not clear. The result was decentralisation.

Then the animal edict of the twenty-sixth year, which is the strangest document in the corpus and the most specific. He declares a long list of creatures inviolable — parrots, mainas, ruddy geese, wild geese, bats, queen-ants, terrapins, boneless fish, skate-fish, tortoises, porcupines, squirrels, bulls set at liberty, iguanas, the rhinoceros.[^31] Then it stops listing species and starts describing situations:

> Those (she-goats), ewes, sows (which are) either with young or in milk, are inviolable, and also those (of their) young ones (which are) less than six months old. Cocks must not be caponed. Husks containing living animals must not be burnt. Forests must not be burnt uselessly or in order to destroy (living beings). Living animals must not be fed with (other) living animals.

**Then the calendar**. Fish are inviolable and may not be sold on the three Chaturmasis, and on the Tishya full-moon for three days, and on every fast-day.[^32] No castration of bulls, he-goats, rams or boars on the eighth, fourteenth and fifteenth of the fortnight, on Tishya, on Punarvasu, on the three Chaturmasis or on festivals. No branding of horses and bullocks on Tishya, on Punarvasu, on the Chaturmasis.

The list is not random and three specialists have worked on why. Norman finds parallels with Jaina texts and an organised structure — two talking birds, a run of water birds, aquatic animals, legged and legless reptiles, three of the pigeon family.[^33] The zoologist Sunder Lal Hora points out that five of the fish are inedible and not worth killing anyway — sharks, eels, porpoise, skate. **Which is a point about whose table you are picturing**. Tribal and fishing communities may well have eaten anything they caught, and it may be them he is addressing.

And the dates turn out to have biology in them. The closed days for fish fall in the rainy season, July to September, which is when several species breed.[^34] Less obviously, some freshwater fish — carp, hilsa — spawn on a lunar rhythm, with peaks at new moon and full moon. Those are the days he closes.

Two things sit inside that edict at once. A ruler asking people to spare a pregnant or lactating she-goat, and her young under six months, is doing something nobody else in the ancient world is doing.[^35] He is also **accepting that the slaughter goes on**. It is a protection of breeding, not an abolition.

His officials did take it seriously somewhere. An epigraph at Deotek near Nagpur records a lord's command prohibiting the capture and slaughter of animals, with punishments specified for anyone who disobeyed.[^36]

Whether it changed what anybody ate cannot be established, and the chapter is careful about that. At Raja Nala-ka-Tila in Uttar Pradesh nearly 1,600 fragments of animal bone came out of the early historic levels, and fish appear earlier but not in the Mauryan phase.[^37] **The period that shows the drop is longer than his reign**, so nothing about his exhortations follows from it.

The Seventh Pillar Edict is on one pillar only, at Topra, and nobody knows why.[^38] It is the last thing he wrote and it is a review of the whole attempt. Earlier kings had also wanted men to progress by the promotion of morality, and men were not made to progress. So he asks himself the question three times over — how might men be made to conform, how might they be made to progress, how could I elevate them — and answers it:

> I shall use proclamations on morality, (and) shall order instruction in morality (to be given).

**What he concludes, looking back, is that restrictions imposed from above do not work and persuasion does**. That is a man who spent thirty years running an empire on stone messages, saying at the end that the messages were the method and the orders were not.[^39]

*Read: lines 2297–2459.*

---

## Ch. 12 — Half a myrobalan

Then he stops talking. No more messages on rocks and pillars, no more addresses to administrators or to the populace.[^40] The metaphors stop, the idiom stops, the whole effort to tie his own life to his subjects' lives stops. **He went on ruling for about another decade, to around 232 BCE, and never inscribed anything again**. The silence is sudden enough to be the loudest thing in the chapter.

Which puts the story back where it started. Everything about his last years comes from the same chronicles composed centuries later with an interest in deifying him.[^41]

The *Mahavamsa* gives it in six verses and a run of intervals. In the eighteenth year the great Bodhi tree was planted in Sri Lanka. Twelve years later his consort Asamdhimitta died. Four years after that he raised Tissarakkha to queen. Three years after that, in the pride of her beauty, she destroyed the Bodhi tree.[^42]

There is a possible explanation for the silence buried in that arithmetic. Asamdhimitta seems to have died in 241 BCE, **within a year of the Seventh Pillar Edict**.[^43] Grief and private preoccupation would account for a man who had nothing further to say in public.

What the chronicle actually cares about is a contrast between two women. Sanghamitra carries a sapling of the tree to Sri Lanka and protects it; Tissarakkha destroys the tree at home.[^44] The faith prospers on the island and fails in the land of its origin, and the two queens are the figures that carry it. **A wife in this literature is good or bad according to whether she helped or hindered his Buddhism**, which is most of what the tradition preserves about any of them.

His own stone says otherwise about at least one. Karuvaki appears in his epigraphs as a self-possessed, strong-willed consort who wanted an act of philanthropy recorded as hers.[^45]

The northern tradition gives the same villain more room and a stranger motive. In the *Ashokavadana*, Tishyarakshita's jealousy of the Bodhi tree starts because she did not know what Bodhi was.[^46] He gave his most precious jewels to Bodhi, so she took Bodhi for a woman and a rival.

Then Kunala, his son by Padmavati, named after a bird because his eyes were like its eyes, a boy who grew into a prince who liked being alone.[^47] She wanted him and he refused her.

Her cure for the emperor's illness is the most extraordinary passage in these chapters and it is worth having in the source's own words. She tells the doctors to bring her anyone suffering from the same disease. An Abhira man falls ill, his wife goes to a doctor, and the doctor sends the man straight to the queen.[^48]

> She, in secret, had him killed, and when he was dead, she split open his belly…

She finds the worm. Peppercorns do not kill it. Long peppers and ginger do not kill it. Onion kills it at once. Then she goes to the king with the prescription:

> 'Queen', the king objected, 'I am a ksatriya; how can I eat an onion?' 'My lord', she replied, 'this is medicine; take it for the sake of life!'

**He eats the onion and recovers**, and the grateful monarch grants her a boon.[^49] She asks to be monarch for seven days. She uses them to send a letter to the people of Taxila ordering that Kunala's eyes be put out.

The shape of that is the shape of his own youth run again. A son sent to Taxila to deal with a provincial matter, a father falling gravely ill immediately afterwards, and the succession settled by intrigue — by ministers in Bindusara's court then, by the chief queen now.[^50]

The end is quieter and it is about giving. He had been trying to match what the householder Anathapindaka gave the Buddha, a hundred *kotis* of gold, and had reached ninety-six.[^51] Falling ill, he started sending gold to the Kukkutarama monastery to close the gap.

**So his own heir shut off the treasury**. Sampadin, who was Kunala's son, and the state counsellors issued an order forbidding it.[^52] He went round them by giving away the gold dishes his food was served in, then the silver ones, then the copper ones. When they were gone, all he had left was half an *amalaka*, half a myrobalan fruit.

He sent that. He gave it to a man to carry to the monks at Kukkutarama, with the instruction that this last offering be distributed so that it was offered to and enjoyed by the whole community — and half a fruit was mashed into a soup and shared out among them all.[^53] The verse the text puts on it is the sharpest thing in the book:

> A great donor, the lord of men, the eminent Maurya Asoka, has gone from being lord of Jambudvipa to being lord of half a myrobalan.

Then the last flourish, and it is a legal one. His powers are restored to him on the strength of that gift, and he immediately donates the whole earth to the Sangha, keeping back only the treasury.[^54] He seals the document and dies. **A successor could only take the throne after the ministers of the court bought the earth back**, paying four *kotis* of gold to make up his shortfall.

And his stated reason for the gift is not merit and not rebirth. He gives it with faith, he says, in order to obtain something that cannot be stolen, is honoured by the aryas and is safe from all agitation: sovereignty of the mind.[^55]

*Read: lines 2460–2565.*

---

## Epilogue — Remembered for everything except what he said

The dynasty went on and left almost no trace. Maurya kings ruled for decades after him, and the historical events of their reigns are not known even as legend.[^56] The Sri Lankan chronicles lose interest in the line entirely once his Buddhist children are established on the island. The Puranas name between four and seven successors; the Buddhist texts name between two and five.

Exactly one of them exists as a historical figure, and he exists for the same reason his grandfather does. Dasharatha cut an inscription in stone.[^57] The Vahiyaka cave, it says, has been given by Dasalatha, dear to the gods, to the venerable Ajivikas, immediately on his accession, to be a place of abode during the rainy season **as long as the moon and sun shall endure**.

That did not happen, and how it failed is legible in the rock. In the Barabar and Nagarjuni caves, one word was later removed or defaced from the Maurya inscriptions: *Ajivikehi*.[^58] Somebody took the caves and scratched out the name of the sect they were given to.

Buddhism, meanwhile, grew without needing a king. The stupas and viharas and chaityas that went up afterwards were paid for by pupils of particular teachers, lay worshippers, bankers, merchants, mothers, housewives, monks and nuns.[^59] They came from Vidisha and Ujjayini, and from as far off as Prathisthanapura and Pokhara.

**He does not appear in the earliest Buddhist art at all**, and that is not because kings are absent from it.[^60] Pasenadi of Kosala and Ajatashatru of Magadha are both at Bharhut, because both were contemporaries of the Buddha. What is at Bharhut of Ashoka is his furniture — the *vajrasana* he donated at Mahabodhi, now serving as one of the symbols that stand in for the Buddha, who was not yet shown in human form.

Two centuries later he arrives in person, and the sculptors put a defeat on the gateway. The southern *torana* at Sanchi shows his visit to the Ramagrama stupa, going to take one of the original relic deposits — in a chariot, with turban and ewer and fly whisk, elephants and armed troops.[^61] **And the Nagas, carved worshipping the stupa, resist him and successfully stop him getting the relics**.

By the second century CE, at Kanaganahalli in Karnataka, he is labelled by name — *Raya Asoko* — and he is not in a narrative at all.[^62] He and his queen fill the register, with female whisk-bearers and a female umbrella-bearer. A portrait, in the local Satavahana manner.

The Chinese pilgrims then describe an India where every site is one of his. Faxian in the fifth century explains practically every place through Ashoka legends, some from the Chinese *Ashokavadana* and some told him by local people.[^63] Xuanzang in the seventh finds his pillars at Sravasti, Varanasi, Niglihawa and Lumbini, notes that the Lumbini pillar is broken in the middle — brought down by the contrivance of a wicked dragon — and admires one near Varanasi as bright and shining as a mirror, glistening and smooth as ice.

**And here is the thing the whole Epilogue turns on**. The memory that he had put up stone pillars survived for a thousand years. What the pillars said did not survive at all.[^64] Niglihawa's was still known to be his, and was believed to record something about the nirvana of an earlier Buddha. Later even that connection was forgotten.

Legend kept filling the space. Xuanzang has a stupa outside Taxila marking the spot where Kunala was blinded on his stepmother's orders, and reports that when the blind pray before it with fervent faith, many of them recover their sight.[^65]

Some places held on to him accurately for a very long time. In the twelfth century Kumaradevi, queen of Govindachandra of Kanauj, recorded that she had restored the Lord of the Turning of the Wheel at Sarnath **in accordance with the way in which he existed in the days of Dharmasoka, ruler of men**, and even more wonderfully.[^66] That is fourteen hundred years after him, at a place his own epigraph shows he was close to.

Elsewhere he acquired a career he never had. Kalhana's twelfth-century Kashmiri chronicle has him reigning over the earth, freed from sins, having embraced the doctrine — and obtaining, through austerities, a son called Jalauka who then exterminated the Mlecchas from Kashmir.[^67] **No such son appears in any other source, and the family name Maurya is missing from the account entirely**. Four centuries later Abu'l Fazl mentions that chronicle in the *Ain-i Akbari*, so the chain of memory runs unbroken for about 1,700 years.

What ran along that chain, though, was one of the two men. The Buddhist convert survived — the royal patron, the pilgrim, the builder of stupas, the disciplinarian of the Sangha.[^68] The other one did not: the compulsively communicative and accessible emperor, reachable in the bed-chamber and on the march, who told his subjects what he had done at Kalinga and how it had felt. **There is no recollection of that man in the Buddhist chronicles at all**.

In the 1960s a sculptor put him back. Meera Mukherjee cast a massive metal Ashoka as a protest against the violence of the Naxalite movement in Bengal — big enough to carry the emperor's power, with the sword turned down.[^69]

And the chapter's last line is about what was lost rather than what was kept. If his own words had survived in their full nuance, the way the memory of his Buddhism did, **he might have been remembered as the founder of a political model of humane governance** — which is a good deal closer to the man who actually wrote them.[^70]

*Read: lines 2566–2682.*

# Below the Line

*Everything from here down is speculative by design. Above the line, every claim carries a footnote and a line range. Below it, the writing is allowed to weigh alternatives, run counterfactuals and hand the decision to advisors from other traditions — because that is the job of these sections*.

## Ch. 10 — Roads Not Taken `[SPECULATIVE]`

**A live alternative, and it is what nearly every other patron did**. Money spent on religious building normally goes to the patron's own religion. He was a declared Buddhist with an enormous stupa programme, and the obvious course at Barabar was four Buddhist caves. Instead the named beneficiaries are Ajivikas — the sect that has no modern adherents, whose founder was a rival of the Buddha's, and whose predictions his own legend used to legitimise him.

**A constructed alternative**. Suppose Barabar had gone to the Sangha. He loses nothing immediately and gains a coherent policy; the twelfth edict's concord becomes a phrase rather than a hillside. The forecast is that the caves survive exactly as well — they are granite — and that the defacement recorded in the Epilogue never happens, because there is no sect name to scratch out. **What would be missing is the only physical proof anywhere that the tolerance was ever more than rhetoric**. A man who funds his own church has demonstrated nothing. The caves are expensive precisely because they are the wrong caves.

## Ch. 11 — Counsel From Elsewhere `[SPECULATIVE]`

Take the fourth pillar edict: independence for the country officers, inspection for the city judges, and no reason given.

**An advisor working from [[ARCHIVES/concepts/behavioral-mechanics/shih-and-strategic-depth|shih]]** would say the split is correct and that the asymmetry is the whole of it. A *rajukka* in the countryside cannot be supervised in any real way — the distances defeat it — so the choice is between formal authority he actually has and formal authority that is a fiction. A city judge sits where an inspector can reach him every five years. Grant the discretion where you cannot enforce and keep the check where you can, and you are describing the empire as it is rather than as the manual says.

**An advisor working from [[ARCHIVES/concepts/history/stoic-dichotomy-of-control|the dichotomy of control]]** reaches the same arrangement from the other end. The emperor cannot control what a man two thousand kilometres away decides in a village court. He can control what he asks of him, and what he tells him a good decision looks like. So the fifth edict's list — envy, anger, cruelty, hurry, want of practice, laziness, fatigue — is not moralising. It is the only lever available at that distance, and he had already used the same list on the judges of Kalinga, where he did have an inspector.

**They converge, which is the useful part**. Both read the autonomy as an admission rather than a gift. The chapter says the reason is not clear and wonders whether the administration had been demoralised by too much intervention; the advisors both suggest something plainer, that he had worked out where his orders stopped arriving.

## Ch. 12 — Roads Not Taken `[SPECULATIVE]`

**A live alternative, and somebody in the room chose it**. Sampadin and the counsellors could have let a dying emperor empty the treasury into a monastery. They stopped him instead, and then had to buy the earth back from the Sangha with four *kotis* of gold before anyone could succeed him.

**A constructed alternative**. Suppose they had let him give. The Sangha ends the reign holding a fortune and a sealed deed to the empire, and the next king inherits a state whose legitimacy runs through a religious corporation. The forecast is not piety but a fight — and the Epilogue shows which way such fights went, with *Ajivikehi* chiselled out of his caves within a generation or two. **The counsellors' refusal is the least admirable act in the chapter and probably the one that kept there being a dynasty to record**. The half myrobalan is what an emperor has left when the people around him have correctly decided he can no longer be allowed to decide.

## Epilogue — What Transfers `[SPECULATIVE]`

**Decision type: choosing what will carry your meaning after you**.

The mechanism the Epilogue exposes is a split between medium and message that nobody could have predicted. The pillars lasted. The pilgrims saw them, admired them, measured them, and wrote about them for a thousand years. **What was cut into them was illegible within a few centuries, because the script died and nothing carried the language forward**. So the object survived and the content did not — and into the vacated content went legend, which is why Niglihawa's pillar ends up recording an earlier Buddha's nirvana and Kashmir acquires a son called Jalauka.

Meanwhile the message that did survive travelled by a completely different route: monks copying texts, in a religion with an institutional interest in remembering him a particular way. That route preserved the convert and dropped the administrator entirely.

**Scope conditions**. A durable medium preserves meaning only while a living community can still read it. Where the medium outlasts its readership, it does worse than fail — it becomes an authoritative-looking blank that later generations fill in. Institutional transmission is the opposite: fragile in the object, robust in the meaning, and heavily filtered by whatever the institution needs. Neither is sufficient alone. The Ashoka who is recoverable now exists because the stone survived long enough for a nineteenth-century decipherment to reach it, which is luck rather than strategy.

**Modern equivalent:** an archive on a durable format nobody can still read, versus a story an organisation keeps telling about itself. The first is trusted and empty; the second is legible and shaped. Anything meant to last needs both, and the interesting question is always which of the two is currently doing the work.

---

## Evidence

Read from `RAW/books/Ashoka in Ancient India.md`, lines 2051–2682: ch. 10 (2051–2296), ch. 11 (2297–2459), ch. 12 (2460–2565), Epilogue (2566–2682).

**Where the evidence changes character, and the book says so**. Chapters 10 and 11 rest on his own inscriptions and on excavated structures, and they are the most secure material in the book. Chapter 12 rests entirely on the *Mahavamsa* and the *Ashokavadana*, composed centuries later with an interest in deifying him — the chapter opens by saying the story is back where it began, embedded in unverifiable tradition. Everything about Tishyarakshita, the worm, the onion and the half myrobalan is reported here at that weight.

**Where dating is inferred rather than known**. The chronology of the edifices cannot be fixed the way the edicts can: only some carry dates, some carry no inscription at all, and the attributions then rest on literary claims or on diagnostic features like Mauryan polish and brick size. The Vaishali stupa breach is a real archaeological fact with a contested cause.

**Where the source's own judgement is doing the work**. That no emperor in the ancient world expresses comparable concern for the underprivileged and for animals is the author's assessment. So is the closing verdict that the surviving memory preserved the Buddhist and lost the governor. Both are reported here as hers.

**Bounded absence**. No claim is made about material outside lines 2051–2682. The Appendix table of inscriptions beginning at line 2683 was not read for this pass.
