# Below the Line

*Everything from here down is speculative by design. Above the line, every claim carries a footnote and a line range. Below it, the writing is allowed to weigh alternatives, run counterfactuals and hand the decision to advisors from other traditions — because that is the job of these sections*.

## The two piles, chapters 5–8 `[SPECULATIVE]`

**Paradigm-obvious**. Meeting an enemy general under a flag of truce with hidden troops in the woods is not an invention; both sides in these chapters plan for treachery and Shahaji's letter advises taking an oath first because there may be treachery. Sacking a rich enemy city for its cash is what every army in the century did. Writing a submission you do not mean, which he does to Jauhar exactly as he had to Aurangzeb, was standard Deccani correspondence.

**Paradigm-breaking, and each one cost him something**.

Paying the widows and the wounded after Pratapgad, on a published scale, and sending captured enemy soldiers home with money and food. That is expensive, and the going rate for prisoners in this book is ransom or execution.

Going into Lal Mahal himself. Every advisor around him would have said the same thing, and the chapter says his mother and his council were frightened. A ruler with sixty forts does not need to be the man in the room at midnight, and if he had died there the state died with him.

Stopping the killing at Surat after an attempt on his own life, then ordering mutilations instead. That is neither mercy nor policy in the ordinary sense — it is a man choosing, in the middle of his own rage, to convert a massacre into a punishment with a countable number attached.

## Ch. 5 — Roads Not Taken `[SPECULATIVE]`

**A live alternative, argued at the time and by the enemy**. Afzal Khan wanted the meeting on the plains of Wai, where ten thousand horse would decide it. Shivaji wanted it under Pratapgad. That is the entire negotiation, conducted through two envoys over several letters, and the flattery was the instrument.

**A constructed alternative**. Suppose he had gone down to Wai. The forecast is not that he loses a battle — it is that there is no battle, because on open ground with those numbers the meeting itself becomes the arrest Afzal Khan had promised the durbar. What the hills gave him was not cover for an ambush so much as **a place where the enemy's main advantage could not be brought to bear at all**, which is the same asset the Mavals and Jaawali gave him earlier and Umbarkhind gave him later. The letters were the cost of moving the venue, and flattery is cheap.

## Ch. 7 — Counsel From Elsewhere `[SPECULATIVE]`

Take the decision to lead the raid on Lal Mahal in person.

**A Stoic advisor**, working from [[ARCHIVES/concepts/history/stoic-dichotomy-of-control|the dichotomy of control]], would object on the grounds the chapter itself supplies. A man in a bedroom at midnight has handed the outcome to a hundred things outside his power — a sleepless cook, a guard who is awake, a door that has been bricked up since he lived there. The plan required the interior layout of a house to be unchanged after three years of another man's occupation, and that was not his to know.

**An advisor working from [[ARCHIVES/concepts/behavioral-mechanics/shih-and-strategic-depth|shih]]** would answer that the raid is not an attack on a man but on a position. Shaista Khan's whole standing rested on being untouchable in the middle of an army; take three fingers off him and the position is gone whether he lives or dies. And it worked exactly that way — Aurangzeb moved him to Bengal, and the Mughal chronicle could only manage three sentences about it.

**They do not converge, and the split is the honest outcome**. One reads it as an unrepeatable gamble that happened to come off; the other reads it as a precise strike on the one thing an occupying general cannot afford to lose. **Both are right, which is why it is in the paradigm-breaking pile**: it cost him a risk nobody in his position would have been advised to take.

## Ch. 8 — What Transfers `[SPECULATIVE]`

**Decision type: attacking an opponent's revenue instead of his army**.

Surat is the clean case. He could not beat Shaista Khan's numbers in the field and had spent three years watching his own villages burned. So he went four hundred kilometres to a city with no walls, took a crore and a half in four days, and left before the relief column arrived. The English president, an unfriendly witness, read the intent correctly: not altogether riches but revenge.

**Scope conditions**. This works where the target is undefended *because* it is commercial — a place whose wealth is the reason nobody thought to fortify it — and where the raider can leave before a field army arrives. It requires accurate intelligence about the route, which is why the chapter names the spy who found it. And it fails permanently the moment the opponent responds structurally rather than punitively: Aurangzeb sacked the governor, which changed nothing, **and ordered a stone wall, which did**.

**The second-order effect is the one worth keeping**. The raid's largest yield was not the money. It was that report hath made him an airy body, and added wings — a reputation for being in six places at once, which then did work for him in every subsequent negotiation. A commercial target produces witnesses who write letters, and the letters travel further than the army ever could.

**Modern equivalent:** hitting a competitor's revenue channel rather than its product. Same conditions, same limit — it works until they build the wall, and by then the reputational effect has already been banked.

## Evidence

Read from `RAW/books/Shivaji-India's Great Warrior King.md`, lines 818–1855: ch. 5 (818–1025), ch. 6 (1026–1211), ch. 7 (1212–1425), ch. 8 (1426–1855).

**Where the accounts disagree, and the book keeps them apart**. The killing of Afzal Khan comes down through several versions that differ on who struck first and in what order; the report here reflects that. Shaista Khan lost three fingers by Sabhasad's account and a thumb by Khafi Khan's. Baji Prabhu's death has two endings, one plain and one heroic, and the plainer one is in the more reliable chronicle. How a hundred Marathas got through the gates of Pune has two explanations and neither is confirmed.

**What the book rejects outright, and on what grounds**. The Katraj pass torches are from a late and unreliable chronicle. The reading of the Rajapur arrests as early anti-colonial insight is called reading history backwards, and the narrower thing that *was* known — that the English wanted forts — is stated instead. Sarkar's explanation for sparing Anthony Smith is corrected from the English records themselves. Cosme da Guarda's secret pact between Shivaji and Jaswant Singh is neither endorsed nor discarded: it is treated as evidence of what people in the Deccan were saying, which is a different and smaller claim.

**Whose voices these are**. Parmanand and Sabhasad were his officials. Khafi Khan's father served in Shaista Khan's army. The English letters are commercial correspondence never meant to be read outside the Company, which is why they swing from "noble" to "perfidious" inside a year and why they are useful. Bernier, Manucci, Tavernier, Thevenot and da Guarda were foreigners collecting talk.

**Bounded absence**. No claim is made about material outside lines 818–1855.

# What the Deccan Took For Granted — Chapters 9–13

## Ch. 9 — The man who asked for full powers before he started

The third general Aurangzeb sent was a Hindu, and he was the one who nearly finished it. Mirza Raja Jai Singh of the Jaipur royal house had entered Mughal service as an orphan at eight and distinguished himself from Balkh and Kandahar to Bijapur.[^1] He brought 14,000 troops with him, and the men left over from Shaista Khan were still in Maratha country.

The first thing he did was ask the emperor for something the other two never asked for. He wanted full freedom of decision at every level — local appointments, payments, civil and military matters — without the Mughal bureaucracy in the way.[^2] He got it, and then he moved.

He was not satisfied with being ahead on numbers. He wanted crushing superiority, and to get it he used persuasion, force, bribery and threats as each occasion required.[^3] That meant working on everybody else first. He sent two Portuguese men in his employ to Goa asking for cooperation, and complained that some Portuguese had been actively involved with Shivaji.[^4] He set about sowing dissension in Bijapur — bribing Adil Shahi fort commanders, offering office and cavalry to Bijapur generals — so that the two could not combine against him.[^5]

Then he picked his camp with the same care. Not Pune, the obvious choice, but Saswad to the east, which put him between Shivaji's state and Bijapur at once.[^6] And in Saswad stood Purandar. What he told Aurangzeb about method is the technical heart of the chapter. All the Deccan territory was needed, but *we have primarily to attack the hill forts* — so send the big guns already in Mughal hands and the cannons recently cast.[^7]

Then he wrote back with what the guns had proved:

> But our campaign has established one thing. It is indeed possible to carry the big guns half-way up the hill forts, to the very place the people of these regions called the machi. From that spot, a highly effective assault can be launched on the fort. [^8]

That single paragraph is the end of Shivaji's basic advantage. Until then the belief had been that cannon worked only against forts standing near the ground.

The rest of the campaign was designed to break a mind rather than a wall. Jai Singh explained his reasoning to the emperor: he wanted to show Shivaji that a siege at Purandar would not stop the Mughals doing everything else at the same time.[^9] So more than six thousand troops went out under Daud Khan and others with orders to **depopulate and reduce to ashes** the whole region around Rajgad and Sinhagad. Every village along the route to Rajgad was torched and the cultivation destroyed.

And the seduction ran alongside the burning. Jai Singh gloated that Shivaji's troops, collected over so long, were seduced by us — **passports and promises of safety, and then imperial service with proper ranks and stipends**.[^10]

The defence of Purandar produced the chapter's one clean refusal. Murar Baji Deshpande, the Maratha commander, was offered a *kaul*, an assurance of safety, by Diler Khan, with promotion attached: *you are an extremely intrepid soldier, I will promote you*.[^11] The reply:

> What is your kaul? Do I, a soldier of Shivaji Raje, take your kaul?

He raised his sword and stepped forward, and Diler Khan had his bow ready and shot him first. About three hundred Marathas died there.[^12] So Shivaji concluded that the best available option was to stop fighting.[^13] Afzal Khan had been hard, Shaista Khan twice as hard, and this was several times harder — and almost everything he had taken, except southern Konkan, was overrun.

What he negotiated matters more than what he gave up. One condition he insisted on, and got, was that **he would neither hold military rank in Mughal service nor be obliged to attend the emperor's court**.[^14] The whole subsequent chapter turns on that clause being broken.

He did not want to go to Agra and the book is clear about why. He had no trust in a man who had neutralised and murdered three of his own brothers to get the crown.[^15] Jai Singh promised everything — including religious promises, as one Hindu to another, that no one would so much as touch him.[^16]

Before leaving he arranged the government. His mother Jijabai would be regent, assisted by the prime minister.[^17] He left Rajgad on 5 March 1666 with his nine-year-old son, and with a promise in his pocket that had already been broken once on paper.

*Read: lines 1856–2239.*

## Ch. 10 — Made to stand behind a man his soldiers had beaten

The crowds came out before he arrived. At Khadki, an early stop on the twelve-hundred-kilometre road to Agra, he found his reputation already there — in an age with no newspapers, people had lined the streets to see him.[^18]

He was to appear at court on 12 May 1666, the emperor's fiftieth birthday by the lunar calendar, with extraordinary pomp planned.[^19] He arrived in style himself: 250 mounted men, and an eyewitness in Jai Singh's own employ took his measure:

> Lean and short, very handsome and wonderfully fair in complexion… Even without finding out who he is, one does feel instinctively that he is a ruler of men. [^20]

The reception was a series of small insults, and it is not clear how many were planned. Aurangzeb had told Jai Singh's son Ram Singh to ride out a day's journey to meet him.[^21] Ram Singh sent a clerk instead. The next day he sent the clerk again, then rode out late by a different road and missed him. The delays meant no rest after three months on the road in the summer heat, and they missed the public audience.

Then the durbar. He bowed three times and presented a thousand gold *mohars*, two thousand rupees and five thousand more as offerings.[^22] And then he was placed in the ranks — **at a level below the rank his nine-year-old son had been given without appearing at court at all**.

His outburst is quoted at length because the grievance is precise rather than vague:

> What? My son is nine years old, and he was made a paanch hazari without even having to turn up before the Emperor in court. Netaji Palkar, who works for me, is a paanch hazari. After all the services I have rendered… is this low rank what I'm going to get? [^23]

Then he asked who the man standing in front of him was. Ram Singh said Maharaja Jaswant Singh, and Shivaji went apoplectic: **an umrao like Jaswant Singh? My soldiers have seen the back of him!**[^24] That is the man whose troops had sat still in Pune the night Shaista Khan lost his fingers.

Robes of honour were being handed out, and he refused his. What he said in front of the assembled court was not a complaint about protocol but a resignation:[^25]

> The Emperor has deliberately made me stand behind Jaswant Singh. He knows what kind of a man I am, yet he has willfully kept me standing. I decline the Emperor's mansab. I will not be his servant. Kill me, imprison me, if you like…

Somebody tried to explain it away with a joke about the weather. The tiger is a wild animal of the forests, he feels hot, something has happened.[^26] May in Agra was ferociously hot and that was not what had happened.

The book's reading of the whole scene is a plan rather than a slight. Shivaji was the most stubborn of rebels — he had attacked Mughal lands, looted rich cities and put a fancied governor to flight in the night.[^27] **Humbling him in front of the assembled nobility said something to the nobility**: if he can be subdued like this, the rest of you are easy pickings.

And what made the rage come out is worth separating from pride. He had not wanted to come. Jai Singh had persuaded him, on assurances that he would be received well and treated with respect.[^28] What broke in the marble hall was the discovery that the assurances had been worth nothing — and that leaves a man with nothing further to protect.

Then house arrest, and a plan. He was told he might live in Allahabad fort, where state prisoners were kept.[^29] So he pretended to be seriously ill, and began sending out sweetmeats in wicker baskets to Mughal officials and holy men, day after day, until the baskets going past the guards were routine.

**On the afternoon of 17 August 1666 he told his guards he was very unwell and should not be disturbed**.[^30] His half-brother Hiroji Farzand, who resembled him, lay on the bed with an arm out and Shivaji's golden bracelet on it. He and his nine-year-old son folded themselves into two baskets and were carried out past the rows of guards.

In the morning Hiroji walked out with a servant, telling the guards the Raja was resting.[^31] The guards' own report, when they found the room empty, is the best thing in the chapter:

> The Raja was in his own room. We visited the room repeatedly to inspect, but he disappeared all of a sudden. Whether he has fled, or entered into the earth, or gone up in the sky – we don't know. We have been very close to him. He vanished in our view.

Aurangzeb was far too rational to believe any of that and ordered a search across Agra and down every road to the Deccan.[^32] The route he took is the last piece of the method. He was twelve hours ahead, and he did not go south.[^33] He went north and north-west to Mathura, then drew an arc through Bundelkhand, Gondwana and Golconda to come home. The boy could not keep up and was left in Mathura with three Deccani Brahmins.

He shaved off his moustache and beard, smeared himself with ash and travelled as a *sanyasi*, carrying a staff **with the gold coins for the journey hidden inside it**.[^34] He reached Rajgad about 12 September, twenty-six days out of Agra, having covered more than a thousand kilometres from Mathura, and fell seriously ill from the exhaustion of it.

*Read: lines 2240–2553.*

---

## Ch. 11 — Three years of measuring land

A hero came home with almost nothing. Time, men, materials, resources and most of his forts were gone, and his closest aides were still prisoners.[^35]

What Aurangzeb got in the same period was a letter from Persia telling him he was weak.[^36] The Persian ruler wrote that most of the zamindars of India were in rebellion because their ruler was weak, incompetent and without resources, and that the chief of them was the impious kafir Shiva —

> who had long lived in such obscurity that no one knew his very name; but now, taking advantage of your lack of means and the retreat of your troops, he has made himself visible like the peak of a mountain.

The man who carried that letter was stripped of his rank for it.[^37] Both sides then bought time from each other. Shivaji wrote that he had fled Agra not from insubordination but in fear of his life; Aurangzeb accepted with alacrity, believing none of it.[^38] And once again Shivaji avoided taking a rank himself in the empire he was fighting.

Then the part of his life that nobody makes a film about. **For three years he made no move that would invite retaliation**.[^39] He put Annaji Datto to measuring his lands so that revenue could be set by rule instead of by whoever was collecting it.

The reform is specific and every piece of it removes somebody's discretion. Dues were fixed in cash and grain according to the yield of a village, and officials could no longer extract rents arbitrarily but only at centrally fixed rates.[^40] Officials could not pay themselves — payment came by orders on the treasury, which ended random collection and misappropriation. And he stopped appointing *jagir* holders altogether, cutting out a line of authority that had become notorious.[^41]

He chose the harder tax and the honest one. The *batai* system takes a share of what a farmer actually grew; the *bighawani* system taxes at flat rates by land quality.[^42] **He took forty or fifty per cent — and the book's point is that with him it meant exactly that**, where earlier collections had been random, unsystematic and without any proper count.

Which is why the chapter can ask its best question. Why did none of his enemies ever cite a single instance of the population in his territories protesting against his rules?[^43] And why did the local people — as distinct from some *watandars* — stay with a newcomer when they could have sheltered under older and far bigger powers?

The wasteland policy is the other half of the answer. New farmers coming to settle were given cattle, grain and money for seed — not as gifts, with the sum realised over two or four years.[^44] A letter of the 1670s says that a farmer with the ability and the workforce but no oxen should be given cash to buy them, and the advance recovered gradually according to his ability, **without charging any interest**.

And there were losers, which is how you tell a reform from an announcement. A temple complex at Chinchwad near Pune had long enjoyed the right to buy goods from neighbouring districts at concessional rates, with the exchequer absorbing the loss, and that stopped.[^45]

The other reform is about what an official is for. Every state in the seventeenth-century Deccan was a military state and almost every civilian official was also a military one, and officials naturally saw more glory in soldiering.[^46] He insisted that civil administration mattered as much as military efficiency and valour.

The Goa episode of 1667 is where the book does its hardest source work. He invaded Bardez in November 1667 with a thousand cavalry and five thousand infantry, and the provocation was that the Portuguese were sheltering the *desais* he had evicted, who kept coming back to harass the population.[^47] Bardez itself was in the grip of serious religious frenzy at the time, which is exactly the coincidence that produces a theory.

An Englishman's letter of 30 November 1667 said the priests were killed for refusing to convert to Hinduism. The treaty and the Portuguese envoy's own note of instructions both show what the quarrel was actually about, and it was the *desais*.[^48] The treaty says Goa will not shelter them.

That is not the same as indifference, and the book keeps both facts side by side. He restored and rebuilt the temple of Saptakoteshwara at Narve in November 1668, on the spot where it had stood.[^49] **In the same years Aurangzeb demolished Somnath and the Vishwanath temple at Kashi and put a mosque on the site**.[^50]

*Read: lines 2556–2789.*

## Ch. 12 — A gold throne and a mother who died twelve days later

Three provocations arrived together at the end of 1669. Aurangzeb confiscated parts of Sambhaji's *jagir*, ostensibly to recover the lakh of rupees advanced for the Agra journey.[^51] And he told Shivaji to back off from Janjira — **while the treaty between them had told him to take as much Bijapur territory as he could**.

The first place he went for was in view from his own window. From the top of Rajgad he could see Sinhagad, one of the earliest forts he ever took, given up in 1649 for his father, retaken, and given up again in 1666 under the Treaty of Purandar.[^52] In places the climb is almost vertical.

Tanaji Malusare offered to lead it, against a Rajput commander of similar reputation — Udaibhan Rathod, thirty-eight, from Jodhpur, with mostly Rajputs under him.[^53] At around midnight on 4 February 1670 two Mavale went up the precipice and fixed a rope ladder.

The book pauses to kill a story here. The claim that the garrison were stupefied with opium is dubious, and it is what let a filmmaker stage a scene of delirious revelry.[^54] The two commanders met, Tanaji's shield broke, a second did not arrive in time, and he was killed.

The Marathas took it and set fire to the stacks in the stables as a signal, and Shivaji, who had stayed up all night, saw the flames.[^55] Then the recovery, and the numbers are the finding. They had lost twenty-three of thirty-five forts to the Mughals. They took almost all of them back inside four months.[^56] The book says plainly that familiarity with the terrain cannot account for it and that, apart from Sinhagad, no records survive to explain how — only that most attacks were at night and turned on surprise.

The English watched him change register: he *now marches not before as a thief but in gross with an army of 30,000 men, conquering as he goes*.[^57] On 3 October 1670 he sacked Surat again, with about fifteen thousand men.[^58] **And this time he had written ahead, demanding the *chauth*, a quarter of the annual revenue, for the third and last time:**[^59]

> As your Emperor has forced me to keep an army for the defence of my people and country, that army must be paid by his subjects. If you do not send me the money speedily, then make ready a large house for me, for I shall go and sit down there and receive the revenue.

That is a tax demand, delivered by a man who is not their ruler, in the form of a threat to come and collect it in person. The word *chauth* is doing work there. He is not asking for plunder; he is asserting a standing claim on their revenue.

The coronation in 1674 is where the chapter's real subject is, because it turns out to require rebuilding him as a person. He was a Kshatriya, one of the twice-born castes — and his family had dropped the practices that went with it.[^60] There had been no sacred thread ceremony, which in that period in the Deccan was largely confined to Brahmins. He had not worn one at any of his marriages.

So he had to be given the thread, and then married to all his surviving wives again, before he could be crowned.[^61] Gaga Bhatt was brought all the way from Benares to conduct it. The ceremony ran a week from 30 May, and the moment fixed for the enthronement was a few minutes before five in the morning on 6 June.

Henry Oxenden of the East India Company was there and left the description. The throne was made of thirty-two maunds of gold, its eight pillars studded with gems, with one of the eight ministers standing at each.[^62] Water from the seven holy rivers. And Raigad itself:

> fortified more by nature more than art, being of very difficult access, and [it has] but one advance to it, which is guarded by two narrow gates.

The decision inside the decision is the one about language. He appointed eight *pradhans* and gave their offices new Sanskrit names, doing away with the long-established Persian titles.[^63] That is the seal of 1646 carried all the way up into the machinery of a state.

He weighed himself against gold — about 160 pounds of it — and distributed that weight in gold, and then the same again in silver, copper, tin and iron.[^64] Then Jijabai died, twelve days later.[^65] She had been, in the book's phrase, the real *chhatra* of the Chhatrapati. She had issued orders in her own name, settled matters, made donations to religious places, and held the state as regent through the months in which nobody knew whether her son would come back from Agra alive.

And grief brought out an opportunist immediately. A tantric priest, Nischalpuri Gosavi, had felt sidelined by the Vedic priests who ran the coronation and had probably received fewer gifts than he expected.[^66] A man who has just buried his mother is a market.

*Read: lines 2790–3250.*

---

## Ch. 13 (numbered 14) — The last letter

The heir apparent had grown up wrong-footed. Sambhaji was barely two when his mother died in 1659, was raised by his father and his grandmother, and had been in Agra in a basket.[^67] Once his father was king he was heir — and the household had the trouble royal households have.

Soyrabai, the senior surviving wife, had borne a son, Rajaram, in 1670.[^68] When Shivaji fell severely ill for a month early in 1676, rumours ran across the Deccan that he had died, and news of serious differences inside the household spread with them.[^69] The grandmother who had been Sambhaji's solace was gone.

So he went over to the Mughals, and what brought him back was watching how they made war.[^70] He was with Diler Khan when the Mughal governor took Bhupalgad in April 1679. On the way back from a failed siege of Bijapur, Diler Khan did things to the ordinary population that Sambhaji — raised where wanton harassment of civilians was not the norm — could not stomach. He escaped and came home.

His father's words on the reunion are recorded by Sabhasad and they are the words of a man handing over:

> My boy, do not leave me. There is enmity between us and Aurangzeb. He intended to commit treachery against you… Now you, my eldest son, have grown big… I shall henceforth meditate on the Sri. [^71]

Sambhaji answered that his fortune lay at his father's feet, and that he would live on milk and rice and meditate there. It is the only conversation between the two of them preserved anywhere.

Then the letter to Aurangzeb, dictated to the secretary who wrote his Persian, and it is the fullest statement of the position the whole book has been circling.[^72] The occasion was the *jizya*, the tax on non-Muslims — imposed, Shivaji says, because the war against him had emptied the treasury.

His argument is historical before it is theological. Akbar ruled fifty-two years treating Christians, Jews, Muslims, Dadupanthis, stargazers, atheists, Brahmins and Jains with peace and equality.[^73] Jahangir twenty-two years, Shah Jahan thirty-two, all of them successful in whatever direction they turned. Every one of them had the power to impose *jizya* and did not:

> But they felt that all men [and women], big and small, were the children of God, and all religions but means to the worship of the Almighty.

Then the threat, unhedged: during your regime many provinces and forts have gone out of your hands, and the remaining ones will too. I will not spare any effort to ruin your provinces.[^74]

Then the theological point, which is made from inside the Quran rather than against it:

> Your Majesty, in the Quran, God has been described as the Rabbul Alameen, the Lord of the entire universe, and not as Rabbul Mussalmin, the Lord of the Mussalmans. [^75]

And then the sting, which is a piece of political advice disguised as a suggestion. If the tax is really justified on grounds of religion and justice, collect it first from Raja Raj Singh, for he is the leader of the Hindus.[^76]

The last year is administration and illness. A peace treaty with the British early in 1680 over the island of Khanderi, which the Marathas had fortified and held.[^77] Siddi Masaud of Bijapur going over to the Mughals. Janjira still not taken.

In March he celebrated his younger son's marriage at Raigad, to the daughter of a lieutenant who had died in his service.[^78] Then came the illness that finished it, and he was fifty.

What he said as they gathered is one sentence, and it is not about the state. There is nothing in it about Sambhaji, the forts, the Mughals or the sea:[^79]

> The term of my life has ended. I am going to Kailas to see my Sri.

At those words, Sabhasad wrote, everyone's throat was choked and tears began streaming from their eyes. Then he sent them all out, bathed, put ash on his body and the *rudraksha* beads on, and died about noon on Saturday, 3 April 1680.[^80]

The other side's obituary was six words. Khafi Khan wrote that the infidel, the unbeliever, had gone to hell.[^81] The English would not believe the news eight months later, having heard too much about him to accept that he had simply stopped.

His own chronicler's summary claims the sea as well as the land — authority invoked from the Narmada to Rameshwar, territories taken from four sultanates on land, and the twenty-two Badshahs of the sea.[^82] Nobody in his family had owned a boat when he was born.

What happened afterwards is the measure of it. Aurangzeb came down to the Deccan and spent close to twenty-five years there and never went back north.[^83] He destroyed Bijapur and Golconda and took their rulers captive. He captured Sambhaji, killed him, and had the severed head carried round the main cities of the Deccan for everyone to see. **The Marathas crowned the younger son at Raigad and kept going**. Aurangzeb died at Aurangabad in February 1707 with Shivaji's people still growing and his own empire in decline.

*Read: lines 3251–3402.*

# Below the Line

*Everything from here down is speculative by design. Above the line, every claim carries a footnote and a line range. Below it, the writing is allowed to weigh alternatives, run counterfactuals and hand the decision to advisors from other traditions — because that is the job of these sections*.

## The two piles, chapters 9–13 `[SPECULATIVE]`

**Paradigm-obvious**. Suing for peace when your forts are falling and your commanders are dead. Escaping captivity by a trick — every prisoner in the century tried it, and the basket is a good trick rather than a new idea. Sacking Surat a second time, having done it once profitably. Losing a son to the other side, which happened to Shah Jahan, to Bimbisara and to half the families in this book.

**Paradigm-breaking, and each one cost him**.

Refusing the robe of honour in open durbar. Every incentive in the room said take it, bow, go home and break the agreement later — which is what he had done with every previous agreement. He chose house arrest instead, and it nearly killed him and his son.

Spending three years measuring fields. A ruler who has just lost twenty-three of thirty-five forts is expected to raise men and take them back. He spent the window on revenue rates, ox advances at no interest, and taking the collection out of officials' hands. The chapter's question — why did nobody in his territory ever revolt against his rules, and why did the local people stay — is answered by that ledger rather than by charisma.

Cutting the Persian titles out of his own administration on coronation day. That is a cost with no military return whatever, paid in the confusion of renaming an entire working government, and it is the seal of 1646 finally arriving in the machinery.

Writing the *jizya* letter. He was fifty, ill, at peace with nobody, and the letter guaranteed there would be no further accommodation with Aurangzeb in his lifetime. The book's word for it is that he was happy to burn all his boats.

## Ch. 9 — Roads Not Taken `[SPECULATIVE]`

**A live alternative, and Jai Singh took it**. The first thing he asked Aurangzeb for was full freedom of decision at every level. Shaista Khan and Afzal Khan had commanded larger reputations and neither is recorded asking for that. It is the only difference between the three campaigns that is visible before any fighting starts, and it is the campaign that worked.

**A constructed alternative**. Suppose the emperor had refused, and Jai Singh had run the campaign through the normal Mughal chain — local appointments and payments cleared upward, sieges argued over by committee. The forecast: the bribing of Bijapur's fort commanders does not happen at speed, the Portuguese are not leaned on in time, and the guns do not go up the *machi* because nobody at Agra believes they can. **What defeated Shivaji was not a bigger army. It was one man being allowed to decide things where he was standing** — which is exactly the arrangement Shivaji himself ran, and the only time in the book that an opponent matches it.

## Ch. 10 — Counsel From Elsewhere `[SPECULATIVE]`

Take the refusal of the robe of honour, in front of the assembled Mughal nobility, from a man who had already killed three brothers.

**A Stoic advisor**, working from [[ARCHIVES/concepts/history/stoic-dichotomy-of-control|the dichotomy of control]], would be on his side here and not on the side of prudence. The rank, the place in the line and the emperor's opinion were never his. What was his was whether he consented to them, and consent given in that hall would have been the one thing he could not later disown. He had broken every treaty he signed; he could not have broken a bow.

**An advisor working from [[ARCHIVES/concepts/behavioral-mechanics/shih-and-strategic-depth|shih]]** would answer that he had walked into a position with no depth behind it — no forts, no terrain, no escape route, a nine-year-old son in the room, and a chaperon whose father had made the promises being broken. In that position the correct move is to take the robe, spend nothing, and leave. Every asset he had ever used was two thousand kilometres away.

**They split, and the split is real**. One says the refusal preserved the only thing he still owned; the other says it cost him four months of captivity and a flight that nearly killed him, in exchange for a gesture. The book itself lands closer to the Stoic reading — that what came out was not pride but the collapse of an assurance, which leaves a man with nothing left to protect.

## Ch. 11 — What Transfers `[SPECULATIVE]`

**Decision type: using a forced pause to rebuild the thing nobody attacks**.

He had three years in which any movement would have brought the Mughals back. He could have spent them recruiting quietly. He spent them on land measurement, fixed revenue rates, treasury-order payments, abolition of *jagirs*, and interest-free ox advances to farmers who had none.

**Scope conditions**. This works where the pause is genuinely enforced — where activity is the thing that would be punished — and where the neglected system is the one that actually generates the resource everything else runs on. It requires that the reformer be able to absorb the losers: the Chinchwad temple lost its concessional rates and the *watandars* lost their discretion, and he could carry that because he had no rival claimant inside his own country. And it fails where the pause is short, because measuring land takes years and produces nothing in the first one.

**The check on whether it worked is in the chapter and it is a negative**. No enemy could cite a single instance of the population in his territories protesting against his rules. That is not proof of contentment; it is proof that his opponents, who were looking for exactly such evidence and would have used it, did not find any.

**Modern equivalent:** the enforced quiet period spent on the ledger, the pipeline or the data rather than on visible activity. Nobody applauds it at the time, and it is what the next expansion is paid for out of.

## Ch. 13 — Roads Not Taken `[SPECULATIVE]`

**A live alternative he had used all his life**. Every previous letter to Aurangzeb had been submission with a knife behind it — contrition, professions of loyalty, a request to hold conquered land on the empire's behalf. It had bought him a decade. The *jizya* letter throws that instrument away.

**A constructed alternative**. Suppose he had written the usual letter instead — deploring the tax mildly, professing loyalty, asking for confirmation of his territories. He is fifty and ill; the accommodation buys his son a calmer succession. The forecast is that it makes no difference at all to the war, because Aurangzeb had already written him off privately as the son of a dog and came down to the Deccan anyway within a year of his death, and stayed twenty-five years. **What the letter did buy was the one document in the whole corpus stating a position rather than a manoeuvre** — and it survived, which the manoeuvres did not, because his own letters to Aurangzeb were burnt and this one was copied.

**Scope conditions on that, since it is the transferable part**. A statement of position outlives the correspondence around it only where it is addressed upward and made public, and where the writer has nothing further to lose by it. Written earlier, from weakness, it would have been read as a bargaining posture and filed with the rest.

## Evidence

Read from `RAW/books/Shivaji-India's Great Warrior King.md`, lines 1856–3402: ch. 9 (1856–2239), ch. 10 (2240–2553), ch. 11 (2556–2789), ch. 12 (2790–3250), ch. 13 (3251–3402).

**Whose account each part rests on**. Chapter 9 is largely Jai Singh's own dispatches to Aurangzeb, collected in the *Haft Anjuman* — which is why the Mughal campaign is the best-documented military operation in the book and why its boasting is visible as boasting. Chapter 10 combines Sabhasad, Sarkar's translations of Persian and Rajasthan records, and Oxenden's English report. Chapter 11's reforms rest on Shivaji's own administrative letters. Chapter 13's *jizya* letter is a Persian document dictated to his secretary.

**Where the book corrects the received story**. The opium-stupefied garrison at Sinhagad is called dubious, and named as the source of a film scene. The claim that the Goa invasion of 1667 had a religious motive is traced to one Englishman's letter and set against the treaty and the Portuguese envoy's own instructions, which say the quarrel was about the sheltered *desais*. The rumour that Shivaji had died in 1676, and the household stories that travelled with it, are reported as rumours.

**Where the author states a view**. That Aurangzeb humiliated him in durbar deliberately, as a demonstration to the other nobles, is the book's reading and is marked here as such. So is the judgement that what produced the outburst was the collapse of Jai Singh's assurances rather than pride alone.

**Bounded absence**. No claim is made about material outside lines 1856–3402. The bibliography and acknowledgements from line 3403 were not read.

## What Runs Through All of It

Every hereditary official in this world holds his post because a sultan let him. The *patil* collects in the village, the *deshmukh* in the district, and the *watan* passes down the family — and it can be taken away the moment the ruler is displeased. That single arrangement produces almost everything in the book. It is why a boy visiting his father's estate frightens Bijapur, why Afzal Khan writes to the *deshmukhs* before he marches, why Kanhoji Jedhe has to tip water off his right hand to renounce his own inheritance, and why Jai Singh can buy Shivaji's cavalry with passports and stipends.

**So the decision he takes at twenty is the one everything rests on: he paid his own soldiers directly**. Not out of a *deshmukh*'s coffers. It was slower, dearer, and it forfeited ready-made levies from men who knew the ground. It is also why, when several of those men changed sides, his army stayed his.

Second, he built where the incumbents had written the ground off. The Mavals were country officials would not walk on and they gave him his men. Jaawali was terrain Bijapur's own troops would not enter and it gave him his capital. The sea had been conceded to the *firangs* by every land power in India, partly on a ruling that crossing it polluted you, and it gave him a navy with two Muslim admirals and a Bhandari. And each time, the neglect ended the moment the position started to matter — the Portuguese locked his first ships inside his own creeks the year they were finished.

Third, submission is a document rather than a state of mind, and everyone in the book knows it. He writes contrition to Aurangzeb while robbing a revenue convoy. He writes surrender to Siddi Jauhar the week he goes down the fort in the rain. Aurangzeb grants him a pardon in April and calls him the son of a dog in a private letter the same year. Goa instructs its captains to refuse the Siddis help ostensibly and to give it secretly. **This is a world where the written word and the intention have been formally decoupled**, and the letters are all still written, because they buy time.

Which makes the one refusal enormous. At Agra he would not take the robe.

Fourth, the identity is asserted through language before it is asserted through anything else. At sixteen he cut his seal in Sanskrit while his father, his mother and his father's agent all sealed in Persian. At forty-four, on coronation day, he renamed his eight ministries out of Persian into Sanskrit. Between those two dates he restored a temple the Portuguese had demolished while Aurangzeb was pulling down Somnath, kept up the grants his predecessors had made to mosques and tombs, ordered his soldiers to treat the Quran with respect, and told Aurangzeb that God is called the Lord of the universe rather than the Lord of the Muslims.

**The book's own answer to what kind of state that was is a refusal of both easy readings**. Not secular, not a theocracy: a Hindu polity that was broadly inclusive and made no difference of treatment between Hindus and non-Hindus. It then names the two groups who cannot claim it — those who want him overstated as a defender of the faith, and those who want the words Hindu and Hinduism denied altogether.

Fifth, the paperwork was burnt, and that shapes every chapter. Most Maratha records went in the Mughal assaults or were destroyed by the Marathas themselves after his death. **Not one of his letters to Aurangzeb survives**. So the correspondence with the empire has to be reconstructed from the empire's replies, the birth date is still contested, and the biography leans on the archive built by Rajwade and the Pune scholars two and a half centuries later.

Sixth, he treats the people who feed the army as an asset rather than a resource. Not a blade of grass, not a grain taken by force, and punishment for the soldiers who did — because otherwise, he wrote, the villagers would think of them as worse than the Mughals. Pensions for widows and graded payments to the wounded after Pratapgad. Captured enemy soldiers sent home with money and food. Oxen advanced to farmers who had none, recovered gradually, without interest. And no enemy of his ever found a single instance of the people in his own territories revolting against his rules.

## Which dimensions the book never reached

**Women, and the book says so rather than filling the gap**. Contemporary chroniclers did not describe the interior or exterior lives of women like Jijabai, which the author names as a serious hole for a modern biographer. What survives is a mother who chased a fleeing clan waving a dead man's Spirit Banner and held the state as regent while nobody knew whether her son would come back from Agra, and a wife, Karuvaki, who wanted an act of philanthropy recorded as hers. He married eight times and the other seven are names.

**Almost nothing on ordinary religious life**. There are temples, a pilgrimage bath at Gokarna, priests brought from Benares and a tantric opportunist working a bereaved king — and no account anywhere of what the Mavale believed, which is striking given that the whole state was built out of them.

**No economic account of the empire from inside it beyond the revenue reforms**. The trade is visible from the outside — English, Dutch and Portuguese letters, ivory, pepper, the value of a sack — and the internal picture stops at what the state took from a field.

## Where two chapters pull against each other

**Ch. 5 and ch. 10 give two accounts of what his word is worth**. Under the canopy at Pratapgad both sides broke an agreement they had negotiated in writing, and the book reports it as a contest of cunning that he won. In the durbar at Agra his refusal to accept a rank turns on the fact that a promise made to him — no military rank, no attendance at court — had been broken. The book does not reconcile these and neither does this report.

**Ch. 8 and ch. 11 disagree about how a state is paid for**. Surat is a crore and a half taken out of somebody else's city in four days. The three quiet years are revenue measured field by field at fixed rates, with the collection taken out of officials' hands. Both are his, four years apart, and the second is what the first was for.

**Ch. 9 is the chapter that breaks the book's own pattern, and it is the one the legend forgets**. Every other opponent is out-thought. Jai Singh asks Aurangzeb for full freedom of decision before he starts, gets it, buys the *deshmukhs*, isolates Bijapur, picks a camp between his enemy and his enemy's possible ally, and proves that cannon can be carried up to the *machi*. He wins. The author says outright that the Marathi telling of what happens next treats Shivaji as the sole driver of predestined events, and that the truth is the reverse.

## What the by-chapter reading recovered

The merged whole-book report had the rebellion, the coronation, the two Surat raids and the question of what kind of state it was. It could not have had these, because each appears once:

- Dadoji Konddev paying a bounty for dead wolves to get people back into a ruined Pune (ch. 2).
- The *patil* of Ranjhe sacked for a sexual offence, his hands and feet cut off, in the first letter that carries the Sanskrit seal (ch. 2).
- The Mores telling him he is an upstart of yesterday and inviting him to come and see what kind of reception Jaawali gives (ch. 3).
- Goa instructing its captains to refuse the Siddis help ostensibly and give it secretly (ch. 4).
- Kanhoji Jedhe renouncing his hereditary *watan* by tipping water off his right hand (ch. 5).
- Rai Bagan, a widow riding in the Mughal ranks at Umbarkhind, talking her own commander into surrender (ch. 6).
- A boy dressed as a bridegroom with drums and music getting a hundred Marathas through the gates of Pune (ch. 7).
- Anthony Smith's hat coming off in the execution line at Surat, and the reason he was spared being that he had already agreed to carry messages (ch. 8).
- Murar Baji Deshpande refusing Diler Khan's assurance of safety, and being shot before his sword came down (ch. 9).
- Guards reporting that the Raja had vanished in their view and they did not know whether he had entered the earth or gone up into the sky (ch. 10).
- Cash advanced to a farmer to buy oxen, recovered gradually according to his ability, without interest (ch. 11).
- A Kshatriya king having to be given the sacred thread and married to all his wives again before he could be crowned (ch. 12).
- The suggestion that if the tax on non-Muslims is really justified, it should be collected first from Raja Raj Singh, who is the leader of the Hindus (ch. 13).

## Evidence

Read from `RAW/books/Shivaji-India's Great Warrior King.md`, lines 22–3402, in fourteen runs. The per-chapter footnotes and line ranges live in the three parts; this file cites none of its own, and every claim in it is traceable to a run.

**What kind of book this is**. A biography written against a living cult, in a state where its subject is a working political symbol. The author separates himself from that repeatedly and specifically: the oath at Raireshwar is a forgery, the renaming of Sinhagad is backwards, the Bijapur court story is apocryphal, the opium-stupefied garrison is dubious and named as the source of a film scene, the anti-colonial reading of the Rajapur arrests is reading history backwards, and the religious motive for the Goa invasion rests on one Englishman's letter and is contradicted by the treaty.

**Where the author states a view rather than a finding**. That the state was a Hindu polity and neither secular nor theocratic. That conquest and empire-building are male megalomania of a revolting form. That Aurangzeb humiliated him at Agra deliberately as a demonstration to the other nobles. All three are his and are reported as his.

**Bounded absence**. The gaps named above are gaps in lines 22–3402, not claims about the book as a whole or about the seventeenth-century Deccan in general.

# What the Bolsheviks Took For Granted — Preface to Chapter 5

> **Preface, Prologue, Introduction and chapters 1–5 of Edvard Radzinsky, *Stalin*** — the archive that was opened, the birth date that was changed, a boy in Gori, the seminary, the underground, and the man who came out of it.
