## Ch. 8 — The steppe inside the Forbidden City

A man builds a temple to his ancestors and then will not go inside it. In 1263 Khubilai ordered an ancestral temple raised for his family and told his ministers to perform the Chinese ceremonies for the dead there. He stayed well away from them himself, because Mongols avoided anything touching death.[^1] The following year he put up Chinese-style ancestral tablets. In 1277 he gave his dead ancestors Chinese names and had portraits made of all of them, so that steppe warriors came out on the wall looking like Mandarin sages.

So what counts as real here is not the ceremony. It is the picture the ceremony leaves in the head of somebody watching. He changed his reign name in 1264 to Zhiyuan, "complete beginning," and in 1271 turned that into the name of the dynasty itself — Da Yuan, "great origins."[^2] A new start for his Chinese subjects, and a new start for his Mongol ones too. He won control of China by looking more Chinese than the Chinese, or at least more Chinese than the Sung.

The educated men of China had wanted one country for centuries and had almost never had one. They shared a written language, the classics, a style of painting. Below them the common people spoke different languages inside a shifting patchwork of temporary states and ruling families.[^3] **A barbarian from the grasslands could offer them the thing their own dynasty had failed to deliver**, and that is what he offered.

What makes things happen, in his hands, is patience applied to a whole civilization at once. He did not chase quick popularity. He ran a policy of nearly two decades aimed at the loyalty of a continent.[^4] The Sung did not fall in a battle. Soldiers deserted. Officials deserted. Merchants took their trade north. Priests and scholars found they could move about more freely under the Mongols. In the end Chinese generals came over with whole regiments of soldiers and sailors, and the dynasty came apart by erosion rather than by conquest. Bayan took Hangzhou in 1276.

Time here runs on Heaven's approval, and approval is something you can be seen to be gaining. Every small victory in the field was read as another sign that Heaven had moved its Mandate off the Sung and onto him.[^5] The Sung leaders were painted as soft men who loved showing off their money more than fighting. The Chinese masses, oddly, found more of their own taste in the Mongols than in their own court officials.

Now look at where he actually slept. Behind high walls at the middle of Khanbalik, guarded by Mongol warriors, the royal family went on living as Mongols. There were large open areas for animals in the centre of the city, which no Chinese capital had ever had. **This Forbidden City was a small piece of steppe kept alive inside the Mongol capital**, and it was full of gers.[^6] The court often preferred to live and eat and sleep in them. Pregnant wives of the khan made sure their children were born in a ger. The children took their school lessons in one as they grew.

Inside those walls a person is a Mongol and behaves like one. They drank hard, slurped their soup loudly, and cut meat with knives at the table — which the Chinese found disgusting, since carving belonged in the kitchen.[^7] Outside the walls the same man was a Chinese emperor. The friar Odoric of Pordenone came in the 1320s and described a Green Mount inside the palace grounds, trees planted on it, a lake beside it with geese and ducks and every kind of waterfowl. It sounds almost exactly like the older descriptions of Karakorum.

The city itself was built to be looked down. In 1272 he ordered a capital raised on the site of the old Jurched city his grandfather had taken in 1215, and connected it by canal to the Yellow River.[^8] Chinese cities of the day were mazes of winding alleys. This one had broad straight streets on a north-south grid, so the guards at one gate could see clear through to the guards at the opposite gate. The boulevards were wide enough for nine horsemen to gallop abreast, in case the people ever rose against their foreign rulers.

How people should relate, in law, changed in a direction nobody expected from a conquering army. He cut the number of capital offences in China from 233 to 135.[^9] Records survive for thirty of the thirty-four years of his reign. The worst year was 1283, with 278 executions; the best was 1263, with seven. Fewer than 2,500 people were executed in more than three decades. Where he could, he swapped fines for beatings, and set up a way for a criminal who repented to be pardoned.

Torture needed evidence first. The Mongol code of 1291 said officials had to have real evidence that this person committed this crime, not a suspicion, before a confession could be beaten out of anyone.[^10] And there is a small rule in there that shows exactly whose world it was. Chinese authorities tattooed a man's crimes on his forehead so he carried them forever. Mongols held the forehead to be where the soul lives, so **even a criminal's forehead could not be written on**. The tattoo went on the upper arm for the first two offences and the neck for the third. Where the practice did not already exist, it was not allowed to start.

What replaced writing on the man was writing on his house. Officials preferred to put the offence on a wall in front of the criminal's home, so the whole neighbourhood could keep an eye on him.[^11] They printed books on criminal investigation so ordinary citizens and small local councils could use them. They set minimum standards for what an official had to do at a crime scene, including how to handle and examine a body, with the report filed in triplicate and drawings showing where the wounds were.

How you know a man is fit for office is the sharpest break of the chapter. China selected administrators by examination in poetry and calligraphy, after years of study. He abolished the exams.[^12] In their place he took Tibetans, Armenians, Khitan, Arabs, Tajiks, Uighurs, Tangut, Turks, Persians and Europeans, and staffed each office by quota — northern Chinese, southern Chinese, foreigners — so every official sat surrounded by men of another religion and another language. He promoted cooks, gatekeepers, scribes and translators upward, which made them loyal to him and left them with no local people to be loyal to instead.

And with no ranked mandarins to run the districts, he put in the steppe's own machine. Wherever it could be done, the bureaucracy was replaced by councils built on the small *khuriltai*, the assembly where a steppe decision got argued out.[^13] They met daily. Any new measure needed the seal of at least two officials. The council had to debate and reach agreement, and the decision belonged to the group rather than to one man. By Chinese standards this was slow and impractical. The lower administration was salaried, too, instead of being unpaid scholars who lived off what they could extort from people needing a stamp.

None of that survived him. The Ming went straight back to offices and rule from above, and paid councils were not tried again in China until the twentieth century, when the founders of the republic and then the Communists reached for local councils and citizen participation all over again.[^14]

What is worth having, for a peasant, gets rewritten from the bottom. Farmers had always sat at the end of a long line of officials who ran the intimate details of their lives. He broke them into units of about fifty households, called a *she*, and handed the unit real authority.[^15] The *she* ran local farming, looked after the land and the water, and held food back against famine. It also had to educate the peasant children.

Public schools for everyone came out of that, including the children of farmers. Until then only the rich had the time and money to educate a child, which is how one family kept power over an illiterate village for generation after generation. The Mongols noticed that in winter a peasant child has time to learn. So the teaching was done in the spoken language rather than classical Chinese, and the lessons were practical.

Money went the same way — from a thing you carry to a thing you agree on. Paper currency was expanded until it ran the empire. Marco Polo describes it as made from mulberry bark, cut into rectangles of different sizes, marked with its value and stamped with a vermilion seal.[^16] Coins were bulky and slow to ship; paper was not. To refuse the paper carried the death penalty. Where there is paper there is credit, so the law let a merchant declare bankruptcy twice. On the third, he could be executed.

What a good evening looks like also changed, and it changed downward toward the crowd. Actors and singers had ranked in China about level with prostitutes. The Mongols raised them to professionals and built theatre districts so that plays did not have to happen in markets, brothels and taverns.[^17] Courtiers wanted acrobatics, loud music, bright paint and colourful costumes. It is reported, though nobody can check it, that no play was censored in his reign. Chinese drama plus Mongol patronage of music is where Peking Opera comes from.

There is a whole category of entertainment they would not have. No gladiators. No bear baiting, no dogfights, no bullfighting. **Executions were never allowed to become a public show**, the way beheadings and hangings and burnings were in European cities.[^18] A people who would flatten a city would not watch a man die for fun.

Then the sea, where all of it stopped working. In 1274 an armada of about nine hundred ships carried 23,000 Korean and Chinese infantry across the 110 miles to Japan, along with Mongol horsemen.[^19] The samurai rode out for single combat, as their own honour required. The Mongols held formation, fired exploding missiles and buried them in arrows. The Japanese fell back inland to a fortress, and the Mongols would not follow into country they had no intelligence on. They reloaded onto the ships. That night a fall storm came in off the ocean and smashed the hurriedly built boats against the rocks. Some thirteen thousand men died, most of them drowned.

Both sides then decided they had won. He told his court the invasion had succeeded, because the land battle was a victory and the loss of nearly the whole navy mattered less.[^20] He sent envoys back the following year telling the Japanese emperor to come in person and submit, after which he would be reappointed to rule Japan. In 1279 the Japanese executed the envoys. The second invasion in 1281 was bigger and worse — 3,500 Chinese ships that arrived late, a stone wall along the shore, men penned in the heat of June, sickness, and small Japanese boats coming out at night.

Java went the same way with a different insult. In 1289 an envoy asked for the same submission the nearby kingdoms had given. The Javanese king branded the man's face and sent him home.[^21] A thousand ships and twenty thousand soldiers sailed in 1292. The Mongol leaders were lured into an ambush at what was supposed to be a ceremonial submission, and the survivors left the island humiliated.

The old hunting instinct did not transfer to water, and four defeats drew the map. Poland, Egypt, Java and Japan — between 1242 and 1293 those four fights marked the outer edge of the Mongol world, and it never went past them.[^22]

The last picture in the chapter is the one that tells you where the tradition ended up. Every spring the cranes came north over China, and he waited for them in the countryside, lying on a silk couch under tiger skins in a gilded pavilion mounted on the backs of four elephants taken from Burma.[^23] He was too fat to sit a horse and gout hurt him. When he was ready, the roof rolled back and the cranes were so thick overhead they looked like cloud. Hundreds of falconers pulled the hoods off their birds, and the gyrfalcons and eagles went up and tore the cranes out of the sky one at a time.

His grandfather had made a law against hunting in spring, hunting being for winter. He found winter cold, even under ermine and sable with tiger skins on the floor, so he changed the law and moved the season.[^24] Tigers travelled with the procession in cages pulled by oxen; leopards rode on the hindquarters of horses behind their trainers. Astrologers, diviners, shamans and Tibetan monks came along to clear the clouds and the rain out of the sky ahead of the hunter.

The camp that met them each night was a portable city, with a pavilion that held a thousand guests. Everyone wore a *deel* of the same colour for the day, with rank showing in the jewels and pearls sewn into it and silver on the boots.[^25] A trained tiger walked in among the guests, bowed to the khan, and sat down beside the throne for the evening. Servants wore a silk veil across the nose and mouth so their breath would not reach the food. There were bull testicles fried in oil and basted with saffron, mutton tail fat dusted with flour and baked with leeks, and mare's milk from a herd of pure white mares kept for the khan alone.

Three generations after the founding, the Spirit Banner still rode in front of the column. It was leading a hunting party.[^26]

*Read: lines 1834–2027.*

---

## Ch. 9 — Priests instead of siege engines

An English king stands up in church for a monk from Beijing. During Mass in the winter of 1287–88, Edward I rose from his throne to honour Rabban Bar Sawma, envoy of Khubilai Khan, and then took the communion bread from the envoy's hand.[^27] Bar Sawma had probably travelled farther than any official envoy in history — some seven thousand miles overland from the Mongol capital, through the cities of the Middle East, and on into Europe. He had already seen the Ilkhan in Persia, the emperor in Constantinople, the cardinals in Rome and Philip IV in Paris.

What surprised him about Europe says more than what he was sent to say. He found that only one religion was allowed.[^28] He found that its leaders held political power over whole nations, and everyday power over ordinary lives. As a Christian he was pleased that his own religion had the monopoly. It was still nothing like home, where many religions flourished on the condition that they served the empire's needs before their own.

He failed. Not one monarch and not one church official signed anything. The single thing he got was a promise from the pope to send teachers to the Mongol court, which Khubilai had asked for several times already.[^29] He went back to Persia and told the story, and it was written down in Syriac.

So the empire stopped sending siege engines and started sending priests. Scholars later named the fourteenth century the Mongol Peace.[^30] **What could not be taken by arms was now to be got by trade and diplomacy** — the same old aim of putting everybody under one sky, pursued by other means.

What actually drove all of it was not a love of commerce. It was *khubi*, the system of shares.[^31] Every soldier, every widow and orphan had a right to a measure of anything seized in war, and Genghis Khan had made that formal. Every member of the Golden Family held a share of the wealth of every part of the empire. Hulegu ruled Persia and still owned twenty-five thousand households of silk workers in China under his brother. He owned valleys in Tibet. He had a claim on furs and falcons from the northern steppe, and pastures and horses and men back in Mongolia.

Each branch of the family demanded its proper share of astronomers, doctors, weavers, miners and acrobats. An army of clerks moved about the empire checking goods in one place against accounts in another.[^32] Persia sent spices, steel, jewels, pearls and textiles to the relatives in China; China sent porcelain and medicine back. Khubilai imported Persian translators and doctors and ten thousand Russian soldiers.

That is why the empire's politics could break without its economy breaking. Khaidu was often in open rebellion against Khubilai, and Khaidu also owned craftsmen and farmers around Nanjing.[^33] Between bouts of fighting his cousin he collected his Nanjing shipments, and let Khubilai collect his horses off the steppe. Refuse a man his share and he refuses yours. Money held the family together after loyalty had stopped.

Under that pressure the war roads turned into trade roads. Shelters were stocked every twenty to thirty miles along the routes, with transport animals and guides for hard country.[^34] In 1281 an expedition went out to find and map the source of the Yellow River, which the Mongols called the Black River, and opened a route from China into Tibet. Officials were told to seize maps and atlases in every camp and city they took. Under Jamal al-Din, craftsmen built globes for the khan in 1267 that showed Europe and Africa alongside Asia.

Armies move fastest on horses and cargo moves best on water, and they worked that out and acted on it. The Grand Canal was lengthened. Dams and reservoirs went up in Yunnan that lasted into modern times. The failed invasions had taught them shipbuilding, and the knowledge was turned to trade.[^35] In the first years the Mongols moved about 3,000 tons of food by sea. By 1329 it was 210,000.

How a person ranks in society was reordered by decree, and it was the merchants who won. Aristocrats from China to Europe held trade to be dirty and beneath them. A European manor was supposed to feed itself; what left it went to buy jewels and relics for the lord, not goods for the peasants.[^36] Chinese administrators had built walls partly to keep the country's wealth inside them. The Mongols put merchants second only to government officials, ahead of every religion and profession, and dropped the Confucian scholars from the top of society to the ninth rank — below prostitutes, above beggars.

Once you believe that a commonplace thing in one country is exotic in another, you go looking. The later decades of the century were a frantic hunt for anything that could be sold somewhere.[^37] Dyes, paper, drugs, pistachios, firecrackers, poison. The names of the cloths still carry the routes: satin from the port of Zaytun, damask from Damascus, muslin from Mosul.

The best small example is playing cards. Merchants and soldiers wanted a game they could carry, and cards weigh nothing next to a chessboard.[^38] To make them fast and cheap, printers used the carved blocks meant for religious scripture. The market for the cards turned out to be much bigger than the market for the scripture.

Now the thing that makes this empire unlike the others. Rome put its language, its gods, its wine and its olive oil into every province, and built the same city from Ephesus to Cologne.[^39] The British put Tudor houses in Bombay; the Dutch put windmills in the Caribbean. **The Mongols brought no architecture, no crop and no religion of their own to impose.** They mostly forbade non-Mongols to learn their language. And no single city swallowed the empire's wealth the way Rome or Babylon had — goods and people moved constantly from one part to another instead of piling up in a capital.

What they did instead was move people who knew things. Translators, scribes, doctors, astronomers and mathematicians were rounded up and parcelled out among the families in exactly the same shares as the musicians, cooks, goldsmiths, acrobats and painters.[^40] In 1261 the Office for the Stimulation of Agriculture was set up under eight commissioners to raise yields and look after the farmers, which was a real change of attitude for a government of herders. In Persia they set up the same kind of office as soon as they took the country, brought seeds and shoots and whole trees from China, and mixed the citrus varieties of India, China and Persia together. A Cotton Promotion Bureau followed in 1289.

Knowledge had to travel with the goods or the goods were worthless. A drug nobody knows how to use is not a trade item.[^41] So Persian and Arab doctors went into China and Chinese doctors went to the Middle East, and a House of Healing near Tabriz worked as hospital, research centre and training school for the medicine of both ends of the world. In 1313 Rashid al-Din published the first book on Chinese medicine to appear outside China, with illustrations made in China.

And you can see a whole worldview in which technique crossed and which did not. Acupuncture failed in the Middle East because putting needles around a body meant too much touching for Muslim custom.[^42] Pulse diagnosis succeeded everywhere, because the doctor only takes the wrist. It let a physician treat a woman without dishonouring her family.

Time had to be standardised, and that turned out to be an imperial problem rather than an astronomical one. A ruler with Heaven's Mandate has to show he can mark time — the phases of the moon, the turn of the seasons, and above all the eclipses.[^43] One court with one capital needs one calendar and can ignore everyone else's. An empire holding many peoples with many ways of counting the year cannot. So they built observatories almost as soon as they took a place, and standing orders went out to find the astronomers, the instruments and the charts in every conquered land.

Counting people broke the arithmetic they had. Censuses of people, animals and buildings, yearly settlements of goods sent back and forth, the movement of herds and soldiers and merchants — the numbers got too big for the methods.[^44] Clerks worked on the abacus. Administrators found European and Chinese mathematics too simple for the job and took what they needed from Arabic and Indian work instead. The word *algorithm* comes from al-Khwarizm, and it was under the Mongols that zero, negative numbers and algebra came into China.

Then the volume of paper beat the scribes. Records and letters could still be copied by hand; agricultural manuals, medical treatises, atlases and astronomical tables could not.[^45] Ogodei had ordered regional printing houses across northern China from 1236. Printing with movable type had probably started in China a century earlier, but a Chinese press needs thousands of characters and the Mongols had an alphabet, where the same few letters come round again and again. A printing office went up in 1269 to spread government decisions. Books got cheaper every year of the dynasty.

What is worth having, across all of it, is whatever works. **Because they had no system of their own to force on anybody, they were free to take systems from everywhere and bolt them together.**[^46] Their astronomy did not have to agree with the Bible. They looked for the thing that worked and then carried it somewhere else.

Europe was never ruled by them and profited most. It got the trade, the technology and the awakening without paying for the conquest.[^47] Water and wind power came into mining and milling and metalwork; the improved blast furnace arrived along the trade roads and let metalworkers reach higher temperatures. Paper replaced parchment, which had needed a herder, a slaughterer, a skinner and weeks of scraping and soaking and stretching for a single page. Gutenberg printed two hundred Bibles in 1455.

Francis Bacon, in 1620, named printing, gunpowder and the compass as the three things the modern world was built on, and said no empire or sect or star had exercised greater power over human affairs.[^48] What the Renaissance was reborn out of, on this account, was not Greece and Rome. It was the Mongol Empire, picked up and adapted.

You can see it in the paint. Pope Nicholas IV called for a new mother church at Assisi in May 1288, weeks after receiving Bar Sawma and the letter and gifts he carried.[^49] The Franciscans had closer ties to the Mongol court than any other group in Europe. In the frescoes at Assisi the life of Saint Francis is literally wrapped in silk, with painted and figured textiles framing the scenes and draped below them. Mongols appear in Christian pictures in their own clothes and headgear and with their own bows, and horses start turning up drawn in the Chinese manner. European painting had been flat for the whole Middle Ages, and what came out of the mixing was a style of depth and light and cloth and horses.

Then it gets specific enough to be unmistakable. In a Padua painting of 1306, the Robe of Christ is Mongol cloth in the Mongol style, and the gold trim along it is written in the square Phagspa script Khubilai commissioned.[^50] In the same church the Vice of Infidelity wears the pith-helmet hat the khan favoured, and Old Testament prophets hold open scrolls covered in undecipherable Mongol writing.

The ideas travelled with the cloth. Nicolaus of Cusa wrote "On the Peace of Faith" in 1453, an imaginary conversation among representatives of seventeen nations and religions about how to get global peace.[^51] His Tatar speaker calls his own people simple worshippers of one God who are astonished at the variety of rites among people worshipping that same God, and who laugh at circumcision and branding and baptism alike. That is almost word for word what Mongke Khan had said to a French envoy: the Jews say they got the commandments from Moses, the Arabs from Muhammad, the Christians from Jesus, so how shall we arrive at concord? The Mongol answer had been that only the state can hold religions in one peace.

By 1390 the terror had turned into a story to entertain pilgrims. In *The Canterbury Tales*, the Squire tells a romance about Genghis Khan — hardy, wise and rich, just and merciful, true to his word, honourable, and there was nowhere such another man.[^52]

## Ch. 10 — The fleas in the grain sacks

A man is well at breakfast and dissolving by evening. Fever came on hot, then chills, then vomiting and diarrhoea.[^53] Blood began to seep under the skin and discolour it, and lumps formed and broke while the family stood and watched. In 1332 the royal family stayed on at the summer capital past the end of summer, and whatever they did to keep it quiet, it was clear the dynasty was in trouble. Between 1328 and 1332 at least four members of the Golden Family held the office of Great Khan, one of them a seven-year-old, amid assassinations and disappearances and deaths nobody could explain.

What makes things happen, in the end, is an animal too small to see. The plague lives in fleas, the fleas travel on rats, and the rats travel in shipments of grain and tribute.[^54] Fleas do not usually take to humans, and the smell of horses drives them off — but a sack of grain or a bundle of clothing will carry them anywhere people go. Once they reached the Gobi they found marmot burrows and rodent colonies and have lived there ever since. **A nomad camp is close to horses, thin on people and short of rats, which is why the disease could never get going there.** A Chinese city was the opposite in every particular.

The numbers do not fit inside a normal history. Chroniclers recorded that ninety per cent of the people of Hopei died in 1331.[^55] By 1351 China had reportedly lost between half and two-thirds of its population. A country of some 123 million at the start of the thirteenth century was down to as low as 65 million by the end of the fourteenth.

And it moved along the roads that the peace had built. Graves near the trading posts show the plague crossing the Tian Shan by 1338 and wiping out a Christian trading community near Lake Issyk Kul.[^56] It reached Sarai on the lower Volga in 1345. **This was an epidemic of commerce**, carried by the same caravans and rest stations that carried the silk.

One famous story about it is thinner than it looks. Yanibeg was besieging the Genoese trading post at Kaffa when plague broke out in his army and forced him to lift the siege. A European report says he had the bodies of the dead catapulted over the walls into the city.[^57] The only known source is the papers of a lawyer, Gabriele de Mussis, who worked near Genoa and said he had heard it from some sailors. It is repeated constantly and rests on nothing anybody saw.

The ship turned out to be better than the city. Humans, rats and fleas shut in together, and neither horses nor fire anywhere near them.[^58] When the Genoese fled Kaffa by boat they carried it to Constantinople, and from there to Cairo and to Messina. In 1348 it went through the cities of Italy and reached England by June. By the winter of 1350 it had crossed the North Atlantic through the Faeroes and Iceland to Greenland. It may have killed sixty per cent of the Icelanders, and it was probably what finally finished the Viking colony in Greenland.

Between 1340 and 1400 the population of Africa fell from about 80 million to 68 million, and Asia from 238 million to 201 million.[^59] Europe went from around 75 million to 52 million. World population dropped from roughly 450 million to somewhere between 350 and 375 million — over a million people a year, every year, for the rest of the century.

What people did about it says what they thought was real. Milan sealed up any house where plague appeared, with everyone inside — sick and well, friends and servants alike — and Milan came through.[^60] Other cities rang their bells, or banned the ringing of bells. In 1348 the small Tuscan city of Pistoia barred anyone from an infected area, banned imported second-hand cloth, and forbade the sale of fruit and the slaughtering of animals, because the smell of death was suspected. The tanning trade was stopped, so the leather trade stopped with it. Anyone returning from elsewhere could bring about thirty pounds of baggage. No gifts to a house where someone had died, no visits there, and nobody was to buy new clothing.

Boccaccio wrote down what it did to people, having lost family and friends to it in Florence in 1348. Husbands left wives. Mothers left children.[^61] Priests had no time for services, gravediggers could not keep up, and bodies went into group pits or were left for the dogs and pigs. Ten young nobles flee the city in his book and pass the time telling stories.

Nobody had the cause, but everyone could see the association with trade and with strangers moving in and out of cities. So the two reactions were to leave the city or to shut it, and either one killed commerce, communication and transport at a stroke.[^62] Delegations and letters stopped. The Catholic church lost contact with its missions in China. In Europe Christians turned on the Jews, who were tied in people's minds to trade and to the east. Some were shut in their houses and burned; others were racked until they confessed. Clement VI issued a bull in July 1348 telling Christians to stop, and it did not stop.

Now watch what the disease did to the share system. The Mongols in Persia could no longer get the goods off their own lands and workshops in China. The family in China could not get its goods out of Russia or Persia.[^63] The interlocking ownership that had held cousins together through open warfare simply came apart. Their subjects had outnumbered them by as much as a thousand to one and had tolerated them because the goods kept coming long after the army had gone soft. With no trade and no prospect of Mongol reinforcement, each branch was on its own.

So they went looking for legitimacy in religion, and religion split them. The Golden Horde in Russia became Muslim before their cousins in Persia and promptly allied with Egypt against them.[^64] When the Ilkhanate converted it moved between Sunni and Shiite as the moment required, and under Oljeitu there was a hard persecution of Buddhists and Jews. The one rule that had held the whole thing together — that every religion is protected and none rules — was the first thing to go.

In China they did the opposite of what had worked, and did it on the advice of a dream. Members of the court reported dreams in which Genghis Khan appeared and demanded new measures to hold the Chinese down.[^65] Officials concluded that the Chinese had been given too much freedom. Rumours ran of plans to kill Chinese children in numbers, or to kill everyone bearing particular family names. The even-handed treatment of religions was dropped in favour of Tibetan Buddhism, precisely because it stood furthest from Chinese ideas. Local people along the new road to Tibet had to feed and house and carry the monks and their goods, and the monks took the hatred that could not safely be aimed at the Mongols.

Cut off from their subjects and helpless against the plague, the court went inward. The monks told them the troubles of society were illusion and the thing to work on was one's own soul.[^66] Freeing a prisoner earned merit toward a better next life, and the monks turned that into a trade. In one ceremony a monk rode through the palace gates on a yellow ox wearing the Emperor's gown. Tantric rites promising enlightenment through sexual acts became court practice, with elaborate dances and the Great Khan himself taking part under the eyes of the lamas. The secrecy fed Chinese suspicion that human sacrifice was going on to keep the khan alive.

Outside those walls, the money died. Paper currency had turned out to work by rules more complicated than the officials understood.[^67] Every sign of weakness in the administration knocked confidence in the paper, which pushed up the value of copper and silver, which fed the inflation.

Persia collapsed in 1335 and China in 1368. The Ilkhanate simply vanished, killed off or absorbed into the far larger population it had ruled.[^68] Togoon Tumur got out of China with some sixty thousand Mongols and left about four hundred thousand behind to be killed or absorbed. Those who got home went back to herding, almost as though the whole Chinese episode from 1211 to 1368 had been a long stay at the southern summer camp.

The Ming set about scrubbing it off. Chinese were forbidden to wear Mongol dress or give their children Mongol names.[^69] The Muslim, Christian and Jewish traders the Mongols had settled were expelled. The failing paper money was abolished outright and the country went back to metal. Tibetan Buddhism was rejected. They moved the capital south to Nanjing, which was a more Chinese place — and then had to move back, because in the minds of most people a united China was ruled from the northern city. They rebuilt the Forbidden City in their own style, and Beijing is still the capital, inside roughly the borders the Mongols drew.

Then the strange part. Having purged it, they could not let it go.[^70] The Ming hunted for the official Mongol seal, and kept Mongol as the language of diplomacy — as late as 1453 the Chinese court was still sending its letters in it. The Manchu, who overthrew the Ming in 1644, married into the descendants of Genghis Khan so they could claim to be his heirs in blood as well as in spirit. **The front of the empire stayed standing for centuries after the building behind it had fallen down.**

Timur is what happens when the front is all that is left. He was a Turkic warrior who claimed descent from Genghis Khan on flimsy evidence, took much of the old territory from India to the Mediterranean, and paid for books linking the two of them.[^71] He piled pyramids of heads outside the cities he took and enjoyed public torture. To the people underneath, one Mongol looked like another, so what Timur did was assumed to be the Mongol way — and got assigned backwards to Genghis Khan, who had been dead for a century and a half.

His descendants ran India. Babur founded the dynasty in 1519, thirteen generations down from Genghis Khan's second son.[^72] Akbar, his grandson, ruled from 1556 to 1608, abolished the tax on non-Muslims, organised his cavalry in the old units of ten, built a civil service on merit, raised the standing of women against both Muslim and Hindu custom, and tried to fold every religion into one Divine Faith.

And Europe never got the news that the empire had ended. When the communication system broke, the reports stopped.[^73] So in 1492 Christopher Columbus persuaded Isabella and Ferdinand that he could reopen contact with the court of the Great Khan, more than a century after the last one ruled China. He sailed with a printed Marco Polo full of his own notes, treating it as a practical guide. Reaching Cuba, he believed he was on the edge of the khan's realm. When he could not find it, he decided these people must be the Mongols' southern neighbours in India — which is how the native peoples of the Americas came to be called Indians.

Now the reputation turns, and it turns for reasons that have nothing to do with Mongols. Voltaire took a Mongol-era Chinese play and rewrote it as *The Orphan of China*, first staged in Paris in 1755 while he sat safely in Switzerland.[^74] His Genghis Khan is ignorant and cruel and ends the play asking what he gained by all his victories. His real target was the French king, whom he did not dare attack directly. Giovanni Casti did the same thing to the Hapsburgs and Catherine the Great, using an opera about Kublai with music by Salieri.

Then the scientists made it permanent. Blumenbach, a professor of medicine at Göttingen, sorted humanity by skin colour, hair, skull shape and the size of noses and lips, and on the theory that Asians came from Mongolia he filed all of them under "Mongol."[^75] Robert Chambers, in an 1844 bestseller, ranked the races as stages on the way to the highest, which was European. Theorists then noticed that Asians sat with folded legs like an orangutan.

The worst of it lands on children. Because some children with learning disabilities have Asian-looking features, it seemed obvious that they belonged to the Mongoloid race.[^76] In 1867 John Langdon Down, running an asylum in Surrey, formalised the categories in a paper on the ethnic classification of idiots. To explain why European children should have Asian features, scientists reached back to the thirteenth century: marauding Huns, Avars and Mongols had raped white women, and here were the descendants. A British physician published *The Mongol in Our Midst* in 1924 and listed the stigmata — small earlobes, small genitals. The conclusion was that these children did not belong in their own communities.

Meanwhile the people the theory was aimed at picked him up as a hero. Across Asia, a generation trying to get out from under Europe found in Genghis Khan the greatest Asian conqueror in history and a direct answer to the doctrine of European superiority.[^77]

The clearest case is a man in a prison cell. On New Year's Day 1931 Nehru learned that the British had arrested his wife and put her in another prison, and that she had been badly treated.[^78] Their thirteen-year-old daughter could see her parents once a fortnight. So he began writing her letters, four or five pages nearly every day for three years, to give her a history that was not the one taught in colonial schools. Working through Genghis Khan, he wrote that the Mongols had built a real civilization without cities, that their victories came from discipline and organisation, and that Alexander and Caesar seem petty before him.

The armies of the twentieth century read him as a manual. The Soviets, the Japanese and the Germans all raced to translate and interpret the newly available *Secret History*, hoping for the key to how the Mongols beat China and Russia.[^79] The tank had just put cavalry and artillery back into one unit for the first time since the mounted archer. The Germans found their version in the blitzkrieg. The Soviets found theirs in luring the Germans deeper and deeper into Russia until they were spread too thin, which is the tactic Subodei used on the Russians themselves at the Kalka River in 1223. Stalin had Timur's body exhumed and sent expeditions to Burkhan Khaldun to look for Genghis Khan's.

The line finally ran out in exile. Sayid Alim Khan, last reigning descendant, emir of Bukhara, died in Kabul in 1944 after a quarter-century away from the city he had ruled.[^80] He had fled in 1920, and as he went, Bolshevik forces attacked the citadel of Bukhara — the same fortress where, exactly seven centuries earlier, the Spirit Banner had led the Mongols to their first victory in central Asia.

And the last thing to go was the banner. Russia and China divided his homeland between them for most of the twentieth century. *Pravda* warned in April 1964 against putting the bloodthirsty barbarian on a pedestal.[^81] The purges that followed destroyed a whole generation of Mongolian linguists, historians and archaeologists whose work touched him even at a distance. Somewhere in the 1960s, eight centuries after his birth, the *sulde* — the Spirit Banner he had carried across Eurasia — disappeared from wherever the authorities had been keeping it.

## Epilogue — A pile of stones in the wind

Nine geldings walk out onto the steppe in April 2000 to retrace a chase from eight centuries earlier. The party was following the path Temujin's family took when they fled the Merkid who came to kidnap Borte.[^82] The local herding boys riding with them were about the age of the ones whose trail they were on, just as good with horses, and wearing the traditional *deel* with a gold silk sash wrapped tight below the waist. Under it, sometimes, jeans. On a few heads, a baseball cap.

They did not have to search for the route. The descriptions of the horses in the *Secret History* are precise enough that the party could have matched their own animals to them by age and colour and shape.[^83] Instead they took the horses an old and slightly drunk herder said were right for the job, and followed the nomads' own sense of where a horse and rider would have gone.

What a person is, here, is somebody with a history that happened last week. For the herders and the scholars alike, the past around them was neither abstract nor far off.[^84] Professor Lkhagvasuren had ridden this country many times with his teacher, the archaeologist Perlee — and when the authorities put Perlee in prison, they arrested Lkhagvasuren's father too. The knowledge had been forbidden inside living memory, which is why the herders wanted a stone cut. They asked for it so their children would know.

Time on this ground has almost no depth to it. He came back to Burkhan Khaldun after every victory, for rest and recovery.[^85] He changed the world and let nothing change in the country he was born in. Hawks still go over in spring. The insects still sing in summer. Nomads still move to the hills in autumn and wolves still hunt in winter.

**And the long war he fought the last great campaign of was already lost when he fought it.** He was the heir of ten thousand years of fighting between the herders and the farmers, the same quarrel as the Bedouin against the idols of the city and the Romans against the Huns.[^86] It did not stop with him, but it never again reached that pitch. Sitting Bull and Crazy Horse, Red Eagle, Tecumseh, Shaka Zulu — none of them had ever heard of him, and all of them fought his war and lost it. Settled civilization won. The future went to the people who stay in one place and keep pushing outward.

What is worth having, at the end of the ride, weighs almost nothing. The party came back to the windy place where they thought Borte had been taken, and stood quiet.[^87] Old campsites were marked on the ground by the big stones once used to hold gers down in the wind. One by one, people walked off to gather a few stones and piled them on the spot, the way nomads have marked places for thousands of years. The senior horseman collected dried horse dung and set it in front of the stones, and the others spread their *deels* open to block the wind while he lit it.

Then Professor Sukhbaatar sprinkled ground cedar into the fire, and everyone stood up straighter.[^88] How you know when to cut the stone was settled the same afternoon. A student was sent to fetch the professor's worn almanac, and he squinted through smudged glasses at the charts, made notes with a stub of pencil, did the sums, and named the day that would be right for it. One man would write the text, another would design the Old Mongol calligraphy, and the students would find the stone and cut it. Professor Lkhagvasuren pulled a bottle of vodka out of his *deel*, sprinkled it on the stones, threw some into the air and touched it to his forehead.

Each man took off his hat, knelt in front of the stones and put his head to the frozen ground.[^89] Then each pulled something small out of a pocket and left it there — the stub of a sugar cube, a few matches, a sweet wrapped in crinkling paper, a scatter of tea leaves. Small gifts of food and warmth, left eight centuries late, for a frightened young woman being carried off on a horse.

# Below the Line

*Everything from here down is speculative by design. Above the line, every claim carries a footnote and a line range. Below it, the writing is allowed to weigh alternatives, run counterfactuals and hand the decision to advisors from other traditions — because that is the job of these sections.*

## Ch. 8 — Roads Not Taken `[SPECULATIVE]`

**A live alternative, on the table at the time.** The chapter names one course that was available and rejected: keeping the mandarin examination system. Every Chinese administrator in the empire expected it, and the men who had spent their youth studying for it were the natural pool of officials for a new dynasty. Khubilai refused, and took Tibetans, Armenians, Persians and Europeans instead. The cost is visible in what happened afterwards — the exam class stayed outside the government for a century, and was waiting when the Ming arrived.

**A constructed alternative.** Suppose he had kept the exams and staffed the empire from the Chinese scholar class. He gains an administration that runs itself and a literate elite with a stake in the dynasty. He loses the thing his grandfather built everything on: officials with no local ties, promoted from the kitchen, whose whole career depends on the khan. The forecast — a forecast, not a finding — is that the dynasty lasts longer and stops being Mongol sooner, and that the *she* units and the peasant schools are never tried at all, because a mandarin has no reason to teach a farmer's son to read.

## Ch. 8 — Counsel From Elsewhere `[SPECULATIVE]`

Take the decision to move the hunting season out of winter because the khan found the cold unpleasant.

**A Stoic advisor**, working from [[ARCHIVES/concepts/history/stoic-dichotomy-of-control|the dichotomy of control]], would not object to the discomfort. He would object to the direction of the fix. The cold is outside your power and your response to it is inside it. A man who changes his grandfather's law rather than his own habit has quietly swapped which of the two he takes to be adjustable. The law was the easier thing to move, and that is the tell.

**An advisor working from [[ARCHIVES/concepts/behavioral-mechanics/shih-and-strategic-depth|shih]]** — position built up in advance so the situation does the work later — would read it as spending stored advantage on nothing. The winter hunt was a rehearsal. The tumens spread left and right, the encirclement, the drive. Move it to spring for comfort and you keep the shape and lose the training, and the shape without the training is a parade.

They converge, from unrelated doctrine, on the same point. The change looks small because what it changed was a date. What it actually changed was which of two things the khan treated as fixed.

## Ch. 9 — What Transfers `[SPECULATIVE]`

**Decision type: holding a coalition together after the reason for it has gone.**

The transferable pattern is the share system. Cousins at open war went on shipping each other goods, because each held property inside the other's territory and could be cut off in return. The bond was not loyalty and not ideology. It was mutual hostage-taking of assets, and it outlasted every political agreement in the empire.

**Scope conditions, which is where it fails.** It holds only while the assets keep producing. The plague did not break the alliance by turning cousins against each other. It broke the alliance by making the shares worthless, and the loyalty underneath was found to be nothing. So the pattern works where the shared asset is durable and its yield is roughly independent of the relationship. It fails wherever one shock can flatten the yield everywhere at once, because then every party discovers at the same moment that they have nothing to lose by walking.

**Modern equivalent:** cross-shareholding between rival firms, and supply chains built so each side holds something the other cannot replace. Same strength, same single point of failure.

## Ch. 10 — Roads Not Taken `[SPECULATIVE]`

**A live alternative, named in the chapter.** After the plague, the Mongol rulers of China chose repression and Tibetan Buddhism. The chapter says plainly that Khubilai's own method was available and was not understood by his successors — he had made himself powerful by appearing Chinese, and his descendants went the other way on purpose, trying to be as un-Chinese as possible. The Middle Eastern branch did adopt the local religion and the local law, and got a longer hybrid afterlife out of it in the Turco-Mongol states.

**A constructed alternative.** Suppose the Yuan court had gone further into Chinese practice as the crisis deepened. Restore the exams, promote the Confucian scholars back up the ranks, take the plague as the emperor's own failure in the way a Chinese ruler was expected to. The forecast is that the dynasty still falls, because the money was gone and the trade was gone. But it falls as a Chinese dynasty that failed, rather than as foreigners who were expelled, and the Ming purge of everything Mongol does not happen edict by edict. The difference between the two endings is not military. It is a matter of which story the survivors could tell about who had just fallen.

## Ch. 10 — Counsel From Elsewhere `[SPECULATIVE]`

Take the court's turn inward — the monks advising that the world's troubles are illusion and the work is on one's own soul, while the currency collapsed outside the walls.

**A Buddhist advisor working from [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/anicca-impermanence-constant-flux|impermanence]]** would not be on the monks' side here, and that is the interesting part. Impermanence says everything made of parts comes apart. That cuts against the dynasty, and it cuts just as hard against the merit accounting the court had bought into. Buying prisoners' freedom to bank credit for the next life treats merit as a store of value that lasts. It is the same mistake the paper money made, moved into another currency.

**A Confucian advisor**, of the kind whose cultivation content [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/why-the-cultivation-content-of-confucius-vanished|got hollowed out of the tradition]], would say something blunter. The ruler's inner state is not private. It shows up in the granary, in whether the roads are safe, in whether the magistrate can be bribed. A ruler working on his own soul behind a wall has misunderstood where the soul was supposed to be visible.

The two converge from unrelated doctrine. Both treat the withdrawal as a mistake about categories rather than as cowardice. The court thought it had chosen the spiritual over the worldly. Neither advisor accepts that those were two different things.

## Ch. 10 — What Transfers `[SPECULATIVE]`

**Decision type: managing a reputation you no longer control.**

Timur is the mechanism, stated cleanly. He claimed the name, did his own atrocities under it, and the atrocities were assigned backwards to the man whose name he had borrowed. Nobody underneath could tell one Mongol from another, so the borrower's conduct rewrote the lender's record — a century and a half after the lender was dead, with nobody left to object.

**Scope conditions.** This works on the borrower's side only where the original is famous, distant and unable to answer, and where the audience cannot tell members of the category apart. It fails where the audience has direct contact with the original, or where the category is small enough that individuals stay visible. Reverse it and the same conditions give you the defence: the way to protect a name from a claimant is to keep the audience close enough to tell people apart.

**Modern equivalent:** a discredited franchisee, a movement's most violent faction, an imitator trading on a founder's name. In every case the record of the original gets set by the loudest current claimant rather than by the original's own conduct. The correction, if it comes at all, arrives centuries late and through people with a separate reason to want it — as it did here, through a man writing letters to his daughter from a prison cell.

## Epilogue — What Transfers `[SPECULATIVE]`

**Decision type: recovering a history that was made illegal.**

The herders asked for the stone because the knowledge had been forbidden in their own lifetimes, and they wanted their children to have it in a form that could not be taken away again. That is the same instinct this vault has already met in [[ARCHIVES/concepts/history/archive-as-resistance|keeping a record as an act of resistance]] and in [[ARCHIVES/concepts/history/chimalpahin-annals-indigenous-historiography|the annals written by the conquered in their own language]]. Three peoples, no contact between them, the same move. When the handing-down is broken by force, put it into the most durable object available and let the interpretation come later.

**Scope conditions.** The stone works because it is illegible to nobody and expensive to remove. It fails wherever the occupying power is thorough enough to destroy objects as well as forbid speech — which is exactly what happened to the *sulde* itself, kept by the authorities and then simply gone. So the pattern holds where suppression works by prohibition, and fails where suppression works by confiscation. The herders' stone and the missing Spirit Banner are the two halves of that condition, in the same book, sixty years apart.

---

## Evidence

Read from `RAW/books/Genghis Khan and the Making of the Modern World.md`, lines 1834–2441: ch. 8 (1834–2027), ch. 9 (2028–2221), ch. 10 (2222–2385), Epilogue (2386–2441).

**Hagiography check.** This is an openly rehabilitative account, and chapters 8 and 9 lean hardest. The legal reforms, the peasant schools, the printing and the religious tolerance arrive as one package, and the reader is not shown much of what the Chinese peasantry made of any of it. Two details from the chapter itself push back, and both are kept above the line — the boulevards built nine horsemen wide against an uprising, and the ethnic quotas designed so that no official could trust his colleagues. Both describe a governing class that expected to be hated.

**Survivor bias.** Ch. 10 is unusual in that it shows the losers. Timur's version of the Mongol name survived and Khubilai's did not, and the chapter says so — the practices assigned to Genghis Khan in later centuries are Timur's.

**Single-source flag.** The catapulted plague corpses at Kaffa rest on one lawyer's report of what some sailors told him, and the text says so directly. Reported here at that weight and no stronger.

**Bounded absence.** No claim is made here about material outside lines 1834–2441.

# What Runs Through All of It — Genghis Khan and the Making of the Modern World

> **Closing pass across all eleven chapter runs of Jack Weatherford, *Genghis Khan and the Making of the Modern World*.** Read from `RAW/books/Genghis Khan and the Making of the Modern World.md`, Introduction through Epilogue. Written last, out of the finished runs.
>
> **Siblings:** [[LAB/Worldview Reports/weatherford-genghis-khan-worldview-archaeology-part-1|Part 1 — Introduction and Chapters 1–3]] · [[LAB/Worldview Reports/weatherford-genghis-khan-worldview-archaeology-part-2|Part 2 — Chapters 4–7]] · [[LAB/Worldview Reports/weatherford-genghis-khan-worldview-archaeology-part-3|Part 3 — Chapters 8–10 and the Epilogue]]. No sibling thread map exists for this source yet.
>
> ⚠ **Supersedes** [[LAB/Worldview Reports/weatherford-genghis-khan-worldview-archaeology|the original whole-book report]], which merged eleven chapters into one account and was built from vault concept pages rather than from RAW.

*Source ingest: [[ARCHIVES/sources/weatherford-genghis-khan-and-making-of-modern-world|Jack Weatherford, Genghis Khan and the Making of the Modern World]]*

---

## What Runs Through All of It

Nothing important in this world stays inside a body or a building. A man's soul lives in the horsehair on his spear, out in the weather. The one God cannot be shut in a house of stone, which is why a conqueror asks whether the mosque is the sultan's house before he will walk into it. A person's soul is in their smell, so you sniff a child instead of kissing them, and a widow sends her husband away holding her blouse. The forehead is where the soul sits, so a criminal's forehead may not be tattooed. And Fatima was killed by having every opening in her body sewn shut, so that nothing of her soul could get out.

**That is one belief, appearing in six chapters, doing something different every time** — a banner, a refusal, a farewell, a legal reform, a torture. It is the assumption the whole book rests on and it is never argued anywhere in the book, because nobody inside it needed it argued.

The second thing running end to end is that authority has to be visibly given, and can be visibly withheld. A *khuriltai* was a vote where you voted by turning up, and staying home counted against. He waited a year for one before taking the title. His followers stood him on a black felt carpet, told him his authority came from Heaven, then lifted the carpet over their heads. Before invading the Jurched he called an assembly so anyone could refuse by absence, then went off alone for three days while the whole nation fasted bareheaded. Sorkhokhtani won an election she could not convene in the capital by holding it in the homeland instead, where nobody could refuse to come.

And it kept working after it stopped meaning anything. **Khubilai put the same assembly into China as a daily council of two seals and consensus, in a country that had run on ranked mandarins for a thousand years** — and the Ming abolished it within a generation. What survived him was the shape of the thing without its purpose: the Spirit Banner still riding in front of a column, and the column a hunting party on elephants.

Third, and this is the one the book returns to most often: aristocrats are the enemy, everywhere, and the poor are the resource. The Tayichiud who put his family out to die were his own close kin, and the family that fed him in captivity had no kinship tie to him at all. He abolished inherited titles at his own installation and made all offices belong to the state. In the Muslim cities the Mongols killed the aristocrats first, in an age when everybody else was ransoming them. He promoted from the bottom. Khubilai abolished the examinations, promoted cooks and gatekeepers, and taught peasant children in winter in their own spoken language.

Nothing about that is sentimental. Killing the rich cut the head off the enemy's social system and produced officials who owed everything to the khan and had no local people to owe anything to. **The same move reads as cruelty in chapter five and as social reform in chapter eight, and it is one move.**

Fourth, a habit of mind more than a policy: they carried things rather than making them. They founded no religion, wrote few books, grew no new crop, and their own craftsmen could not weave, cast, throw a pot or bake bread. The only structures he built were bridges. Chinese gunpowder plus Muslim flamethrowers plus European bell-casting became the cannon. Persian doctors went to China and Chinese doctors went to Persia. The Arab and Indian arithmetic came into China because the censuses had outgrown the abacus. Printing spread because a Mongol alphabet reuses a few letters where a Chinese press needs thousands.

The chapters give the reason plainly and it is not a virtue. **Having no system of their own to impose, they were free to take anybody's and bolt them together**, and their astronomy never had to agree with anyone's scripture. Rome put its own city down in every province. These people put nothing down.

Fifth, information is a weapon they use better than anybody and cannot use on themselves. Orders were composed in rhyme so illiterate officers could carry them exactly, and the laws were set to music so every man knew them. Terror was spread by the pens of scribes rather than the acts of warriors, and he simply let the worst stories about him circulate uncorrected. Jamuka frightened the Naiman with Mongols who had chisels for noses and bodies of copper. Persian chronicles recorded 1,747,000 dead at Nishapur, a number that would need every Mongol to kill a hundred people.

Then the same machinery ran backwards on them and nobody could stop it. Timur borrowed the name and his atrocities were assigned to a man dead a century and a half. Voltaire needed a stand-in for the French king. Blumenbach needed a name for a race. **The reputation was built by other people's pens from the beginning, which is exactly the arrangement he chose**, and the eight centuries afterwards are that choice collecting interest.

Sixth, the empire is held together by property rather than by loyalty, and everybody in it knows this. *Khubi*, the share, starts as the orphan's and the widow's right to a measure of the loot. It becomes Hulegu ruling Persia while owning twenty-five thousand households of silk workers in China. Cousins at open war went on shipping each other goods, because refusing a man his share meant losing your own. It is the most durable structure in the book and it fails in one stroke: the plague stopped the yield everywhere at once, and there was nothing underneath.

## Which dimensions the book never reached

**Nothing here on what a person is made of inwardly, and nothing on what happens after death beyond where the soul lives.** The report has plenty on the soul's address — the banner, the smell, the forehead — and almost nothing on its fate. Death rites are all about handling the body: carried home in leather bags on camels, buried secretly with animals driven over the grave, no tomb and no tombstone. Nobody in eleven chapters explains what the dead person is now doing.

**No account of childhood or education among the Mongols themselves.** Boys learn hunting, trading, herding and fighting as one seamless thing from the time they can ride, and that is the whole of it. When universal schooling appears it is Khubilai's, for Chinese peasants, and it is described as a policy rather than as a view of what a child is.

**Almost nothing on illness, medicine or the body until the plague.** Doctors are traded as assets in the share system, and the medical crossing of the empire is told from the outside — which technique moved and which did not. What a Mongol thought a disease was is not in the range read.

## Where two chapters pull against each other

**Ch. 5 and ch. 8 give two answers about killing.** In the Muslim cities the policy is to kill the soldiers and the aristocrats and to let the terror travel by letter, and the book insists this was not accompanied by torture or mutilation — the deviation from the standard practice of the age. In Khubilai's China execution is rare enough to be counted year by year, torture needs evidence first, and public killing is never allowed to become entertainment. The same people, sixty years apart. The chapters do not reconcile this and neither does this report.

**Ch. 3 and ch. 6 disagree about what a fixed place costs.** He built no cities and no walls and kept the centre of power moving, and the book names that as a primary cause of Mongol success. Ogodei decided a kingdom conquered on horseback could not be ruled on horseback and built Karakorum — which then had to be fed from elsewhere, which is exactly the lever Khubilai used to starve it out from under his brother. Karakorum lasted three decades and the Mongols themselves pulled it apart.

**Ch. 7 and ch. 10 give the religious settlement two endings.** At Mongke's court the religions argue as equals with a panel of three judges and a rule against insulting each other, and finish the evening drinking together while Louis IX is burning Jewish books in France. A century later the Golden Horde is Muslim and allied with Egypt against its own cousins, the Ilkhanate is persecuting Buddhists and Jews, and the Yuan court has handed itself to the Tibetan lamas. **The one rule that made the empire portable was the first thing each branch gave away when it needed local legitimacy.**

## What the by-chapter reading recovered

The merged whole-book report had the soul-in-the-banner, the meritocracy, the trade network and the reputation swing. It could not have had these, because they each appear once:

- The Mongols composing military orders in rhyme, to fixed melodies, because the officers could not read (ch. 4).
- Peasants classified with the same vocabulary as cows and goats, and rounded up with the same precision, because in Jurched country there were people and no animals (ch. 4).
- Torture requiring substantial evidence before it could be applied, under the code of 1291 (ch. 8).
- The tattoo moved off the forehead onto the arm and the neck, and forbidden to spread to peoples who did not already do it (ch. 8).
- Pulse diagnosis crossing the empire and acupuncture failing, on the question of how much a doctor may touch a woman (ch. 9).
- Playing cards printed from the blocks cut for scripture, and outselling it (ch. 9).
- Fleas repelled by the smell of horses, which is why a nomad camp escaped a plague that took two-thirds of China (ch. 10).
- A herder's family asking for a stone to be cut in 2000, because the history had been illegal inside their own lifetimes (Epilogue).

## Evidence

Read from `RAW/books/Genghis Khan and the Making of the Modern World.md`, lines 112–2441, in eleven runs. The per-chapter footnotes and line ranges live in the three parts; this file cites none of its own, and every claim in it is traceable to a run.

**The book's own position, in one line.** This is a rehabilitation, written against eight centuries of the opposite, and it says so. The strongest check on it is internal: the boulevards built nine horsemen wide against an uprising, the ethnic quotas designed so officials could not trust their colleagues, and Fatima sewn shut. All three are in the book, and all three describe something the argument does not need.

**Bounded absence.** The dimension gaps named above are gaps in lines 112–2441, not claims about the book as a whole or about Mongol belief in general.
